docs.title: Deploy a project with your CLI or CI pipeline
When you need it
docs.text:
This project is a standard Databricks Bundle. Deploy it with your own CLI profile or existing CI/CD service account. No GitHub workflow or company adapter is required or generated. Authentication stays in the CLI/CI environment; do not put tokens or passwords in these files.

This page covers project deployment, identities, access, compute and retry settings. Use endpoint setup to expose a registered model, and project upgrades to migrate an existing generated layout.

flowchart LR
    A["deployment/targets.yml and variables.yml"] --> B["bundle validate --strict -t test"]
    B --> C["bundle deploy -t test"]
    C --> D["Jobs: train, score, monitoring"]
    D --> E["bundle run train"]
    E --> F["Score and monitoring runs"]

Deploy only creates or updates job definitions and uploads files. Running a job is a separate step.

docs.title: Files and environments
docs.text:
databricks.yml includes deployment/variables.yml, deployment/targets.yml and the job files under resources/. Optional feature/online selections add separate jobs to the three standard jobs. Keep the train, score and monitoring job keys: changing them can recreate deployed jobs and lose their history.

Target Intended use Output/model names Workspace files test, syst, prod Shared deployment, usually through existing CI/CD Shared names Team-managed project directory test_development, syst_development, prod_development Optional personal work in the selected environment _<env>_dev_<user-id> suffix Personal directory per environment

There is no separate dev target. With personal targets enabled, test_development is the only default. Otherwise no target is default: select test, syst or prod explicitly with -t. Shared targets use production mode, including test: the name test describes the environment, not a personal development deployment. Different targets may use one workspace with different catalogs/schemas, or different workspaces. Configure distinct shared destinations when environments use the same workspace. The template does not create catalogs, schemas, users or service principals.

The personal_development_targets answer controls whether the three additional personal targets are generated. Detailed setup asks it; quick setup and an answer file without it keep false. Read the generated deployment/README.md for the project's selected value. Personal targets do not receive shared service-principal identities or shared job ACL overrides. Their resolved suffix uses the workspace user ID, not just an email prefix, so two users named alice cannot share output/model names accidentally. Use each developer's own profile; one shared service account represents one identity, not several developers.

Personal job names are dev_<user>_train, dev_<user>_score and dev_<user>_monitoring, without a project or environment label. Shared test/syst/prod jobs keep <project>_train, <project>_score and <project>_monitoring, without a user prefix. Environment-specific roots and output suffixes keep targets distinct when users choose to share one workspace.

Personal names isolate deployments; they do not replace Unity Catalog grants. Reading production inputs still requires permission. Personal model/output schemas must also allow that developer's writes. If the company disallows writes in production schemas, set the environment's development output and metadata schema variables to approved sandbox schemas while retaining the source schema. Do not give personal accounts production model ownership to make a trial work.

docs.title: Deployment identity and run identity
docs.text:
The credentials executing bundle deploy are the deployment identity. Job run_as controls execution. The deployment_identity answer selects the shared job behavior. Detailed setup asks it; quick setup keeps deployer.

Choice Shared train/score/monitoring configuration deployer Emit no run_as override; preserve standard job ownership or externally managed identity shared_service_principal All three jobs use shared_service_principal separate_service_principals Train uses train_service_principal; score and monitoring use score_service_principal

Monitoring reuses the scoring identity in separate mode. Arrange its monitoring source reads and evidence-store writes explicitly; this does not require model ownership. There is no additional monitoring principal to configure.

The optional online_feature_lookup_setup, online_publication and daily_rollout jobs get no run_as override in any mode. They run as the deploying identity, even with shared_service_principal. Add a job-level run_as under the target in targets.yml if they must run as a service principal.

For explicit service principals, configure application IDs, not account display names. A deployment service account may also be the shared run identity. Separate deployment and execution accounts are supported, not required. Override the identity variables under the corresponding target when each environment has its own accounts. The deployer needs permission to use the selected run identity. deployer is an omission of configuration, not a command to change an existing job's owner or reset an existing run identity. Inspect existing jobs on migration.

For a user-based shared installation, edit that target's job-level run_as to user_name instead of service_principal_name; do not specify both keys. Personal targets already use their normal deployment identity without inheriting shared overrides. Keep identities at job scope so later unrelated resource types do not inherit execution settings they cannot support.

docs.title: Job access
docs.text:
Every target grants CAN_MANAGE to the deploying identity and to ${var.pipeline_owner}. Entries here apply to every job in that target, including optional feature and online jobs. Shared test, syst and prod targets also grant CAN_VIEW to a workspace group when detailed setup was given one. Personal targets have their own list, with the two managers only:

permissions:
  - level: CAN_MANAGE
    user_name: ${workspace.current_user.userName}
  - level: CAN_MANAGE
    user_name: ${var.pipeline_owner}
  - level: CAN_VIEW
    group_name: "YOUR_ENVIRONMENT_VIEWERS"

pipeline_owner is a variable in deployment/variables.yml. Its default is the setup answer, or the deploying user when the answer was blank; listing the same user twice is accepted. CI/CD can set it per deployment with --var pipeline_owner=<email> or BUNDLE_VAR_pipeline_owner. Change a view group by editing group_name in deployment/targets.yml; remove the entry to grant none. When CI deploys as a service principal, current_user.userName is its application ID: change that entry's user_name key to service_principal_name.

Use the optional per-job lists below when the jobs need different access. Avoid duplicating the same principal at target and job scope.

manage_job_permissions controls the explicit shared job ACL resources for train, score and monitoring. Detailed setup asks it; quick setup keeps false. When false, a new project omits explicit shared job ACL resources so your existing deployment/platform setup can manage them. Changing an existing deployment from managed to external ACLs requires an intentional state/permission handoff: removing a previously managed permissions resource can reset existing nonadmin access. Review the deployment plan before changing this choice. When true, configure the train_permissions, score_permissions and monitoring_permissions lists in variables.yml or per-target variable overrides. The default lists are empty; they do not create operator access.

For example, a train ACL can contain:

train_permissions:
  type: complex
  default:
    - group_name: YOUR_JOB_MANAGERS
      level: CAN_MANAGE
    - group_name: YOUR_LIFECYCLE_OPERATORS
      level: CAN_MANAGE_RUN
    - group_name: YOUR_JOB_VIEWERS
      level: CAN_VIEW

Use existing groups. Keep broad management privileges limited to trusted job/code maintainers. CAN_MANAGE_RUN applies to the whole train job, including its supported train/approve/reject/rollback parameters; it is not an approve-only role. Job access does not grant data or model access to the caller.

Job-to-job calls run under the caller's execution identity. Arrange CAN_MANAGE_RUN on each called job where the workflow requires it, through the corresponding permissions list or existing external governance:

Calling Run as identity Called job / ACL list When required Train Score / score_permissions Automatic score handoff Score, or another authorized producer Monitoring / monitoring_permissions Submitting independent monitoring requests Monitoring (the score principal in separate mode) Train / train_permissions Opting into on_drift=retrain

Each child retains its configured run_as; invocation does not transfer the caller's data/model privileges. No cross-job grants are added automatically. Granting monitoring access to run train permits the whole train lifecycle, including approve/reject/rollback parameters. Keep on_drift=disabled unless that authority is acceptable; the setting alone is not a permission boundary. See Databricks job privileges.

docs.title: Data, model and experiment access
docs.text:
Configure Unity Catalog and workspace access with your existing governance process. The Bundle does not silently create UC objects, transfer ownership or grant privileges on existing resources.

Execution identity Required access to arrange Train/lifecycle Read training inputs; create/register model versions in the model schema; own the models whose aliases it changes; write the project's MLflow experiment Score Read scoring inputs; execute/read the pinned registered models and their artifacts; create/write prediction tables, generations and views in the designated output schema Monitoring Read configured source, prediction and label tables; read/write the central monitoring store and references; write monitoring reports to the configured experiment; use serverless compute All three Use the required catalogs/schemas and read deployed code/wheel assets; train/score also need their selected serverless compute or approved cluster policy

Grant experiment access explicitly through your workspace governance, or manage an experiment resource at exactly ${workspace.root_path}/experiment in a separate approved Bundle resource file. An experiment's workspace permissions and a UC model's privileges are different controls. Keep model/schema creation and grants optional and explicit; do not take over existing objects on deploy.

For enforced writer separation, the score/monitoring identity must not own the registered models or inherit model ownership through a group. Broader inherited permissions can defeat the intended separation even with different service principal IDs. A single account can run the project, but it cannot prove that scoring is forbidden from changing aliases. Keep the existing one-run train/score queues and ensure another job or operator is not independently writing the same aliases/output namespace.

docs.title: Runtime packaging
docs.text:
deployment/requirements.txt records the generated skyulf-core[mlflow] release pin (for example, ==0.9.3) from the package index. Change that one version to a published release to upgrade Core, then redeploy. Serverless environments and policy-cluster task libraries load the same shared requirements; monitoring and optional online jobs inherit the same Core pin. Ensure each job can reach the package index.

Use the Core release that matches the template you generated from. A project generated from an unreleased source checkout needs a Core build of that same checkout on every job and locally; a different published release can lack the APIs and YAML support that smoke, preview, training and scoring use. Package installation alone does not establish runtime compatibility. Install deployment/train-requirements.txt locally for smoke and preview tools. Saved models retain exact producer runtime checks and certified worker source snapshots; validate compatibility or retrain before upgrading production.

deployment/requirements.txt is shared by all jobs and includes exact project pins from src/features/requirements.txt. It also includes the packages of the models and ensembles selected at generation. Optuna and optuna-integration are pinned only when the optuna search strategy was chosen. Update those pins when changing model, ensemble or search declarations in config/training.yml. deployment/train-requirements.txt adds training-only report packages. These direct pins do not fully lock transitive dependencies.

Override job_tags through target variables. For train and score, configure serverless_environment_version and serverless_budget_policy_id, or policy-cluster spark_version, node_type_id, min_workers and max_workers.

Monitoring always uses an independent serverless environment, including when train/score use policy clusters. Configure monitoring_environment_version (default 4) and monitoring_budget_policy_id (default blank) separately. Train/score runtime and budget overrides do not affect monitoring. A blank budget policy uses workspace defaults. Set the monitor's approved policy even when the model jobs use a classic cluster policy. Validate runtime/package compatibility, serverless availability and policy access in the intended workspace before use; local Bundle validation only verifies the generated settings.

Training/scoring schedules and source-window rules are independent. See training source windows for snapshot selection, calendar windows, availability cutoffs and their relationship to CV/sampling. Shared scheduled targets can run after deployment; personal targets start paused. Test the target's identities and permissions before enabling schedules.

retraining_mode and scoring_mode are asked only in detailed setup. Quick setup keeps both manual, so the train and score jobs have no schedule.

Schedule Variables in deployment/variables.yml Training, when retraining_mode: scheduled was answered retraining_cron_expression, retraining_timezone_id, retraining_pause_status Scoring, when scoring_mode: scheduled was answered scoring_cron_expression, scoring_timezone_id, scoring_pause_status Monitoring monitoring_cron (UTC; default 0 0 * * * ?) and monitoring_pause_status (default PAUSED)

Training and scoring use Quartz cron expressions and IANA timezones. Their pause values are PAUSED or UNPAUSED; manual runs remain separate. Personal target overrides explicitly pause generated clocks. Set each target's values deliberately and redeploy when changing a schedule.

docs.title: Job resource files
docs.text: Training/lifecycle tasks live in resources/train.job.yml; batch scoring lives in resources/score.job.yml. The root databricks.yml includes them through resources/*.yml. Each job has its own schedule and compute settings. Training calls scoring through ${resources.jobs.score.id} when handoff is enabled. resources/monitoring.job.yml holds the monitoring job. Optional selections add online_feature_lookup_setup.job.yml, online_publication.job.yml and daily_rollout.job.yml; local tools can add features.job.yml and dashboard overlays.

docs.title: Inference runtime
docs.text:
Training uses the selected pandas or Polars engine and remains bounded by max_rows and max_input_mb in config/training.yml, including when scoring uses Spark; see local input limits. Monitoring uses its independent Spark/serverless path in every layout.

Generated choice Score execution Environment manager batch_compute: single_node Local pandas/Polars under row and byte bounds Project task environment batch_compute: spark, serverless mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf local, using the declared environment batch_compute: spark, policy cluster mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf virtualenv, installing the recorded wheel and pins

The Spark default prediction batch size is 10000. A manager failure stops scoring without silently changing managers. For certificates, admitted fitted recipes, model-set composition and result receipts, read distributed scoring and feature-table inference boundaries.

docs.title: Install locally and check the source
docs.text:
Run from the generated project root, before the validate/deploy commands below:

uv pip install -r deployment/train-requirements.txt

Source tables must already exist. Enable Delta Change Data Feed on the scoring source before new rows arrive; the default initial_scoring: full_snapshot processes existing rows. Choose from_now before the first score to establish a zero-row checkpoint; see scoring start. Record keys must be unique, nonnull STRING/BIGINT columns. See scoring for publication, receipts and recovery.

docs.title: Configure once, then validate
docs.text:
Setup does not ask for the model and data catalog/schema names. It generates editable bindings for test/syst/prod in variables.yml with REPLACE_* placeholders. The separate monitoring store catalog and schema are asked in both setup modes; see monitoring store setup. An initialization JSON file may still provide catalog and schema to prefill shared test values. These settings reference existing UC objects; they do not create them.

  1. Set the same workspace host in each shared/personal environment pair in targets.yml. Host is a literal because the CLI needs it before resolving Bundle variables for authentication.
  2. Set <env>_catalog, <env>_input_schema, <env>_output_schema and <env>_metadata_schema in variables.yml, or supply these scalar variables with BUNDLE_VAR_<name> / --var in your existing pipeline. Personal targets share the environment catalog, but have separate <env>_development_input_schema, <env>_development_output_schema and <env>_development_metadata_schema values. Point these at approved development schemas, or reuse the shared input schema if that matches your access policy.
  3. Set <env>_root_path to a directory managed by your team. The proposed /Workspace/Projects/<project>/<env> path must have suitable access controls; its name does not create an ACL. Avoid a personal deployer's home and folders writable by unrelated users for a shared production deployment.
  4. Configure the chosen identities and access described above. Review the published Core pin and optional dependencies in requirements.txt and train-requirements.txt. This generated project does not require a project wheel or a dist/ build.

The shared test example is below. If personal targets were generated, choose test_development for your personal namespace instead.

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_TEST_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_TEST_PROFILE

With personal targets enabled, a user already authorized for the production workspace can deploy a personal trial there:

databricks bundle validate --strict -t prod_development --profile YOUR_PROD_DEV_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t prod_development --profile YOUR_PROD_DEV_PROFILE
databricks bundle run -t prod_development --profile YOUR_PROD_DEV_PROFILE train

Scheduled train and score triggers, when enabled, and the monitoring trigger start PAUSED for every personal target. Personal monitoring enrollment and automatic retraining are disabled. Manual train/score runs still work. The target explicitly overrides schedule variables, because a pause preset alone cannot override an explicit job schedule. Only enable a personal schedule intentionally in that target's variables. Shared targets retain the initializer's schedule choices.

An external pipeline uses the same project and standard commands after its own authentication step:

databricks bundle validate --strict -t prod
databricks bundle deploy -t prod

Deploy updates definitions; running any of the jobs is a separate pipeline decision. Bundle variables are deployment-time settings. Use job parameters for individual run inputs, not new deployment-variable values on a previously deployed job.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text: Deployment creates the train, score and monitoring jobs and uploads their code and configuration. Optional feature/online jobs are separate choices. Training and scoring clocks are independent; monitoring starts paused until its reference and store setup is verified. A deploy updates definitions; it does not run training or score automatically.

docs.title: Time limits, retries and notifications
docs.text:
Operational settings live in variables.yml; initialization asks no extra questions. Override them under a target's variables when environments differ.

Variable Default Meaning train_timeout_seconds, score_timeout_seconds 0 Whole-job limit; zero means unlimited train_task_timeout_seconds, score_task_timeout_seconds 0 Notebook-task limit; zero means unlimited score_max_retries 0 Optional finite score retries after failure score_min_retry_interval_millis 60000 Minimum interval between score attempts train_health_rules, score_health_rules [] Optional duration-warning rules train_email_notifications, score_email_notifications {} Optional event-to-email mappings train_webhook_notifications, score_webhook_notifications {} Optional event-to-notification-destination mappings monitoring_timeout_seconds 7200 Whole monitoring job limit; optional online and rollout jobs reuse it monitoring_task_timeout_seconds 3600 Monitoring task limit; optional online and rollout tasks reuse it monitoring_max_retries 1 Retries for each monitoring task, 60 seconds apart

Choose limits from measured project runs. A duration warning does not stop the job; a timeout does. The task limit also applies to generated model/SHAP tasks after refresh_training_graph.py. The train job includes its automatic score handoff, so leave time for that child run when configuring its whole-job limit.

For example, add these values under targets.test.variables in targets.yml:

train_timeout_seconds: 14400
train_task_timeout_seconds: 7200
score_timeout_seconds: 3600
score_task_timeout_seconds: 3000
score_max_retries: 2
score_min_retry_interval_millis: 60000
train_health_rules:
  - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
    op: GREATER_THAN
    value: 10800
train_email_notifications:
  on_failure: ["YOUR_ONCALL_EMAIL"]
  on_duration_warning_threshold_exceeded: ["YOUR_ONCALL_EMAIL"]
score_email_notifications:
  on_failure: ["YOUR_ONCALL_EMAIL"]
score_webhook_notifications:
  on_failure:
    - id: "YOUR_EXISTING_NOTIFICATION_DESTINATION_ID"

Webhook values are existing workspace destination IDs, not URLs or secrets. No destination is created and no recipient is added by default. Configure duration events alongside a health rule. Job-level failure notifications report the final failed job, rather than every failed retry attempt. See the official notification settings. Global defaults apply to personal targets too; use target overrides to keep personal trials separate from shared on-call recipients.

Lifecycle tasks and the automatic handoff always have zero retries. Existing runtime guards also reject lifecycle repair/retry before mutations. Scoring retries are opt-in, finite (never -1), and do not retry timeouts. Serverless automatic optimization remains disabled so it cannot add hidden attempts. See Databricks task retry settings.

Train and score notebook tasks default to max_retries: 0; their serverless tasks also set disable_auto_optimization: true. The optional online_feature_lookup_setup, online_publication and daily_rollout tasks always use max_retries: 0 with automatic optimization disabled. Monitoring tasks are the exception: they retry once by default through monitoring_max_retries. A retried monitoring attempt does not duplicate saved observations, because exact retries deduplicate. A new training run can register another candidate version. Inspect run evidence and registry state before rerunning; these guards do not promise exactly-once training. See Databricks serverless retry behavior.

When rescore_when_history_expires: true was selected during initialization, the same notebook timeout and retry settings also apply to recover_predictions and scoring_report. These tasks use the existing score job's identity, single-run queue, compute and notifications. The recovery_needed condition does not run a notebook or retry scoring. Recovery consumes the score task's pinned request; an exact already committed recovery is a no-op. The final report joins the ordinary and recovery branches with NONE_FAILED, so failed recovery does not publish a success report.

Enable score retries only while the job remains the sole output writer and the configured model/source policies suit another attempt. An attempt re-evaluates the configured model selector and current source watermark; it is not an exact replay of the failed snapshot. Use a concrete score_model_version when recovery must keep the same model. An uncertain write, foreign commit, source replacement or incompatible schema requires inspecting the receipt/history and fixing the cause; retries do not bypass those guards. Expired CDF also requires operator action unless optional CDF recovery is enabled and the expiry is recognized. A timeout cannot undo an already committed write or alias change.

If training/promotion succeeded and only scoring failed, inspect the child run and run only the score job after fixing the error. Use Run with different settings on score to enter the concrete version recorded by the failed attempt, or leave it blank to deliberately use the configured selector. Do not rerun train or approve just to recover predictions. Single/competition versions identify the selected model; multi-target versions identify the complete model set. An unchanged successful replay produces no new prediction writes.

The score output shows the source table and end version, output table, selected model/version, row counts, commit version and no-op status. Previous-write provenance stays labeled separately on a no-op. Raw JSON remains available for automation. These settings and summaries are covered locally; actual timeout, retry scheduling and notification delivery require workspace verification.

docs.title: Existing deployments and verification limits
docs.text:
Moving a deployment root points the CLI at new Bundle state; do not deploy a second writer by accident. To change roots or targets of a deployed project, follow project upgrades. To remove a deployment, see teardown.

Local rendering and strict resolution tests verify configuration, distinct user namespaces, paused personal schedules and identity/ACL wiring. They do not prove real workspace grants, source access, job ownership, model alias denial or queue behavior. Verify those with the intended accounts before treating writer separation as enforced in production.

Symptom Fix Unresolved REPLACE_* values or authentication failure Set literal target hosts and environment catalog/schema variables; select the intended CLI profile Missing input/output privileges Test the actual run_as identity and UC grants, not only the deployer's access A personal run writes to shared output Inspect the resolved target and user-ID suffix; use an approved development schema A deployment appears to create duplicate jobs Preserve resource keys, bundle identity and workspace root; review the migration before deploying Model/runtime admission or worker startup fails Use the template's matching release and verify exact producer/worker compatibility Training succeeded but score failed Inspect the child run and rerun score only with the intended concrete model version

For policy-cluster train/score, review the approved cluster policy, runtime, node type and cost tag. The checkout's skyulf-core/templates/databricks/examples/policy-init.example.json is a starting point. Serverless train/score defaults to Python environment 4; check pinned dependency support in the actual workspace. Monitoring has its own environment and budget-policy settings regardless of that choice.

docs.title: Measure drift and feature data quality
When you need it
docs.text: Use drift to compare production inputs with the verified population used to train a concrete model version. It detects changed distributions, missing declared features and incompatible types without requiring outcome labels. Performance loss instead compares labeled prediction quality with a baseline. Both can independently qualify for guarded retraining.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
Set monitoring_drift_thresholds under the producer target's variables in deployment/targets.yml. These are the current defaults:

monitoring_drift_thresholds: '{"psi": 0.2, "ks_statistic": 0.1, "wasserstein": 0.1, "kl_divergence": 0.1}'

monitoring_drift_thresholds is authoritative for this project's enrollment; {} uses Core defaults and partial objects override named metrics. Defaults are PSI 0.2, KS statistic 0.1, normalized Wasserstein 0.1 and KL divergence 0.1. A value must strictly exceed its own threshold. The displayed KS p-value is diagnostic relative to these effect limits; statistical support is checked separately.

Check Comparison and limit Numeric PSI Compare distributions using reference-derived bins; use psi (0.2). Low-cardinality numeric references use midpoint bins; otherwise reference percentiles supply the bins. Categorical PSI Compare category frequencies; use the same psi limit. KS Maximum empirical cumulative-distribution gap; compare KS statistic with ks_statistic (0.1). The diagnostic KS p-value is never compared with this effect-size limit. Wasserstein Empirical transport distance divided by the reference population standard deviation; with zero standard deviation use the unnormalized distance. Compare with wasserstein (0.1). KL divergence Compare current and reference numeric-bin probabilities with kl_divergence (0.1). Missing schema A declared feature absent from either input records schema_missing; unrelated extra columns are not new declared features. Type drift Incompatible feature types record type_drift. Supported numeric/string and boolean representations are normalized where valid; this is not a blanket raw-dtype inequality check. Missing fraction Nulls and numeric NaNs are missing. Compare with the reference rate, using the quality rule below. Nonfinite fraction Numeric NaN and infinity contribute to the fraction; infinity is a quality issue.

Distribution drift requires both an effect above its own limit and supported sample-aware statistical evidence. Evidence uses Bonferroni correction across feature tests in one report at significance 0.05; repeated windows are not covered by that correction. not_detected is not proof of equal distributions or adequate test power. Schema/type violations are recorded independently.

The missing-rate reference value is not a configurable alert threshold. An increase from a zero reference rate is an issue; otherwise an increased rate uses a one-sided Fisher test at 0.01. Missing input rows without usable saved predictions can also be quality issues. Do not interpret a displayed reference missing percentage as an allowed limit.

docs.title: Choose the reference population
docs.text: The monitor replays original training membership from saved source and split evidence, prepares immutable Spark reference tables, and compares current features from the source snapshots recorded with saved predictions. It does not pick an arbitrary latest table or retrain during measurement. See reference preparation and store reference tables.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
After changing thresholds, validate and deploy the producer, then run activation/scoring registration to update its enrollment. Run a fresh observation from the generated project root:

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

Open monitoring_report in the run for the saved feature metrics and notes, then Drift and data quality in the shared dashboard. Dashboard refresh alone does not calculate a new drift report.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Status Meaning healthy Measured drift/quality checks passed; model accuracy is not an acceptance gate. drift Distribution or declared feature-schema checks detected drift. stale The latest scoring commit (batch) or captured request (online) is older than expected_interval_hours, regardless of the last monitoring run. never_observed No observation exists for the current enrollment configuration. degraded Quality/measurement issues, no usable predicted outputs, or a nonfinite calculated metric. failed Monitoring raised a saved error. no_data The selected reference or current population is empty. disabled Enrollment explicitly paused. unavailable A result exists but the scoring or captured-request time is unavailable.

Counts represent enrollments, not prediction rows. measurement_status retains the underlying measured verdict when freshness changes. No retraining, performance acceptance thresholds or notifications are enabled by the dashboard.

Measured status precedence is no_data for an empty reference/current population, then drift for a detected feature change, then degraded for incomplete checks, quality problems or invalid measured metrics, otherwise healthy. A quality issue does not erase measured drift. Health freshness is based on scoring commit or captured request time, not the time monitoring reran.

docs.title: Read the drift charts
docs.text:
The drift/quality page keeps two history tables and separates charts by model/version/context. Each identity shows its latest observation's top ten feature PSI values beside their own limits, plus feature counts with drift or unavailable checks over time. Each feature is counted once within its observation even if multiple checks flag it. The count axis uses whole numbers; compact UTC date/time labels keep the chart readable. Hover to see the full window and calculation timestamp. For example, data from 09:00 to 10:00 appears at 10:00 even if the checks ran at 11:30. Drift and Performance date filters use the same window end as their time charts. Calculation time remains available separately in the details. The matching-identity table shows which contexts the shared filters include. The full model/table inventory remains on Overview.

KS p-value is not an effect-size threshold. Unavailable checks are shown separately, and missing values never become zero. PSI is only one drift check; the counts and table include other distribution and schema checks too.

Drift columns show each metric's value / its own limit. KS p-value is diagnostic only; it is never divided by the KS statistic's threshold. Missing features and changed types stay visible. Quality rows identify model version, scoring time and feature, with separate missing/nonfinite percentages. Both tables retain observation history.

Filters never select an older report; see latest observations and page filters. The PSI bars retain at most ten features per identity before feature filtering; use the history tables for the rest.

The PSI matrix includes numeric and categorical features. Each cell divides a recorded PSI by its own recorded limit; values above 1 receive a fixed highlight. An absent or nonpositive limit leaves the cell blank. Each identity retains its latest 12 full observations and the 10 features with the largest ratios within that history. Feature and date filters narrow this retained set; they do not retrieve older observations. Observation labels include the year and a sequence number, so separate reports for the same window remain separate cells.

The missing-value matrix uses the same observation and feature bounds, ranking features by their largest missing fraction. Its reference rate is the reference dataset's missing fraction, not an alert limit. A recorded quality issue can depend on a statistical test or unscored inputs. The tooltip identifies that saved decision. Nonfinite fractions remain available in the quality table.

Latest PSI bars use the newest saved report for each context, as described in latest observations. The drift context summary exposes the newest report status even when charts are empty. Mature performance-window-only reports stay in policy history; they do not replace the full feature observation, current model health or confusion matrix.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: What you see What to check no_data Confirm the pinned reference and selected current window contain rows. Empty data is not proof of no drift. degraded or unavailable checks Read the per-feature evidence and quality notes. Unsupported types, too little statistical evidence, unscored inputs and invalid values must be resolved before treating the population as measured. Large PSI but no supported drift Inspect effect and statistical evidence separately; meeting one gate does not establish the other. Drift but no training request Opt into on_drift: retrain only after reviewing the shared request guards. Quality/schema problems, incomplete checks or stale/freshness guards can block a request.

docs.title: Spark measurement limits
docs.text:
Spark computes regression and confusion-matrix metrics from full-population aggregates, and probability AUC/AP from exact tied-score counts. Numeric drift uses exact empirical-CDF KS/Wasserstein effects and reference percentile bins; rows are not sampled. Ordered CDF and probability curves use an ordered Spark window over distinct values, which can concentrate work on one executor for high-cardinality features. Removing the local row cap does not remove compute, shuffle or executor-memory requirements.

Statistical evidence is bounded separately: KS uses the exact lattice calculation when the two population sizes multiply to at most 1,000,000, the Core asymptotic method when either size exceeds 10,000, and explicitly named ks_dkw_union_bound evidence in the remaining range. An inconclusive bound is unavailable rather than evidence of no drift. Small categorical domains (at most 50 distinct non-null reference values) keep their exact-category comparison; Spark accepts at most 1,024 current categories on that path. Larger domains use the grouped comparison below. Classification allows at most 256 saved classes. Temporal/nested feature drift and unsupported cardinalities are explicit failures or unavailable checks. These limits bound summaries and supported algorithms, not observation rows.

Temporal or nested feature checks and unsupported cardinalities stay explicit; missing values never become a zero drift score. Numeric infinities or invalid numeric conversions can make the distribution comparison unavailable while quality evidence remains visible.

docs.title: Categorical features with many values
docs.text:
ZIP codes, cities and product categories can have more than 50 values without being identifiers. With default settings, pandas/Polars and Spark use the same rules:

  1. Count distinct observed non-null reference values. More than 10,000 categories on either side makes the comparison unavailable. The reference must also have at least two non-null observations per distinct value on average: distinct_count / non_null_count <= 0.5. This heuristic excludes mostly unique identifiers; it does not prove that a column is an identifier.
  2. Keep the 50 most frequent reference categories, breaking equal counts by ascending label. Pool all remaining reference and current values into one additional bucket. Current frequencies never select the retained categories. Spark collects bounded category counts, not raw observations.
  3. Calculate psi_categorical and statistical evidence from the 51 buckets. Existing PSI limits, sparse-count tests and feature-family Bonferroni correction still apply. Evidence test names end in _top50_other to expose the grouping. A drift decision still needs both effect and statistical support.

The additional new_category_rate is the fraction of non-null current rows whose label never appeared anywhere in the reference, including its pooled tail. For example, 25 rows with unseen ZIP codes among 100 non-null current rows give 0.25, even if another 100 current rows are null. It is diagnostic: monitoring records threshold: null and has_issue: false. It does not independently trigger retraining. The direct Core DriftMetric retains its numeric threshold field with the harmless upper bound 1.0; has_drift is always false for this metric.

from skyulf.profiling.drift import DriftCalculator
import polars as pl

reference = pl.DataFrame({"zip": [f"zip{i:03}" for i in range(90)] * 20})
current = pl.DataFrame({"zip": ["zip089"] * 75 + ["new_zip"] * 25})
report = DriftCalculator(reference, current).calculate_drift()
column = report.column_drifts["zip"]
print({metric.metric: metric.value for metric in column.metrics})
# Includes new_category_rate: 0.25 and the measured psi_categorical value.
print(column.evidence.model_dump())

Pooling can conceal redistribution within the tail, even when all tail labels change. Inspect novelty alongside PSI; a small PSI does not establish stable rare-category frequencies. Missingness is measured separately by the monitoring quality checks. Columns with 50 or fewer reference categories retain their existing metrics and evidence; they do not gain new_category_rate.

docs.title: Configure thresholds and measurement limits
docs.text:
Use the existing monitoring_drift_thresholds JSON variable in your producer's deployment/variables.yml or target overrides. Register the changed enrollment through normal activation or scoring before the next monitoring job. These are per-monitor settings; changing the dashboard does not change a measurement.

Key Default when absent Meaning and valid range psi 0.2 PSI effect threshold; finite and positive. ks_statistic 0.1 Maximum-CDF-distance effect threshold; finite and positive. wasserstein 0.1 Distance normalized by reference standard deviation; finite and positive. kl_divergence 0.1 KL effect threshold; finite and positive. categorical_top_k 50 Retained reference levels before pooling; integer 1–1,000,000, no larger than max_category_summaries. id_like_uniqueness 0.5 Maximum distinct/non-null reference ratio for the grouped path; (0, 1]. Increase only for known categorical domains. max_category_summaries 10000 Maximum distinct categories per population on the grouped path; integer 1–1,000,000. An explicit override also caps exact-category comparisons. psi_moderate 0.1 Moderate severity wording, separate from the PSI alarm threshold. Positive and below psi_critical. psi_critical 0.25 Critical severity wording. Positive and above psi_moderate. monitor_max_rows Existing observation budget, capped at 1,000,000 Explicit non-Spark observation row budget; integer 1–1,000,000. monitor_max_bytes Existing observation budget, capped at 1 GiB Explicit non-Spark observation byte budget; integer 1–1 GiB. missing_markers None Object mapping monitored integer or floating-point feature columns to 1–100 marker values, for example {"co_gt": [-200]}. Matching values count as missing in both the reference and the current population. See missing-value markers. Monitoring only.

monitor_max_rows and monitor_max_bytes override driver materialization budgets, not feature thresholds. Without them, the producer's budgets remain in effect; direct MonitorConfig defaults remain 10,000 rows and 64 MiB. Overrides stay within the existing 1,000,000-row / 1 GiB safety ceilings. For larger observations use Spark monitoring. Spark validates these keys but does not impose local row/byte budgets on distributed observations. It still bounds category summaries. Very large category limits increase driver memory for count summaries; a large top K also enlarges the statistical test's contingency table and its diagnostic details. Increase them only as needed.

# Target variable override; JSON numbers must be numbers, not quoted strings.
variables:
  monitoring_drift_thresholds: >-
    {"psi": 0.2, "categorical_top_k": 30,
     "id_like_uniqueness": 0.75, "max_category_summaries": 20000,
     "psi_moderate": 0.15, "psi_critical": 0.3,
     "monitor_max_rows": 200000, "monitor_max_bytes": 268435456}

The same dictionary, without missing_markers, can be passed to DriftCalculator(...).calculate_drift(...), which rejects that key; row/byte keys are consumed by monitoring enrollment only. Category evidence names reflect the chosen K, for example chi_square_top30_other. Increasing K preserves more rare labels but increases summary work and can make sparse evidence harder to establish. Changing severity bands changes suggestions, not the independent effect/statistical gates. Omitted keys retain historical output and enrollment fields. With no categorical overrides, the small-domain Spark path retains its 1,024-current-category limit.

These settings do not expose preprocessing probe minimum/sample caps or float tolerances, the PowerTransformer 10% fit guard, SHAP's two-row minimum, Spark's maximum class count or its exact-KS cell limit. Those remain fixed contracts.

docs.title: Missing-value markers
docs.text:
Monitoring measures the raw scoring inputs, before the model's preprocessing. A source that writes a code such as -200 for "no reading" therefore looks like a real measurement: its missing fraction stays 0 and drift includes the code. List such codes per column to count them as missing instead:

variables:
  monitoring_drift_thresholds: '{"missing_markers": {"co_gt": [-200], "hour": [-1]}}'

For a sensor that writes -200 during outages:

Without markers With {"co_gt": [-200]} co_gt missing fraction 0, because -200 counts as a reading The share of rows without a reading co_gt drift Includes the -200 values, so more outages look like a shift in the readings Compares real readings only More outages than in training Not visible A quality issue when the increase is significant Model, predictions and training Unchanged Unchanged
  • Markers apply to the reference and the current population before quality and drift, in Spark and in-memory monitoring alike. Stored reference tables keep raw rows, so changing markers takes effect at the next observation.
  • A marker matches exactly in the column's own type. Integer columns need whole numbers within their range. Floating-point columns need a value that type holds exactly: a 32-bit float column accepts -200 or -999.5, but not 0.1. Decimal, text and other columns cannot carry markers.
  • A marker for a column that is not a monitored feature, or that has no exact value in the column's type, fails the observation instead of being skipped.
  • A marked value is then an ordinary missing value. Missingness above the training rate, and a missing value on a row without a saved prediction (an excluded row), are quality issues.
  • Without missing_markers, reports are unchanged.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
Job failures and measured drift are separate events. A successful monitoring run can report drift, missing evidence or performance loss. Configure native job notifications for failed runs and long durations in your target variables:

variables:
  monitoring_email_notifications:
    on_failure: [ml-operations@example.com]
    on_duration_warning_threshold_exceeded: [ml-operations@example.com]
  monitoring_health_rules:
    - metric: RUN_DURATION_SECONDS
      op: GREATER_THAN
      value: 1800
  monitoring_webhook_notifications:
    on_failure:
      - id: YOUR_EXISTING_NOTIFICATION_DESTINATION_ID

Replace the example email/destination before deploying. Webhooks use an existing workspace notification destination ID, not a URL. Empty defaults send nothing. To notify on monitoring findings, create a separate SQL alert over the shared store's existing monitoring_issues view. For example:

SELECT count(DISTINCT monitor_id) AS models_requiring_attention
FROM my_catalog.skyulf_monitoring.monitoring_issues
WHERE environment = 'prod';

Alert when models_requiring_attention > 0; choose an existing warehouse, notification destination and a schedule aligned with the monitoring job. This view includes drift, quality, policy loss and missing/stale evidence, with current enrollment and configuration filtering. Multiple feature issues for one monitor count once. Open the view or dashboard for the individual reasons. Narrow project or model_name to alert on a particular workload. The Bundle does not create this SQL alert or any recipient automatically.

docs.title: Voting and stacking ensembles
docs.text:
This page covers ensemble candidates in a generated Databricks Bundle's config/training.yml: the voting and stacking model.params fields, nested member search axes, worked voting, stacking and calibrated examples, and the setup questions and defaults for each slot. Read it when one model candidate should combine several learners. The worked examples append a models block to the common setup header in the tuning guide.

Back to Databricks Bundle tuning

An ensemble is one model candidate containing several learners. In contrast, competition evaluates separate candidates and selects one winner. Choose voting_regressor, voting_classifier, stacking_regressor or stacking_classifier; see their model cards for task-specific member menus and defaults.

model.params setting Type/default Effect base_estimators List of distinct member names; model-specific defaults Choose member keys such as ridge, lasso, random_forest, not automatically the top-level model IDs. Unknown, duplicate and empty selections fail. base_estimator_params Mapping, {} Fixed constructor overrides keyed by selected member name. Unknown members/parameters fail. weights Voting only; null means equal Ordered list with one finite nonnegative value per member, or a member-name mapping with omitted selected members defaulting to 1. At least one value must be positive. These weight model votes, not training rows. voting Classification voting only, soft soft averages probabilities; every member needs probability output. hard votes on class labels and has no ordinary predict_proba output. final_estimator Stacking only; ridge for regression, logistic_regression for classification A supported member key for the learner trained on base-model out-of-fold predictions. final_estimator_params Stacking only; mapping, {} Fixed final-learner constructor overrides. cv Stacking only; integer 5, 2..20 Internal out-of-fold predictions for the final learner. prefit is not admitted. passthrough Stacking only; boolean false Also give original input features to the final learner. calibrate_base_models Boolean, false Classification only: wrap each base classifier in probability calibration. calibration_method String, sigmoid sigmoid or isotonic; isotonic needs enough calibration data. calibration_cv Integer, 3; 2..20 Internal calibration folds, separate from shared search CV and stacking CV. tune_base_models Boolean; false without tuning, inserted true by a tuning wrapper if absent With automatic spaces, include selected members' search axes. Explicit true requires a tuning wrapper. A manually supplied space owns its own axes. n_jobs Integer, 1 for Bundle search Keep ensemble and member workers at one during search.

Voting rejects stacking-only fields; stacking rejects weights and voting. Classification calibration controls are different from the downstream decision_threshold policy. Row weight_column is a third, independent concept; all selected members and the final learner must meet the sample-weight contract.

For manual spaces, a member parameter is named <member>__<parameter>, and a stacking final-learner parameter is final_estimator__<parameter>. Calibrated members insert estimator__: for example logistic_regression__estimator__C. Fixed overrides remain fixed in automatic spaces, and conflicting manual axes fail. Do not search structural member lists, weights arrays, or estimator objects as scalar axes.

docs.title: Voting example
docs.text:
Append this alternative models block to the common regression header. It searches ridge while keeping lasso's alpha fixed. To fit the same ensemble once, delete the whole tuning mapping.

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: voting_regressor
      params:
        base_estimators: [ridge, lasso]
        base_estimator_params:
          lasso: {alpha: 0.01}
        weights: {ridge: 2, lasso: 1}
    tuning:
      strategy: grid
      metric: rmse
      max_candidates: 2
      search_space: {ridge__alpha: [0.1, 1.0]}

docs.title: Stacking example
docs.text:
This alternative searches both a member and the final estimator. Its internal cv: 2 happens inside each outer search fit, so it costs more than a single ridge grid even though there are only four candidate combinations.

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: stacking_regressor
      params:
        base_estimators: [ridge, lasso]
        base_estimator_params:
          lasso: {alpha: 0.01}
        final_estimator: ridge
        cv: 2
        passthrough: false
    tuning:
      strategy: grid
      metric: rmse
      max_candidates: 4
      search_space:
        ridge__alpha: [0.1, 1.0]
        final_estimator__alpha: [0.1, 1.0]

docs.title: Calibrated classification example
docs.text:
This block overrides the header's task/target/metric for a classification model. The table must have a binary churn label and enough examples per class for both search and calibration folds. Update the example model's quality threshold to your domain's accuracy gate before deployment.

models:
  churn:
    task: classification
    target_column: churn
    metric: heldout_accuracy
    quality_threshold: 0.7
    stratify: true
    model_name: "{catalog}.{metadata_schema}.churn_model{resource_suffix}"
    model:
      type: voting_classifier
      params:
        base_estimators: [logistic_regression, decision_tree]
        base_estimator_params:
          decision_tree: {max_depth: 2, random_state: 42}
        voting: soft
        calibrate_base_models: true
        calibration_method: sigmoid
        calibration_cv: 2
    tuning:
      strategy: grid
      metric: accuracy
      max_candidates: 2
      search_space:
        logistic_regression__estimator__C: [0.1, 1.0]

docs.title: Spark scoring and serving endpoints
docs.text:
Voting, stacking and calibrated ensembles can score on Spark workers (batch_compute: spark) and behind serving endpoints. Training first checks the fitted ensemble as one model: every member, every calibration estimator and the stacking final learner must be a supported built-in model, and the ensemble's own predictions must give the same results in batches of any size. Spark and online-feature projects run this check automatically; an endpoint-only project enables it with defaults.allow_tested_custom_steps: true. The check, its evidence and the full model list are described in Score on Spark workers.

A linear final learner such as the default logistic_regression can differ in the last floating-point digits between batch sizes. The check allows such rounding differences in probabilities but never a changed label. Voting, including soft voting, and stacking with a decision_tree final learner passed the same checks on real data.

docs.title: Setup questions and defaults for each slot
docs.text:
Detailed setup repeats the ensemble question group for the selected single model, each competition candidate, and each multi-target branch. It asks for the member count (default two), each distinct member and the stacking final estimator where applicable. Regression offers up to 14 member positions and classification up to 13; installed optional packages and weighted-mode eligibility still constrain the choices. Selecting two members exposes two member questions, rather than silently filling every available position.

The wizard does not ask for the settings below. Each slot writes their defaults into model.params in config/training.yml; edit them there, or set them in an answer file before generation:

Setting Answer-file suffix Default Voting weight of member K weight_K 1 Classification voting mode voting soft Stacking folds cv 3 (5 when omitted from hand-written YAML) Stacking passthrough passthrough false Calibrate classification members calibrate (YAML calibrate_base_models) false Calibration folds calibration_cv 3

Calibration method defaults to sigmoid; edit YAML to select isotonic.

The answer-file names follow these patterns, with N the candidate/branch number, task equal to regression or classification, and K the member position:

Scope Answer-file prefix Common suffixes Single model single_ensemble_<task>_ base_count, base_K, weight_K, final Competition slot competition_ensemble_N_<task>_ Same, isolated to that candidate. Multi-target branch branch_N_ensemble_<task>_ Same, isolated to that branch.

For the shared slot suffixes voting, cv, passthrough, calibrate and calibration_cv, omit the task portion of the prefix. Examples are single_ensemble_cv, competition_ensemble_2_calibrate and branch_1_ensemble_passthrough.

For example, competition_ensemble_2_regression_base_1: "ridge" selects the first member of candidate two; its weight_1 key applies only to voting. Setup writes these choices into that model's params; the editable YAML is the place for detailed member overrides, calibration and manual nested axes. Inspect the emitted entry because setup keeps these defaults without asking. Shared competition search settings and per-branch settings still obey the same accepted tuning fields and budgets in the tuning guide.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text:
Use SHAP to inspect which transformed features influenced a fitted model's output. It explains model behavior; it is not a quality gate or proof that a feature causes an outcome. Evaluation charts answer a different question: how well predictions match known outcomes.

Quick setup leaves SHAP off and does not ask the SHAP questions. If you cannot find a shap_* task, first check how the project was generated. Detailed setup asks shap_enabled, default false.

flowchart LR
    A["Enable explainability and dependencies"] --> B["Fit the model"]
    B --> C["Apply saved preprocessing with required history"]
    C --> D["Compute bounded SHAP values"]
    D --> E["MLflow: explanations.json and explanations.html"]
    E --> F["shap_model or shap_name: display saved report"]

shap_name stands for each concrete shap_<name> task of a competition or model set. The SHAP leaf displays an existing report. Computation happens during fit; opening the leaf does not retrain or explain new score requests.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text: For a new project, choose detailed setup, enable shap_enabled and set its three budgets. This adds the config, dependencies and matching report tasks. For an existing project, complete all three changes below.

docs.title: Enable computation and dependencies
docs.text:
Merge this fragment into config/training.yml:

defaults:
  explainability:
    method: shap
    max_samples: 100
    max_features: 30
    max_display_samples: 3

These settings apply to each single model, competition candidate or model-set branch. A named model's explainability mapping replaces the shared mapping; include every override you need. Omit the field or set it to null to disable computation. The example uses the generated defaults. The direct Core config defaults to 10 display samples, capped by max_samples, if that key is absent.

Keep these exact template dependencies in deployment/train-requirements.txt:

shap==0.49.1
matplotlib==3.10.0

The generated training environment installs that file on serverless and policy clusters. Scoring does not compute SHAP and does not need these packages for that purpose. A local installation alone does not update deployed job libraries.

docs.title: Add the report leaf if it was omitted
docs.text:
Projects generated with SHAP off omit src/jobs/shap_report.py and the SHAP tasks. Generate a separate project with the same layout and SHAP enabled, then review and copy the missing notebook, training requirements and relevant task fragment as described in project upgrades.

For a single-model project, the task fragment under the existing train job's tasks is:

- <<: *lifecycle_task
  task_key: shap_model
  depends_on:
    - task_key: train_and_tune
  notebook_task:
    notebook_path: ../src/jobs/shap_report.py
    base_parameters:
      <<: *lifecycle_parameters
      reference_json: '{{tasks.train_and_tune.values.reference_json}}'
      tracking_uri: '{{tasks.initialize_run.values.tracking_uri}}'

This is a fragment for a generated graph: its two YAML anchors already exist there. For competition/model-set branches, use shap_<name>, depend on train_<name> and reference that exact task's reference_json. Keep the SHAP task as an independent leaf with no outgoing dependencies. refresh_training_graph.py can replicate an existing SHAP leaf when branches change; it does not invent a leaf if the graph has none.

Budget Allowed value Effect max_samples 1–200; generated default 100 Maximum training rows used for SHAP computation. Larger values can be expensive, especially for generic explainers. max_features Positive integer; default 30; no fixed upper bound Guard on transformed input width. It does not select the top features or drop columns; exceeding your configured value produces unavailable. max_display_samples 0–50, no greater than max_samples; generated default 3 Number of saved sample waterfalls. Zero keeps global importance without sample waterfalls.

Budgets apply per fitted model: eight candidates can each compute an explanation. Samples are training inputs transformed with saved preprocessing; holdout labels, record keys and time/target metadata are not explanation features.

Set defaults.explainability.max_features in config/training.yml to cover the features produced by preprocessing. For example, four numeric inputs plus 111 one-hot columns produce 115 model features, so max_features: 115 admits that model. A value such as 200 leaves room for a wider fitted model. The setting controls the allowed width, not the number of features displayed in a chart. Higher values can increase SHAP computation time and memory use; use max_samples to choose how many training rows to explain.

Row-independent steps can preprocess only the sampled rows. Steps that need other rows, such as LagFeatures or RollingAggregate, first preprocess the complete training population supplied by the training job, then select the SHAP sample. For example, a sampled May record keeps April's lag even when April is not selected for explanation. An undeclared context also takes this conservative path. The job's training row/byte limits still bound that population; max_samples bounds SHAP computation, not context preprocessing. When more rows were preprocessed than the SHAP limit, preprocessing_rows records their count.

For models with fitted exclusion steps, such as IQR or PowerTransformer, SHAP uses only sampled rows accepted by those saved steps. The report records sampled_rows, explained_rows, excluded_rows and excluded_by_reason; sample_count is the accepted count. For example, 100 sampled rows with 11 IQR exclusions produce explanations for 89 rows and an outlier:<step> count of 11. The HTML shows these counts too. At least two rows must survive; otherwise the result is unavailable with reason too_few_rows_after_exclusions. The sample is not topped up. This describes the fitted preprocessing population, not custom scoring eligibility or business outputs. Models without exclusion steps retain their existing evidence fields.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
From the generated project root, after merging all required files:

uv pip install -r deployment/train-requirements.txt
python src/tools/smoke.py
python src/tools/preview.py --action train
databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run train -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

Use your target/profile. Smoke and preview check declarations, not SHAP computation. New settings affect a new fitting run; old runs are not backfilled.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Start with Workflows > Jobs > your train run > training_report > Output > Where to look for the saved per-model report links and statuses. For the full explanation, open:

Layout Notebook output MLflow artifacts Single model shap_model > Output Fitting run > Artifacts > explanations.json and explanations.html Competition Each shap_<name> > Output Each candidate's fitting run; the selected winner's report is also copied to the parent with its child-run provenance Model set Each shap_<name> > Output That branch's fitting run, not one explanation of the combined business output

The portable HTML contains embedded PNG images, run/model identity and a workspace-relative MLflow link. It needs no JavaScript or CDN; a downloaded copy's relative link needs the original workspace to navigate back to the run. It may contain transformed sample feature values, so use the experiment's existing access and retention controls.

Read mean absolute importance as average contribution magnitude on the sample: a taller bar means more influence, not a positive or negative effect. Read a waterfall from its base value through the feature contributions to the explained output. Red contributions increase it; blue contributions decrease it. The units belong to the explainer: a classifier can show raw scores/log-odds rather than probability percentage points. Do not compare unrelated models' bars without matching output units and sample populations.

Binary sample plots use class index 1. For multiclass explanations the helper uses the predicted class when available (otherwise class 0); global magnitude averages absolute contributions over classes. A sample number is a position in the report, not a business key. Correlated features and training-population choices affect attribution; SHAP is not causal evidence.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text:
Symptom or saved reason What it means and what to do No shap_* task Quick/default setup omitted it. Add config, pinned dependencies, notebook and task, then validate/deploy; the YAML flag alone cannot create a task. No explanation artifact Check whether explainability was off in the fitting run, or whether fit failed before saving it. Absence alone is not a successful explanation. feature_limit_exceeded Transformed width exceeds the guard. Inspect encoded/generated columns; raise the guard only within 100, or train a deliberately smaller feature set. empty_training_frame, missing_input_columns No usable training sample or missing saved input columns. Repair the source/split/feature contract before retraining. too_few_rows_after_exclusions Fewer than two sampled rows survived the fitted exclusion steps. Read the counts and reasons; check the data and fitted thresholds before changing the sample budget. inference_transform_unavailable, row_count_changed, feature_schema_mismatch Saved preprocessing cannot produce the expected row-preserving feature frame. Inspect the transform and context requirements. model_unavailable, shap_unavailable No usable estimator/explainer result. Check training logs, model compatibility and installed dependencies; a supported training model need not be supported by the selected SHAP explainer. shap_feature_schema_mismatch, invalid_shap_result Returned SHAP columns or finite JSON values do not match the saved contract. Keep the failure evidence and investigate the estimator/dependency combination. report_status: unavailable Numerical evidence may exist while rendering failed. Inspect report_reason, the JSON artifact and plotting dependencies. SHAP leaf fails after fitting The independent leaf can fail the overall job without undoing a model decision or retraining. Inspect saved artifacts before retrying; do not repair a lifecycle invocation merely to regenerate a chart.

status: completed means SHAP values were saved, not that the model is accurate or suitable for promotion. Unavailable explanations preserve their reason and do not replace the saved evaluation metrics or quality policy.

docs.title: Prepare feature tables for training and scoring
docs.text:
You can train and score directly from an existing Delta table. Feature tables and a merged table are optional. With the generated config/features.yml left as version: 1 and groups: {}, Skyulf creates no feature job and no merged table: training reads training_table, and scoring reads score_source_table.

Model count and feature-group count are independent: several models can share the same group outputs and merged observation table.

Use this guide when features come from separate sources or require upstream Spark calculations. The example builds company and activity features, joins them to observations, then shows how to select the result for a model. The YAML and generated graph can be checked locally; the SQL, Spark transforms and Delta results below are expected workspace behavior, not a claim that these example tables have been created in your workspace.

docs.title: Choose a data route
docs.text:
What you have or need Configure What it produces One Delta table with all model inputs training.yml and inference.yml; leave feature groups empty No additional feature table or merge. Separate sources to calculate and join features.yml plus src/features/groups/*.py One Delta output per group and one merged observation table. Existing UC feature tables to bind to a saved model training.yml → feature_lookup Native Feature Engineering lookup during training and batch scoring; no explicit merged table required. Endpoint requests carrying entity keys rather than all feature values feature_lookup, online_features, and serving.yml Native lookup from an explicitly provisioned/published online store before saved prediction.

These routes can compose. A group job can produce an offline feature table that another workflow registers or publishes. Producing an ordinary Delta table does not declare UC primary keys, provision an online store, publish it, or deploy an endpoint. See online features for that workflow.

Keep learned imputers, scalers, category statistics and selectors in preprocessing.yml, where fitting occurs inside the training partition/fold. Use upstream groups for fixed formulas, domain aggregations and time-correct source preparation.

docs.title: 1. Define observation identity and create the inputs
docs.text:
Run the following SQL on Databricks in a schema you own. Replace workspace.demo consistently with your catalog/schema. The example names must be unused: these CREATE TABLE statements intentionally do not replace existing tables. The job's Run-as identity needs access to the input tables and permission to create/write the three output tables in that schema.

There are two identities in this example:

  • (company_id, observed_at) is the feature join grain: one observation per company and date. Both keys must be nonmissing and the pair unique in the base and each produced group.
  • observation_id is a stable, unique, nonmissing prediction record key. It is BIGINT, kept outside model inputs. Do not use observed_at as a scoring record key: date/timestamp keys are not supported by the prediction publisher. A company can have many observations, so company_id alone is not the record key.
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS workspace.demo;

CREATE TABLE workspace.demo.company_observations (
  observation_id BIGINT,
  company_id BIGINT,
  observed_at DATE,
  churn BIGINT
) USING DELTA TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = 'true');

INSERT INTO workspace.demo.company_observations VALUES
  (101, 1, DATE '2026-01-31', 0),
  (102, 1, DATE '2026-02-28', 1),
  (103, 2, DATE '2026-01-31', 0),
  (104, 2, DATE '2026-02-28', 1);

CREATE TABLE workspace.demo.company_source (
  company_id BIGINT,
  observed_at DATE,
  employee_count BIGINT
) USING DELTA;

INSERT INTO workspace.demo.company_source VALUES
  (1, DATE '2026-01-31', 10),
  (1, DATE '2026-02-28', 12),
  (2, DATE '2026-01-31', 20),
  (2, DATE '2026-02-28', 21);

CREATE TABLE workspace.demo.activity_source (
  company_id BIGINT,
  observed_at DATE,
  amount DOUBLE
) USING DELTA;

INSERT INTO workspace.demo.activity_source VALUES
  (1, DATE '2026-01-25', 40.0),
  (1, DATE '2026-01-25', 60.0),
  (1, DATE '2026-02-25', 150.0),
  (2, DATE '2026-01-20', 20.0),
  (2, DATE '2026-02-20', 70.0);

The four base rows are enough to inspect joins; they are not a training-quality or split/CV example. Supply a larger representative labeled population before training. The activity dates here represent when the aggregate was available, not raw transaction times from which a monthly cutoff is inferred. Define windows, late-arrival handling and historical availability explicitly in real source preparation.

No implicit string parsing, timezone conversion or duplicate removal runs. Use date/timestamp columns with the same types across all participating tables.

All input tables must be Delta. The group sources need not already have CDF; the feature publisher requires/enables it on its outputs. The scoring source must have CDF before incremental scoring starts.

docs.title: 2. Configure two groups and the merge
docs.text:
Replace the entire contents of config/features.yml with this file. Do not append it to the disabled groups: {} mapping.

version: 1
base_table: workspace.demo.company_observations
output_table: workspace.demo.company_merged
keys: [company_id]
timestamp: observed_at
groups:
  company:
    source_table: workspace.demo.company_source
    output_table: workspace.demo.company_features
    transform: src/features/groups/company.py:compute_features
    columns: [employee_count]
    lookup: exact
    allow_missing: false
  activity:
    source_table: workspace.demo.activity_source
    output_table: workspace.demo.activity_features
    transform: src/features/groups/activity.py:compute_features
    columns: [monthly_amount, transaction_count]
    lookup: asof
    allow_missing: false

These table names are exact three-part names. Unlike training/inference table settings, this file does not expand {catalog} placeholders or add a deployment suffix. Choose separate names for each environment. Every output must differ from every input and other output, with one owning producer.

Field Type / default What you configure version Integer, required 1 Feature configuration format. groups Mapping, required; {} disables production Up to 20 groups. Disabled configuration contains only version and groups. base_table String, required when enabled Existing observations and labels; no transform is applied to the base. output_table String, required when enabled Destination for the merged base and features. keys Nonempty distinct string list Entity keys used by every group join. timestamp String, required when enabled A separate date/timestamp column, already typed consistently across inputs. groups.<name> Lowercase identifier, 1–50 characters Domain/task name; independent of the Python filename. source_table, output_table Required three-part table names Group input and persisted output. transform Required src/features/groups/module.py:function Contained Python module and callable. columns Required nonempty distinct string list Features only; exclude keys, timestamp and labels. lookup exact default, or asof Exact matches key and time; asof selects the latest feature time at or before the base time. allow_missing Boolean, default false Permit unmatched observations with null features, or fail the merge.

An asof match has no built-in maximum age in this group-merge implementation. Use explicit source rules when old feature values must expire. A matching row whose feature value is null still counts as a match; allow_missing controls missing records, not missing cells.

docs.title: 3. Keep the Spark transforms small and explicit
docs.text:
The generated project already contains these editable files. Confirm their columns match your configuration. Each function receives its pinned source Spark DataFrame and must return exactly the keys, timestamp and declared feature columns.

src/features/groups/company.py:

def compute_features(frame):
    """Select one company snapshot at each declared observation date."""
    return frame.select("company_id", "observed_at", "employee_count")

src/features/groups/activity.py:

from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def compute_features(frame):
    """Aggregate the supplied transactions at their declared availability grain."""
    return frame.groupBy("company_id", "observed_at").agg(
        F.sum("amount").alias("monthly_amount"),
        F.count(F.lit(1)).alias("transaction_count"),
    )

Group functions accept only frame; feature-group configuration has no params field. Keep fixed business constants in the module. The file path before : in transform is relative to the project root and the name after it is the callable. Do not call spark.table, toPandas, collect or a table writer inside the function: the job owns pinned reads, validation and publication. Source rows may repeat the key/time when aggregation combines them, but returned rows must be unique and contain no label columns. Activity sums all-null amounts as null; its transaction count still includes those rows. An asof match selects one latest available row, not the sum of all prior months, and it does not fill gaps with zero.

One file can produce several features. The group name does not have to match its filename. Do not return observation_id from these group functions: it belongs to the base observation, while the shared features use company/time.

The run pins input Delta versions and hashes the declared transform file. It does not freeze extra network calls, hidden table reads or undeclared helper files. Keep calculations based on the supplied frame. The root groups/ directory is excluded from the saved model's captured recipe package; keep model callbacks in preprocessing.py, pre_split.py or custom/, and do not import group functions from those modules. Keep Spark dependencies in deployment/requirements.txt. Groups need no __init__.py; smoke still checks their syntax. The transform entry point is one contained Python module, not a general dependency graph. Saved model versions retain their original snapshots.

docs.title: 4. Generate and run the feature job
docs.text:
From the generated project root:

python src/tools/refresh_feature_graph.py
python src/tools/smoke.py
databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run features -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

Replace YOUR_PROFILE with your configured profile. Refresh is local: it reads and validates config/features.yml, then creates resources/features.job.yml and its thin notebook. Smoke does not read config/features.yml; it checks the training configuration and the Python syntax of src/, including the group modules. Neither reads Delta data or executes Spark transformations. Refresh after changing feature configuration or inherited deployment controls, then redeploy. A stale graph/config digest fails before reading source records.

The graph should contain:

flowchart LR
    I[initialize_features] --> C[feature_company]
    I --> A[feature_activity]
    C --> M[merge_features]
    A --> M

Independent groups can run concurrently. The graph inherits training compute, Run-as/permissions, time limits and notification settings. It is a separate job; finishing it does not trigger training, scoring or promotion automatically.
