Branches must share one source version and keys, have distinct targets and models, and exclude sibling targets from features. The coordinator does not move aliases. The YAML fields above are not SDK keyword arguments.

This Databricks cell assumes version 12 of the named table with unique event_id, numeric inputs feature_a/feature_b and numeric labels revenue_target/cost_target. Replace the names and version:

from dataclasses import replace
from skyulf.integrations.databricks import (
    TrainingSpec, TrainingBranch, train_branches,
)

branch_spec = TrainingSpec(
    table="catalog.schema.labeled_events", version=12,
    record_key_columns=("event_id",), input_columns=("feature_a", "feature_b"),
    target_column="revenue_target", split_strategy="random", test_size=0.2,
    random_state=42, drop_missing_labels=True,
    max_rows=10_000, max_bytes=32_000_000,
)
branch_pipeline = {"preprocessing": [], "modeling": {"type": "linear_regression"}}
branches = tuple(
    TrainingBranch(
        name=name, spec=replace(branch_spec, target_column=f"{name}_target"),
        pipeline=branch_pipeline, model_name=f"catalog.schema.{name}_model",
        metric="heldout_rmse", min_improvement=0.0,
    )
    for name in ("revenue", "cost")
)
trained = train_branches(
    spark, branches, tracking_uri="databricks", registry_uri="databricks-uc",
    experiment_name="/Shared/multi-target-demo",
    artifact_path="artifacts/multi-target-demo",
)
print(trained.parent_run_id, trained.source_version, trained.components.keys())

Expect both component names in the result. In MLflow, inspect the parent's saved plan and each child run's holdout and model artifacts. Replaying a saved plan keeps the source version and split settings but is a new attempt; it can create new model versions.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Each registered set version has the tags model_set_model_count and model_set_<branch>_name, model_set_<branch>_version and model_set_<branch>_type. Long names continue in _name_2, _name_3 and so on. These tags are for display; the saved manifest is the execution authority.

The final training_report task (models_report.py) shows Where to look, the set version, the operator blocks and Decision details (JSON). Score results are in the score job's score task.

docs.title: Upgrading Core with model sets
docs.text:
After upgrading Core, retrain the existing set normally. If its champion requires an earlier runtime, training retains that champion's concrete component versions and checks each new candidate against its saved absolute quality gates. The set stays pending; automatic promotion is disabled for this decision.

Review the component metrics and the filled-in approval command in the training report. When every component passes its configured quality_threshold and other gates, run that command on the same Bundle target. For example, replacing set version 4 with candidate 5 on prod:

databricks bundle run train -t prod --params lifecycle_action=approve,candidate_version=5,expected_champion_version=4,allow_unloadable_champion=true

This explicit approval records that the previous champion could not be compared. It rechecks candidate quality and the expected champion before moving the alias. Configured score and serving handoffs use the resulting concrete-version receipt. Never delete the champion alias to recover from an upgrade. Rollback to a pre-upgrade set requires a runtime that can load both sets; the recovery flag applies only to approval.

docs.title: Migrating an older DECIMAL input contract
docs.text:
Older models may have recorded a Spark DECIMAL input as object or string. New training converts that model value to float64 and records the source conversion. If champion comparison reports this schema mismatch, use new registered identities:

  1. In config/training.yml, give every affected models.<branch>.model_name a new name; for a single model, update its effective model_name.
  2. For a model set, also change config/inference.yml → model_set.model_name. Renaming only the set leaves its component champions unchanged.
  3. Train and review the new float64 candidate under the normal quality policy. Keep the old registered versions and their champion records for existing consumers.
  4. Validate the new model's batch output and serving requests before switching destinations. Use a separate prediction table and endpoint/SQL function for this check; update config/serving.yml model and destination names deliberately.

allow_unloadable_champion handles incompatible runtime versions only. It does not approve a changed input schema. The diagnostic names the affected columns and the concrete old champion. See DECIMAL conversion evidence.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Symptom Fix Scoring rule '...' raised KeyError during approval or scoring The shared scoring rules run for every component with only that component's input columns. Read only columns all components receive. Replacement stays challenger No branch improved by its min_improvement; ties alone never promote. Replacement fails quality A branch regressed or failed an absolute gate; read the failed components in the report. Champion belongs to an earlier Core release Retrain, review the pending report, then explicitly approve as described above. Changed branch names are rejected A replacement needs the same branches and component names; create a new set for a new layout. combined_only fails Add saved combined rules, then train and package a new set. Editing rules has no effect Train and package a new set; scoring uses the saved rules. Spark admission rejects the set Read the named rule and check, then follow When the probe fails; or use batch_compute: single_node. Update or delete fails scoring Choose on_source_change: rescore_all deliberately.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text:
Monitoring checks models after they score. It compares production inputs with the training population (drift and data quality), matches delayed outcomes to saved predictions (performance), and can request guarded retraining. Results are saved in one shared Delta store and shown on one shared dashboard. It works the same for single-model, competition and model-set projects.

Monitoring is optional. It runs only when the project has a monitoring destination and monitoring_enabled: "true". Setup asks for the destination; a blank answer creates a project that trains and scores without monitoring. See the setup questions.

docs.title: How monitoring runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["score"] --> B["prepare_monitoring"]
    B --> C["monitor_model: Run Job"]
    C --> D["monitoring job: monitor_model"]
    D --> E["monitoring_report"]
    E --> F["evaluate_retraining"]
    F --> G["refresh_monitoring_dashboard (optional)"]

A successful score hands its receipt to the separate monitoring job. That job measures and saves the evidence, shows it in monitoring_report, and applies any retraining policy you enabled. The dashboard refresh task exists only after you configure it. The monitoring job also has its own schedule, which starts paused, to revisit delayed outcomes without a new score. Monitoring runs only in shared production-mode targets; personal development targets skip it unless they opt in to their own separate store.

docs.title: Read in this order
docs.text:
1. Set up the monitoring store: destination, owned tables and views, permissions.
  2. Enroll models and run monitoring: automatic enrollment, reference preparation, the schedule.
  3. Match delayed labels: the label table needed for performance.
  4. Drift and data quality: thresholds, statuses, charts.
  5. Performance loss: policies, windows, baselines.
  6. Guarded retraining: drift and performance triggers and their shared guards.
  7. Shared dashboard: connect, own and read the dashboard.
  8. Serving monitoring: enroll endpoints and read the Online serving page.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Symptom Fix Train or score fails with Set both monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema. Set both names, or turn monitoring off; see store setup. Scoring succeeds but nothing is monitored Check monitoring_enabled for the target and that it is a shared production-mode target. The dashboard shows old results Run monitoring first; a dashboard refresh only rereads saved evidence.

docs.title: Configure and investigate the shared dashboard
When you need it
docs.text:
Connect a project to the existing AI/BI dashboard, create its single owner if needed, or investigate saved health and lineage. Metric-specific chart reading belongs to drift, performance loss and serving observations.

Choose one project/target to own the dashboard resource. All other projects reuse its published URL. An existing dashboard can remain under its current deployment ownership; using its URL does not create a copy. Keep its dashboard ID and Bundle state when migrating ownership; never deploy a second owner against it.

The native Dashboard job task runs after the existing monitoring job has saved its evidence and evaluated retraining. Configure it in each project as described below. Development or disabled monitoring skips refresh. No email subscription is created.

Updating source data does not automatically invalidate the dashboard result cache. The task performs the explicit refresh after successful monitoring. It runs as the job identity and preserves embed_credentials=false; other viewers keep their own data permissions and caches. This is automatic result refresh, not a continuously pushed update of every already-open browser tab. A separate dashboard schedule can refresh independently of monitoring if desired.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
Set the same monitoring_catalog / monitoring_schema in all production targets. No separate monitoring template or setup Bundle is required. The first activation, scoring registration or scheduled monitoring run bootstraps missing objects. Initialize before validating the dashboard SQL, because its queries need the views.

Dashboards are set per shared target in deployment/monitoring.yml. Each workspace has its own dashboard and SQL warehouse, so test, syst and prod are configured separately; leave a target out for no dashboard. A configured target adds two tasks after evaluate_retraining in the monitoring job: dashboard_refresh_enabled checks that monitoring_enabled is "true", then refresh_monitoring_dashboard refreshes. Existing schedules, policies and compute are unchanged, and no email subscription is created. Development targets have no dashboard block unless development monitoring is on; then test_development can create its own dashboard over the development store. For a dashboard published without shared data permissions, the job's Run as identity needs access to its data and warehouse. See the Databricks dashboard task documentation.

For each target choose one:

Choice What to write under the target Result create the dashboard (with warehouse_id), the link variable and the refresh task bundle deploy creates the dashboard; monitoring refreshes it connect the published URL as monitoring_dashboard_url and its ID in the refresh task monitoring refreshes the existing dashboard and links it in its output nothing omit the target monitoring still saves its results; no dashboard

docs.title: How the refresh task is added
docs.text:
deployment/monitoring.yml does not define a second job. resources/monitoring.job.yml defines the monitoring job for every target, and a target block repeats only its name with two extra tasks:

# resources/monitoring.job.yml (every target)
resources:
  jobs:
    monitoring:
      tasks:
        - task_key: monitor_model
        - task_key: monitoring_report
        - task_key: evaluate_retraining

# deployment/monitoring.yml (only the test target)
targets:
  test:
    resources:
      jobs:
        monitoring:            # same job name: merged, not a new job
          tasks:
            - task_key: dashboard_refresh_enabled   # skip when monitoring is off
              depends_on:
                - task_key: evaluate_retraining
              condition_task:
                op: EQUAL_TO
                left: "${var.monitoring_enabled}"
                right: "true"
            - task_key: refresh_monitoring_dashboard
              depends_on:
                - task_key: dashboard_refresh_enabled
                  outcome: "true"
              dashboard_task:
                dashboard_id: ${resources.dashboards.monitoring_dashboard.id}

On bundle deploy -t test, Bundle merges every included file into one configuration. Jobs with the same name become one job, and their tasks are merged by task_key: a new key is added, an existing key is updated. The deployed test job therefore runs monitor_model -> monitoring_report -> evaluate_retraining -> dashboard_refresh_enabled -> refresh_monitoring_dashboard. A target without a block keeps the first three tasks. deployment/targets.yml uses the same merge to add run_as and permissions to jobs defined in resources/. Run databricks bundle validate -t <target> -o json to see the merged job.

Choose create only in the first project that uses a target's monitoring store; every other project uses connect. The dashboard ID is the 32 characters after /dashboardsv3/ in its URL. The warehouse ID is the 16-character value under SQL Warehouses > your warehouse > Connection details, also visible in the warehouse page URL; syst and prod need IDs from their own workspaces. The file contains both blocks as commented examples to copy.

Setup fills the test target for you. With a monitoring store, answer monitoring_dashboard:

Answer Also asks Result none (default) nothing no target is configured create monitoring_dashboard_warehouse_id (required) test gets the create block connect monitoring_dashboard_url, optional warehouse ID test gets the connect block, with the ID taken from the URL

syst and prod are always set by hand in the same file. monitoring_catalog / monitoring_schema stay in deployment/variables.yml; the monitoring job creates its tables there on its first run, and the dashboard reads from them.

The template's src/monitoring/monitoring.lvdash.json defines SQL, shared investigation filters and five content pages, plus the global filter page. resources/monitoring.job.yml contains the separate Spark measurement, report and retraining job. No separate monitoring Bundle is required.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
After editing deployment/monitoring.yml for a target, validate and deploy it:

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile <profile>
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile <profile>

For a new dashboard, validate every dashboard dataset against the chosen monitoring store first. Other projects connect with the published URL from this deployment. To stop refreshing, remove the target's two refresh tasks. Removing a create block deletes that dashboard on the next deploy, so move ownership deliberately.

Initialize or upgrade the store using the owner notebook before validating every dataset SQL query and publishing the dashboard. The dashboard needs SELECT on complete_observations, monitoring_identities, serving_windows and the other monitoring views. For training summaries, refresh model_version_details to expose training_summary_json.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Dashboard deployment is configuration, not metric calculation. Run monitoring to save new measurements, then the native task refreshes the published datasets. The dashboard retains the selected store across all project layouts.

Use the shared filters on the left: Model (choose one for details), Monitored version and Context. Model names include catalog and schema, so there are no separate catalog/schema controls. Context includes environment, project and a short monitor ID. The selection persists between pages; there are no competing model controls inside the pages. Date, feature, metric, target and job controls refine only the page where they appear.

All models, All versions and All contexts are the initial selections. Drift and Model performance include every matching model/version/context, with the latest result selected independently for each identity. Disabled policies and identities without measurements remain visible. Choose Model, Monitored version and Context to narrow the portfolio. Online serving lists matching endpoint contexts separately. Incompatible explicit selections stay empty; clear Monitored version and Context when switching models. An explicitly selected model never falls back to another model.

Page Scope What to use it for Overview All models with the initial All selections; otherwise all matching registrations. Four summary counts, prioritized issues, current status distributions and daily trends. Training and lineage All matching model/version/context identities. Compare concrete versions, owning training runs and recorded provenance. Drift and data quality Every matching model/version/context, with its own latest observation. Separate feature PSI comparisons and drift histories, with detailed quality measurements. Model performance Every matching model/version/context, including disabled and unmeasured policies. Per-identity prediction/label coverage, metric history, policy comparisons and classification evidence. Online serving All matching serving enrollments, separated by model/version/context; choose Model to narrow them. Distinguish monitored and served versions; inspect captured counts, errors and latency in tables and five window charts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Overview puts the issue list before trends. Four counters show distinct registered models, monitoring registrations, issue rows and distinct scoring-input tables. The issue count can exceed the registration count because one observation may have several issues. The model/table mapping includes prediction and optional label tables; shared tables count once. Two compact status distributions show feature/data health and performance-policy status separately, including missing evidence and disabled registrations. These are current registration counts, not prediction rows or daily totals.

Two line charts show daily drift and performance-policy checks. Each counts one enrollment per UTC window day using the latest saved window, then measurement and report ID to break ties. They include only the current configuration/version; missing or failed evidence stays unavailable. Unrecorded days are gaps, not zero checks or carried-forward healthy models. These are daily recorded checks, not historical snapshots of fleet health.

Healthy feature/data status does not mean accuracy met its baseline. The performance distribution compares each enrollment's current configuration and concrete version against its latest saved policy window. Within tolerance and Performance loss require usable, sufficiently recent evidence. Insufficient evidence includes missing checks, unavailable labels/baselines and stale windows. Policy disabled and Monitoring disabled remain distinct states.

Freshness uses the latest completed UTC policy window after label_delay_hours: a window becomes stale when it trails that boundary by more than expected_interval_hours. Future or immature windows cannot count as success. The dashboard does not initiate training. Retraining retains its independent opt-in and request guards; historical losses remain visible even when the latest window has insufficient evidence.

The Drift and Performance charts show up to two columns and two rows of panels at once; scroll inside a chart for additional identities. Fewer panels use the available width, within the fixed compact card height. Choose Monitored version and Context as well as Model to reduce panels.

docs.title: Latest observations and page filters
docs.text: Latest-observation views pick each identity's newest saved report first, ranked by window end and then measurement time. Page filters for date, feature, target or metric apply afterwards. A filter can hide that report's values, but it never selects an older report instead. A newer empty or failed report likewise hides an older measured value. History tables and trend charts keep every saved observation.

docs.title: Training and lineage
docs.text:
Training and lineage shows every identity matching the shared filters. Choosing All models / All versions / All contexts shows all available identities; an obsolete or incompatible selection leaves empty tables and never substitutes the latest different model. Each table includes its model, version and context. Historical observed versions retain their concrete identities, while NULL versions explicitly say unresolved. The page shows creation time, owning training run, recorded algorithm, artifact digest and available code evidence. Open Training run to inspect that run's native Inputs and artifacts. A source commit is shown only when the owning run already records mlflow.source.git.commit; a project Python source digest is shown only when the saved artifact records one.

Three additional tables explain how each monitored version was produced:

  • Training candidates and recorded selection shows saved candidate scores, metric direction, CV evaluation mode and selection reason. Only the selected, registered candidate has a registered version; losing candidates retain their own training run. A single configured model is identified explicitly, without an invented competition score. Run duration is elapsed run time, not isolated fitting time. Post-selection CV is identified separately from an unbiased estimate.
  • Chosen model parameters lists the fitted estimator's saved settings, including defaults, ensemble and split settings, by parameter name and source. Structured values remain JSON; these are recorded settings, not a new search.
  • Training datasets and provenance shows the saved training/holdout populations, source table and version, membership evidence and feature binding. Delta table identity and Unity Catalog identity are different fields. Version zero is valid. Dataset Inputs run opens the verified run containing native Inputs; in a task-based competition this may be the winning child rather than the registered model's parent run.

All three tables use the same Model (choose one for details), Monitored version and Context selection. They summarize allowlisted metadata only; raw training rows, executable source and complete run configs are not copied into the dashboard. Missing, inaccessible, invalid or oversized evidence is reported independently for each section. Empty evidence never becomes a zero score or a different version's training history. These optional summaries cannot change monitoring or promotion decisions.

Each new observation reads up to three known JSON artifacts and the saved competition's child-run metadata. Competition summaries admit at most 32 candidates; each section admits at most 256 rows and 64 KiB of stored JSON. Oversized sections show too_large instead of truncating or partially ranking candidates. Feature-binding details appear once, on the training-population row.

The summary is copied into the monitoring store. Readers with access to its tables/views can see candidate scores, model parameter values and source metadata even if they cannot open the original MLflow experiment. Grant store access to the intended audience; opening the linked run still requires its own permissions. Lookup details contain table/column names, time-window settings, table identities and versions, not individual lookup-key values or row filters.

In the Alias metadata snapshot table, Aliases at capture describes the concrete version's alias metadata when the monitoring reference was loaded, alongside Captured at. It does not describe historical deployment identity or guarantee today's registry alias assignment. New observations refresh the bounded snapshot in existing evidence_json. Retrying the same observation preserves the first saved snapshot and does not invalidate prepared Spark references. Dashboard refresh only rereads saved evidence; it makes no per-row registry calls and does not move aliases.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text:
Start on Overview → Issues to investigate. The table uses native pagination, with failures first, then recorded quality/drift/performance issues, then missing or stale evidence. The counter gives the full filtered issue count, including rows on later pages. One model can have multiple issues; this is an issue count, not a model count. Use the shared Model (choose one for details), Monitored version and Context filters to narrow the list. Disabled monitoring and disabled performance policies do not create new failures. Never-observed, no-data, failed, stale and insufficient-label results keep their distinct recorded reasons. Missing metric values remain empty.

Open a concrete Model version link for the registry entry, or Evidence run for the monitoring run that recorded that issue. The latter is separate from the owning training run. A missing link means its exact run/experiment identity was not recorded or is unavailable; it does not mean the issue is healthy.

Older reports can show not_recorded, never-observed enrollments have no training metadata, and optional metadata permission failures show unavailable with a reason. Missing creation/code/alias fields remain unavailable rather than inferred. Existing store owners can run initialize_monitoring_store explicitly to refresh owned view definitions; ordinary runs create missing compatible views without replacing existing ones. Viewers retain their own data permissions. For the training tables, refresh the owned model_version_details view to add training_summary_json before publishing the dashboard. The next new observation captures the summary. Refreshing the dashboard or retrying an already saved observation does not backfill historical reports; their section status remains not_recorded.

A refresh only queries the saved summary; it neither rereads training rows nor fits a model. New observations read the saved artifacts again. Incompatible explicit model/version/context choices stay empty; clear Monitored version and Context when changing models.

If a browser still shows old results, use the dashboard refresh control. A browser reload may reuse cached queries. The native job task refreshes published datasets after observation but does not push updates into every open tab. Store/view upgrades and producer runtime upgrades remain separate from dashboard refresh.

docs.title: When you need it
docs.text:
Use this page after store setup to enroll activated or scored batch models, prepare their references, and start observation. For endpoints, use serving monitoring.

Monitoring writes to the shared store only for mode: production deployments (test, syst, prod). By default, personal development targets do not enroll temporary models or create monitoring tables: they set monitoring_enabled: "false", and the monitoring_allowed condition then skips enrollment and the post-scoring monitoring handoff. Training and scoring still run normally, including automatic scoring after activation. Development targets also set monitoring_performance_policies: '{}' and on_drift: disabled.

docs.title: Development monitoring (optional)
docs.text:
To see your own development models, answer development_monitoring: "true" in setup. The question appears with personal development targets and needs a monitoring store; it defaults to off. Setup then asks for the schema name (development_monitoring_schema, default development_monitoring) in the same catalog. Any name works, including an existing schema in your workspace, as long as it is not the shared monitoring_schema. Every *_development target sets monitoring_enabled: "true", and every job receives both names. Change the name later in deployment/variables.yml; a blank name keeps development monitoring off.

Core keeps the two stores apart: in development mode it writes only to development_monitoring_schema and refuses one that is missing or equal to the shared schema; test, syst and prod always use the shared schema. Development models are measured and reported only; automatic retraining stays disabled. Development jobs run as you, so you may need permission to create the schema, or ask for it to be created first. bundle destroy does not remove a development model's enrollment, so old trial models remain in the development store until you clean or recreate it. With monitoring_dashboard: create, test_development also gets its own dashboard over this store; development mode prefixes its name for each user.

flowchart LR
    A["train: register_monitor"] --> B["score"]
    B --> C["prepare_monitoring"]
    C --> D["monitoring_ready"]
    D --> E["monitor_model: Run Job"]
    E --> F["monitoring job"]

Activation enrolls the model in the train job. Each successful score then hands its receipt to the separate monitoring job.

docs.title: If monitoring is not configured
docs.text:
Monitoring runs only when setup answered monitoring: "true", which sets monitoring_enabled: "true". monitoring: "false" sets it to "false": train and score run, register_monitor and prepare_monitoring report disabled, and the score job skips monitor_model. Nothing is enrolled or observed. Enable it later as described in store setup. A configured "false" flag with both names set publishes a pause instead. Without a configured label table, drift and feature quality still run; actual model performance remains unavailable.

Keep model/data catalog, input_schema, output_schema and metadata_schema unchanged. After a successful activation, the train job's register_monitor task registers the version from the verified lifecycle result before scoring. The training graph orders training_report -> register_monitor before scoring_requested in every layout. Initial activation, approval and rollback are supported; pending/rejected candidates do not replace the active enrollment. Merely running bundle deploy does not activate a model. A successful scoring or CDF-recovery task also registers its actual model version and physical Delta prediction generation. It never resolves an alias a second time. No-op scoring also repairs registration without writing duplicate predictions. A registration error fails the task visibly; previously committed predictions remain intact and their receipt makes scoring retries safe. A pending recovery request does not register an output as successfully scored.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
In the generated model Bundle's target variables, configure:

monitoring_catalog: operations
monitoring_schema: model_monitoring
monitoring_expected_interval_hours: "24"
monitoring_revisit_windows: "3" # Includes the latest completed window
monitoring_drift_thresholds: '{"psi": 0.2, "ks_statistic": 0.1, "wasserstein": 0.1, "kl_divergence": 0.1}'
# Optional shared MLflow experiment for the post-scoring task:
monitoring_experiment_name: /Shared/skyulf/monitoring
monitoring_dashboard_url: "https://<workspace-host>/dashboardsv3/<dashboard-id>/published"
# Optional actual results:
monitoring_label_table: outcomes.production.labels
monitoring_result_available_at_column: available_at
monitoring_performance_policies: '{}'

Place this excerpt under targets.<target>.variables in the generated deployment/targets.yml. Performance and delayed labels are optional; choose their policy on the performance-loss page.

The inventory holds the latest enrollment for environment/project/fully qualified model name. A newly scored model version updates that enrollment and keeps old version observations in history. It appears never_observed until the central job measures the new configuration. Removing deployment settings does not delete an existing enrollment. To pause, retain the destination, set monitoring_enabled to false and run scoring, or upsert a disabled MonitorConfig through enroll_monitor. Do not edit only the duplicated config/digest fields by hand. Removing only the destination while monitoring is enabled is invalid. External alias edits do not trigger enrollment.

Automatic registration supports single models, competition winners and model-set components. Model-set activation enrolls each component's concrete version before scoring. Each component retains its parent set name/version/branch and reads its own predictions from the shared physical output table. Use all or separate_views; combined_only cannot supply individual model performance and is rejected before scoring when monitoring storage is configured. No JSON model list is required.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
Run from the generated project root after reviewing its target variables. These commands operate on Databricks; replace YOUR_PROFILE and the target. Deploy updated model, score and monitoring jobs together when changing their shared runtime contract.

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

docs.title: Prepare references for a first pinned candidate
docs.text:
Activation prepares verified training references. A first manual candidate scored by concrete version may be enrolled by scoring without having been activated. In that case, the prediction commit can succeed while the monitoring child fails with Spark reference is not prepared; run prepare_spark_monitoring_reference first. Open the score receipt to confirm publication, then run the existing monitoring job's preparation action for the enrolled identity:

databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE --params monitoring_action=prepare_references

Use the same project, target and monitoring namespace. Preparation reads the saved training evidence and creates/reuses the immutable references; it does not train, promote or rescore. After it succeeds, repeat the original score request to finish its monitoring handoff. An unchanged source/model replay is a prediction no-op; inspect the original commit and the separate child result. Do not delete output rows or invent a new watermark to repair monitoring. The preparation action needs the reference/table permissions of the shared store.

After reference preparation succeeds, set monitoring_pause_status: "UNPAUSED" in the target variables and redeploy to let the existing UTC schedule revisit observations. Keep the generated schedule paused until references and permissions are verified.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Generated producer Bundles always use Spark monitoring; no engine selection is required. Scoring validates its exact receipt, then a native Run Job task calls the independent third monitoring job and waits for its result. Training can call scoring through the same native job hierarchy. Monitoring uses its own serverless environment, timeout and retry settings, and a UTC schedule that starts PAUSED. Prepare and verify references before unpausing it. The scheduled run observes enrolled models and delayed labels even if no new scoring batch arrives. Its tasks run monitor_model -> monitoring_report -> evaluate_retraining; a guarded policy may submit the producer's complete train job.

With monitoring configured and enabled, every successful scoring receipt reaches the dedicated monitoring job. Failed scoring and missing saved batches do not create a successful observation. Dashboard refresh reads saved results; it does not run monitoring and an already open page is not a push stream. Use the dashboard's refresh control to load new observations; reloading the browser can still reuse cached query results. Scheduled monitoring covers late labels even when scoring has not run again.

Open monitoring_report for saved drift, observed performance and policy evidence; Open monitoring dashboard appears when the shared HTTPS URL is configured. evaluate_retraining then applies only explicitly enabled retraining policies.

The score job runs prepare_monitoring -> monitoring_ready -> monitor_model, where the final node is the native child-job call. Calculation, saved drift reports and guarded retraining belong to that child job. The monitoring job's own monitor_model executes src/jobs/monitor_project.py; the scoring job's task with that key invokes the child job. All projects can link to the same monitoring_dashboard_url.

For custom inventory-wide SDK runs, select a suitable observation window. The inventory limit bounds enrolled models, not prediction rows. Refreshing the dashboard does not compute new metrics. Each model failure is saved, other models are attempted, and the notebook then fails if any model failed. Inspect reports before retrying.

Observation identity includes configuration, cutoff, window and snapshot evidence. Exact retries do not overwrite history. Current health ranks the newest window, then its latest measurement; historical backfills cannot replace newer windows. Keep the Delta retention needed for source replay and audit history.

docs.title: Library API and local execution
docs.text:
The library can read a bounded inventory snapshot, default maximum 10,000 entries. The SDK can enroll explicit records and run inventory-wide observations; it does not require a configuration file or a second template.

The public local API observes with pandas or Polars in the Python process. MonitorConfig.max_rows=10000 is its default observation budget; MAX_MONITOR_ROWS=1_000_000 is the local safety ceiling. The local byte budget defaults to 64 MiB and is capped at 1 GiB. Neither local row nor byte budget limits Spark observation rows. These are not two separate Spark limits.

The observation budget bounds local data, while the inventory budget bounds enrolled models. Generated Spark observation rows have neither local row nor local byte caps; drift measurement limits still apply.

docs.title: Library integration entrypoints
docs.text:
Import monitoring helpers from the domain modules below. Paths are relative to skyulf/integrations/databricks/.

File Responsibility observability/monitoring/monitoring_config.py Validated model/table identity, version and bounded policy. observability/monitoring/monitoring_registration.py Activation/scoring enrollment and immutable scoring handoff. jobs/monitoring/monitoring_tasks.py Visible activation enrollment and per-commit scoring observation tasks. observability/monitoring/monitoring_output.py Saved-batch drift report and safe shared-dashboard navigation in task output. observability/monitoring/monitoring_reference.py Registered artifact and original training-reference replay. observability/monitoring/monitoring_sources.py Saved predictions, source snapshots, receipts and delayed labels. observability/monitoring/monitoring_metrics.py Core metric adapters and finite keyed reports for bounded frames. observability/monitoring/monitoring_performance.py Mature performance windows measured against a pinned model baseline. observability/monitoring/spark/ Distributed monitoring measurements, references and source handling. observability/monitoring/monitoring_store.py Owned Delta objects, concurrent registration, inventory reads and report history. observability/monitoring/monitoring.py Inventory observations, engine dispatch, failure isolation and MLflow reports. jobs/shared/job_runtime.py, scoring/incremental/scoring_recovery.py Invoke enrollment after successful scoring/recovery. model_sets/model_set_project.py, model_sets/monitoring_model_set.py Enroll pinned components after activation and scoring.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text:
If train or score fails with Set both monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema., monitoring is enabled or one name is set alone; fix the destination as described in store setup. If nothing is monitored after successful scoring, check that monitoring_enabled is "true" for that target.

A deployment alone does not activate or enroll a model. Run the normal lifecycle/scoring path, then check the concrete version and configuration in inventory. A configured false flag publishes a pause only when registration executes; removing configuration does not delete the previous enrollment.

Reference preparation is a separate, one-time activation or explicit migration step. It replays the original training source under the existing bounded training row and byte budget, validates the original split and writes pinned reference populations. Models without monitoring_source_evidence.json need retraining or verified original source proof; the job never silently reconstructs provenance. Spark freshness checks fail explicitly for unsupported fixed normalizers, custom pre-split filters and custom weight generators. Supported source weight columns still obey the training contract. Training remains local even when inference is distributed. Spark monitoring does not change the training or scoring engine.

Activation enrollment is ordered by the original serialized lifecycle run start. A delayed score cannot replace an activated different version, and repairing an older activation cannot replace a newer activation. Enrollment-only repairs read the verified original receipt without repeating training or alias changes. The private activation-order metadata lives in inventory config_json; table schemas and model configuration digests do not include it. Every job that reads the shared inventory must run a Core release that understands it.

Current-health states and their freshness rules are described on Drift and data quality. If the latest report failed, inspect its saved error before retrying; the dashboard does not reuse an older success.

docs.title: Match delayed labels to saved predictions
When you need it
docs.text:
Use delayed labels when actual outcomes arrive after prediction. Drift can run without outcomes; measured accuracy and performance-loss policies need usable true targets.

Performance explains the number of predictions with matched usable true target values. No configured label source means no measured performance, not zero accuracy. A target in an arbitrary source is not discovered automatically: use monitoring_label_table with the saved record keys and target column, and declare the result-availability timestamp. That table can be the scoring source when it already satisfies this contract and its rows are never updated; when outcomes arrive later, use a separate outcomes table (see Choose a table layout). Fewer than two eligible pairs cannot be scored.

flowchart LR
    P["Saved predictions with record keys"] --> J["Join on keys"]
    L["monitoring_label_table"] --> A["available_at at or before cutoff"]
    A --> J
    J --> W["Mature window after label_delay_hours"]
    W --> M["monitor_model: metrics and policy"]

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
During Bundle initialization, both setup modes accept label_table_name and label_available_at_column. For example:

{
  "label_table_name": "outcomes",
  "label_available_at_column": "available_at"
}

A short table name resolves through the active target's catalog and input schema. A three-part name such as labels.production.outcomes stays explicit across targets. Leave both fields empty to start without label-based measurements. Setting only one fails initialization. These answers generate the two variables below; override them per target if your environments use different sources.

Set these target variables in deployment/targets.yml; the names below are examples.

monitoring_label_table: labels.production.outcomes
monitoring_result_available_at_column: available_at
monitoring_revisit_windows: "3"

The label table must expose the saved record keys, the model's target column and the UTC timestamp when the actual outcome became available. available_at is outcome availability, not the prediction time or the job execution time.

Observation source Required label identity Batch predictions The model's saved record_key_columns, including every component of a composite key. Serving predictions databricks_request_id plus zero-based request_row_index, distinguishing multiple rows in one request.

Both need the saved target column and a valid UTC availability timestamp (or an aware ISO timestamp string). Eligible label keys must be unique. Actuals must use the saved classification classes or finite numeric regression targets.

For endpoint-only projects, monitoring_label_table is a request-outcomes table: databricks_request_id must be a string and request_row_index an integer. The endpoint job checks these columns before creating or updating serving resources. Keep the request ID returned by serving and the position of each input row when recording its eventual outcome. Two requests for the same business record remain two observations; Skyulf does not guess that relationship from a customer or transaction ID.

The table used by training_label_table still joins by the training record keys. It can be a different table. If one automatically configured monitoring label table serves both batch and endpoint observations, it must satisfy both key contracts. For separate outcome tables, enroll the serving monitor with its own request-key label table using the monitoring enrollment configuration. Leave the label table and availability setting empty for operational monitoring and drift alone; those measurements do not require actual outcomes.

For a model set, include the target columns required by each monitored component. Skyulf does not discover an arbitrary target source, generate outcomes, or write labels back into the training table. source_layout: separate_outcomes also configures a read-only training join; in other layouts, monitoring's label binding alone does not enable that join. See training from separate outcomes before enabling retraining.

monitoring_revisit_windows controls how many completed performance windows are checked for late labels. It defaults to 3, includes the latest window, and accepts 1 to 100. Historical windows can update saved evidence, but do not independently submit training. Spark joins saved predictions, pinned feature snapshots and eligible actual outcomes, then writes durable Delta observations. Ongoing Spark measurements do not use the local one-million-row monitoring cap.

docs.title: Which time counts
docs.text:
For batch predictions, three timestamps are involved, and only the prediction commit time places a row in a performance window:

sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Scoring source
    participant J as Score job
    participant P as Predictions
    participant L as Outcomes table
    participant M as Monitoring job
    S->>J: Row inserted, observed_at is when it was measured
    J->>P: Prediction committed, this time picks the window
    L->>L: Outcome inserted with available_at
    Note over P,M: A daily window holds the predictions committed in one UTC day
    M->>P: Read the window after its end plus label_delay_hours
    M->>L: Join on the record key, keep available_at at or before the cutoff
    M->>M: Compare the metric with the baseline
    Note over M: report mode records the first degraded window
  • observed_at is a source column for training windows; it does not decide the performance window. Loading two historical days today puts both into today's window.
  • available_at decides whether an outcome may be used yet. An outcome that arrives later is picked up when monitoring revisits that window.
  • consecutive_windows counts adjacent degraded windows. It decides whether mode: retrain may request training; it does not delay a report.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
Deploy the updated producer settings and run successful activation/scoring registration so the enrollment contains the label source. Run the existing monitoring job to read outcomes available at its observation cutoff.

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

Unpause the monitoring schedule after reference preparation. Revisited windows can acquire late outcomes even without another scoring batch. A historical backfill updates evidence but cannot independently submit training.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
Only saved predictions are scored. Reference loading replays the original training membership, and current features use the source snapshots recorded with predictions. Local SDK enrollments materialize bounded pandas/Polars inputs under their limits; generated Spark enrollments use distributed readers. Labels join by saved record keys and only count when their UTC availability is at or before as_of. Missing labels or fewer than two finite pairs leave performance unavailable; an unavailable value is not zero accuracy.

Full monitoring reports include excluded_rows: the number of saved prediction records explicitly marked scoring_status="excluded". Missing prediction records and missing labels do not increase this count. Spark, pandas and Polars reports retain it in report_json. Existing saved observations are not rewritten; a missing count in an older report means unavailable, not zero.

The saved report exposes scored_rows, labeled_rows and label_coverage. Coverage is eligible usable labeled predictions divided by scored predictions; an empty prediction population leaves it unavailable. The policy separately requires both minimum_labeled_rows and minimum_label_coverage. Its fixed UTC windows wait label_delay_hours after their end before assessment.

A 00:00–24:00 UTC window with a six-hour delay first becomes eligible at 06:00 UTC the following day. Outcome availability is checked against the observation cutoff; an outcome recorded as available later cannot be used early. Window end and calculation time remain separate.

See performance chart interpretation for per-identity coverage, gaps and classification matrices.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: Symptom or error Fix Labels need target and availability columns. Supply the saved target and configured availability column. Invalid or naive label availability timestamp. Provide non-null valid timestamps; strings must include a timezone. Do not substitute prediction time or job execution time. labels has duplicate record keys. Resolve duplicates among eligible outcomes upstream, including every composite key field. The monitor does not pick an arbitrary label. Prediction and label classes must match saved classes. Correct label encoding to the classes saved with this concrete model version. Insufficient labels or blank scores Wait for true outcomes, check keys and cutoff, and meet both policy evidence minimums. Fewer than two finite pairs cannot produce performance. Serving requests have incomplete payloads Check logging errors; excluded payloads cannot contribute prediction/label pairs. A label table changed but retraining remains blocked Labels do not update the training table. Supply fresh eligible labeled training rows under the existing training contract.

docs.title: Set up and upgrade the monitoring store
When you need it
docs.text:
Set up one durable store before enabling production monitoring, or upgrade its owned views before deploying a newer producer or dashboard. Follow Enroll models next.

The end-to-end flow from scoring to dashboard is on the monitoring overview.

Set per-model measurement controls through the existing monitoring_drift_thresholds JSON variable. The complete settings table covers category grouping, uniqueness, summary caps, PSI severity wording and non-Spark row/byte budgets. Empty {} preserves existing enrollment defaults. These settings do not resize Spark compute or change model admission probes.

The canonical dashboard definition is src/monitoring/monitoring.lvdash.json inside the existing Databricks project template. This is not a separate Bundle or another project template. Single, competition and model-set projects write to one configured store and display their evidence in one shared dashboard.

Operation Trigger and effect Measure drift and performance Successful scoring calls the separate Spark monitoring job when monitoring is configured and enabled. A production-mode target is required; development targets bypass shared monitoring. Revisit delayed outcomes Unpause the monitoring job's schedule after setup. The generated schedule starts paused. Clean old references Projects initialized with monitoring include a separate weekly cleanup job, enabled on shared targets and paused in personal development. Review the retention and writer controls below before deployment. Refresh dashboard results The configured native Dashboard task reruns published datasets after monitoring completes. It does not calculate new monitoring metrics. Request training Drift or performance loss can qualify independently when its own policy enables retraining. Shared guards must also pass.

Changing training/scoring compute to a cluster does not enable monitoring, change its storage destination, or enable automatic retraining. The generated monitoring job has its own serverless environment. Use Databricks to inspect job run history, compute usage and billing.

Native AI/BI is the visualization product, distinct from Databricks Data Profiling. This Bundle does not provision a separate native data profile. The older quality_monitors API is deprecated; new integrations use data_quality. An InferenceLog profile can calculate model quality from prediction and label columns, but it requires its own input table, refresh lifecycle and metric tables. It does not replace this project's delayed-outcome matching, concrete training holdout references, consecutive-window policy or guarded training requests. See the current Data Profiling API.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
Setup asks monitoring (on or off) and, when on, monitoring_schema in both quick and detailed mode. An omitted or blank schema defaults to skyulf_monitoring; a different answer is preserved, and existing stores are never moved or migrated. The catalog is not asked: monitoring_catalog defaults to each target's own catalog. Setup writes both to deployment/variables.yml; see the setup questions. To use other names in one target, put this excerpt under targets.<target>.variables in deployment/monitoring.yml. The values are examples; use your existing catalog and a schema reserved for the shared store.

monitoring_catalog: operations
monitoring_schema: model_monitoring
monitoring_enabled: "true"

docs.title: If no destination is set
docs.text:
monitoring: "false" at setup generates monitoring_enabled: "false". Train and score then run normally without enrollment, monitoring or a store. Nothing is written to a monitoring schema, and both generated destination values are blank. To enable monitoring later, set both names and monitoring_enabled: "true", then validate and redeploy.

monitoring_enabled Catalog and schema Result at train/score "false" Both blank Runs without monitoring "false" Both set Publishes a paused enrollment "true" Both set Enrolls and monitors "true", or either value set alone Not both set Fails with Set both monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema.

Development targets skip this check unless they opt in to their own separate store; see development monitoring.

Every project uses the same independent monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema values. These control monitoring storage only; they do not change model, training, source or prediction locations. The catalog must exist. The first configured enrollment or enabled scheduled run creates the schema and missing owned tables/views if its identity has the required permissions. Later runs validate and reuse existing objects without replacing their data or view definitions. Explicit initialize_monitoring_store remains the upgrade API for deliberately refreshing view definitions.

When a release adds views, run that owner upgrade before upgrading producer jobs. Bootstrap still needs CREATE permission for any missing object; a writer with only SELECT/MODIFY fails with the platform's permission error until the owner creates the missing views. There is no fallback to partially initialized storage.

Object First initialization Later runs model_inventory (Delta) Create if absent Producer MERGE inserts/updates one environment/project/model identity. monitoring_results (Delta) Create if absent Monitoring job inserts immutable observations; exact retries deduplicate. complete_observations (view) Create before dependent views Exclude policy-only late-label reports from feature/serving selection; preserve failed and zero-row observations. current_health (view) Create if absent Reuse; read inventory and latest applicable observation. monitoring_identities (view) Create after current_health Include enrolled and historical model/version/context identities, including unresolved versions; latest measurement time counts full observations only. serving_windows (view) Create after complete_observations Share enabled, current-configuration serving windows, error-class fallback and per-context/version ordering across charts. metric_history (view) Create if absent Reuse; expand stored report metrics for dashboard queries. performance_actions (Delta) Create if absent Append request and skip receipts without rewriting observations. retraining_requests (Delta) Create if absent with Serializable isolation Retain request identities, submission receipts, a shared cooldown gate per training job and the store's reference-mutation control row. performance_history (view) Create if absent Reuse; join performance evidence with the latest applicable action. monitoring_issues (view) Create if absent Reuse; read current health and recorded quality, drift and active-policy issues. model_version_details (view) Create if absent Reuse; read concrete version lineage and bounded metadata snapshots from existing reports.

Tables in your workspace explains each of these objects and the reference tables in plain terms. One store serves all enrolled models; inventory, observations and action history are shared rather than recreated per model or score run. Spark reference preparation writes a population and receipt per verified model/training identity, plus an immutable monitor_src_<identity> table shared only by references with identical source content and schema. The population has a recorded boolean membership column so readers recover the original training and seen rows without duplicating tables. Existing format-1 train/source/seen/receipt tables remain readable and are not migrated. See the workspace-tables guide for examples. References are prepared once for their identity and reused; a new model/training identity can require new reference tables. Ordinary monitoring observations append to the shared results table, not to new per-run tables. Existing foreign objects or incompatible table schemas are rejected. Store initialization sets inventory and retraining-request isolation to Serializable. Producer registrations make at most three attempts (two retries) on optimistic Delta conflicts; exhausted conflicts and other errors remain visible. Each project monitoring job serializes its own observations; independent projects share the same store. An inventory read never writes its older snapshot back over another repository's configuration update.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
For jobs without schema/table creation privileges, have the store owner run initialize_monitoring_store(spark, monitoring_catalog, monitoring_schema) before starting those jobs. This also prepares retraining_requests, so the first automatic training request can use the existing table. Grant the runtime identity the required catalog/schema access and table read/write privileges. Reusing a compatible store requires no schema, table or view creation SQL. If any owned table or view is missing, the next enrollment or monitoring run must create it, so either rerun owner initialization first or give that run's identity CREATE privileges. Normal runs refuse incompatible schemas or weak isolation.

Run this cloud-only Python example in a store-owner notebook after installing the Core requirement that will serve the producers and dashboard. Define monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema with the destination selected above.

For an explicit schema/view upgrade, run initialize_monitoring_store after installing the updated Core requirement and before deploying or publishing the updated dashboard. The dashboard reads complete_observations, monitoring_identities and serving_windows; a dashboard refresh does not create these views. In an owner-run notebook:

from skyulf.integrations.databricks.observability.monitoring.monitoring_store import (
    initialize_monitoring_store,
)

namespace = initialize_monitoring_store(spark, monitoring_catalog, monitoring_schema)
for view in ("complete_observations", "monitoring_identities", "serving_windows"):
    spark.table(f"{namespace}.{view}").limit(0).collect()

Grant dashboard viewers SELECT on the new views, using the same access policy as the existing monitoring views, then publish. The initializer checks ownership of every object before changing any of them. Normal producer bootstrap creates only missing views and never replaces existing definitions. The inventory and observation table schemas and saved data stay compatible. Store bootstrap creates performance_actions with the other tables. Any active performance policy, in report or retrain mode, writes its actions there, so the monitoring identity needs SELECT/MODIFY on performance_actions.

Projects on different Core versions share these views. Keep existing columns and their meanings compatible across those versions; coordinate owner upgrades with all consumers before changing a view contract. Owner-run monitoring can replace view definitions using its installed Core version. Adding a result-table column also requires reinitialization to refresh the views' stored column lists. Chart labels and missing-value display text stay in the dashboard, so wording changes do not require a store upgrade.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
The initialization call returns the namespace, and all three spark.table(...).limit(0).collect() checks finish without an error. Existing observations remain in place. Each later enrollment or enabled observation reuses compatible objects. Monitoring metrics appear only after an observation run; initialization does not calculate them.

The producer principal needs access to the central catalog/schema and SELECT/MODIFY on model_inventory for enrollment. The score job's monitoring task also needs SELECT/MODIFY on monitoring_results, read access to the saved model/training/source/prediction/label data, and access to its optional MLflow experiment. First bootstrap additionally requires permission to create the missing schema, Delta tables and views. A complete existing store needs no recurring CREATE/ALTER permission for bootstrap; normal observation/reference/action writes retain their own grants. Foreign objects or incompatible schemas fail visibly. The central monitoring principal needs inventory access, report writes, read access to enrolled models/artifacts, original source snapshots, predictions and optional labels, plus the monitoring MLflow experiment. These table grants assume trusted producer repositories; they do not provide per-row tenant isolation.

Configure the shared dashboard after the store exists. Its training tables also require training_summary_json in the owned model_version_details view.

docs.title: Retain or clean old Spark references
docs.text:
Prepared Spark monitoring references are stored snapshots of training and source populations. They are separate from source tables and historical monitoring reports. The optional cleanup action considers only references whose saved receipt proves they belong to this project and environment in the configured monitoring store. Nothing is cleaned during ordinary observation.

Projects initialized with a monitoring catalog include a separate monitoring_cleanup job. It runs Sundays at 04:00 UTC with confirmation enabled and a 90-day minimum reference age. This schedule is independent of monitoring and retraining; personal development targets keep it paused. Override these variables in deployment/targets.yml:

monitoring_cleanup_cron: "0 0 4 ? * SUN"
monitoring_cleanup_confirm: "true" # false reports candidates without deleting
monitoring_cleanup_pause_status: UNPAUSED # PAUSED stops the cleanup schedule
monitoring_reference_retention_days: "90"

Setting monitoring_enabled: "false" does not pause cleanup in a configured shared target. Use monitoring_cleanup_pause_status: PAUSED to stop its schedule, or monitoring_cleanup_confirm: "false" to keep reporting candidates without deletion.

The job uses the same monitoring identity, permissions, notifications and serverless environment as observation. It only runs cleanup_references; it does not measure drift or request training. Projects initialized with monitoring off have no cleanup resource. Enable their monitoring destination and use the manual action below, or regenerate with monitoring on to obtain resources/monitoring_cleanup.job.yml and its target settings.

Before deploying an enabled cleanup schedule, meet the lifecycle-writer requirements below. Existing corporate tables are not relocated or removed by changing these defaults.

flowchart TD
    A["Reference receipt in the store"] --> B{"Identity recomputed from this project's inventory matches?"}
    B -- "no" --> K1["Another project's: ignored"]
    B -- "yes" --> C{"Owned, unchanged since creation, same table ids?"}
    C -- "no" --> K2["Skipped with a reason"]
    C -- "yes" --> D{"Still needed? Enrolled anywhere, alias, policy baseline or unfinished retraining"}
    D -- "yes" --> K3["Preserved with a reason"]
    D -- "no" --> E{"Older than reference_retention_days?"}
    E -- "no" --> K3
    E -- "yes" --> F["Deletable"]
    F --> G{"cleanup_confirm=true?"}
    G -- "no" --> L["Dry run: listed with its size"]
    G -- "yes" --> H["Recheck everything; drop only what is still deletable"]
    H --> I["Audit intent; drop retired populations and unused shared source; receipt last; audit result"]

If the inventory, registry aliases or retraining state cannot be read, the run stops before any change.

Start with a dry run from the deployed project:

databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE --params monitoring_action=cleanup_references,reference_retention_days=90,cleanup_confirm=false

Inspect the monitor_model output for candidate tables, size and preservation reasons. The default age is 90 days, measured from receipt creation; accepted values are 1–3650. Change the default with monitoring_reference_retention_days in the target variables. Active enrollment in any project sharing the store, a registered alias, a policy baseline or pending retraining can preserve an old reference. Unknown ownership or missing dependency evidence is never permission to delete it.

Before enabling deletion, upgrade every producer sharing this store to the same admission protocol. Updated generated jobs serialize model alias changes, enrollment, reference publication and confirmed cleanup through one control row in retraining_requests. The row uses Serializable Delta writes; it adds no new store table. A competing mutation waits for the verified owner to release, for up to ten minutes by default. Timeout reports the exact owner and job/task; it never takes over an old lock. SDK callers can set wait_timeout_s from 0 to 3,600 seconds. An uncertain claim/write is not automatically retried. During acquisition, a successful claim that loses to another owner, or a Delta write explicitly rejected with a recognized data-conflict condition, can retry within that same wait budget. Retries use bounded backoff and recheck the physical table identity and ownership. Unknown errors, metadata/protocol changes and contradictory ownership evidence stop the operation; an error message merely containing the word "concurrent" is insufficient. This follows Databricks' documented write-conflict boundary. Some Delta Connect versions omit structured error fields. For those versions, Skyulf accepts only a recognized Delta exception class with its matching, allowlisted condition at the beginning of the message. Any supplied structured condition remains authoritative; malformed or contradictory metadata stops retry. Lifecycle evaluation and quality checks run before admission; the first alias write acquires it and retains it through phase completion and failure cleanup. Training computation and ordinary reference preparation run outside the publication lock. First enrollment of a serving monitor retains its existing prepare-before-enroll order and can hold admission longer while preparing that reference.

This is a cooperative protocol. Restrict alias and reference-table writes to the participating job identities. Pause legacy jobs and external UI/MLflow writers that bypass admission, and wait for them to finish before deleting. A separate job with max_concurrent_runs: 1 does not serialize other jobs.

After reviewing the dry run, use cleanup_confirm=true. The action rechecks dependencies while holding admission, records intent and outcome in the owned reference_cleanup_audit Delta table, drops reference populations and drops their receipt last. Cross-service checks and table drops are not one atomic transaction. A shared source is dropped only by its last retiring receipt, after checking all projects' remaining receipts. Unknown receipt state prevents that deletion. If dropping a population table fails, the receipt remains for investigation and recovery. A failure writing the final audit result can occur after every table, including the receipt, is gone; completed deletions are not rolled back. Inspect the table state and recorded intent before retrying or treating an absent final audit row as proof of no deletion.

The action does not delete source/prediction tables, model versions, monitoring reports, jobs or dashboards. Disabled monitoring can still run cleanup when the store destination is configured; personal development targets remain disabled. The caller needs read access to the store, registry aliases and retraining job state, permission to create/write the audit table, and ownership or equivalent permission to drop the selected references. No new dashboard chart is created.

docs.title: Recover a failed reference mutation
docs.text:
A failed remote request can still finish after its response is lost. Admission therefore remains held after a mutation fails or its driver crashes; there is no expiry timer. Normal completion releases it, as does a validation failure before any protected write started. A held owner temporarily blocks other reference mutations in the same store, including model promotion and enrollment, while ordinary observation reads remain available.

Inspect the row before taking action:

SELECT request_id AS owner, status, created_at_ms, evidence_json
FROM workspace.skyulf_monitoring.retraining_requests
WHERE row_id = 'control:reference_mutation';

Generated tasks record their workspace, job-run ID and task key. Stop the original run, wait for it to terminate, and inspect its alias/table/audit state to resolve uncertain writes. From a separate operator notebook, first preview:

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.observability.monitoring.reference_admission import (
    recover_reference_mutation,
)

workspace = WorkspaceClient()  # The same workspace as the saved holder.
namespace = "workspace.skyulf_monitoring"
rows = spark.sql(
    f"SELECT request_id, status, evidence_json FROM {namespace}.retraining_requests "
    "WHERE row_id = 'control:reference_mutation'"
).collect()
if len(rows) != 1 or rows[0].status != "held":
    raise ValueError("No unique held owner to recover; inspect the store first.")
owner = rows[0].request_id
print(rows[0].evidence_json)

preview = recover_reference_mutation(
    spark, namespace, workspace=workspace, owner=owner
)
print(preview)
print(
    "After inspecting the interrupted operation, run:\n"
    "recover_reference_mutation(spark, namespace, workspace=workspace, "
    f"owner={owner!r}, confirm=True)"
)

The helper verifies the saved workspace, run and task. TERMINATED is accepted. An INTERNAL_ERROR parent is accepted only with a positive end time and all tasks either terminated with end times or skipped; the actual holder task must have terminated. An internal-error label alone cannot prove that workers stopped. Running, terminating, unknown or incomplete task state is rejected. These checks use the Jobs run response. After verifying that the original writer cannot resume, explicitly call the same function with confirm=True. It records a recovery intent, conditionally clears only that exact owner, then records the result in reference_cleanup_audit. Recovery does not retry the interrupted operation or restore deleted tables. Review its partial work before starting a fresh job. An audit failure can occur after release; re-read the control row before retrying.

Direct SDK callers must use hold_reference_mutation(spark, namespace) around alias operations that could activate or retire these references. For recoverable job provenance, also pass job_run_id, task_key and workspace_host together. Custom table writers inside that scope must call require_reference_mutation(spark, namespace, owner) immediately before writing; the yielded owner token binds the write to its admission. Skyulf's registry alias operations perform that check automatically. Manual callers without those fields require verified process shutdown and owner-controlled SQL recovery; the helper cannot prove that a local process has stopped. Never clear an owner merely because its timestamp is old.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text:
Symptom Fix Missing view or CREATE permission error after an upgrade Run owner initialization before upgrading producer jobs; grant viewers SELECT on the refreshed views. Dashboard refresh does not install schema changes. Foreign object, incompatible schema or weak isolation rejected Have the store owner inspect the destination and use the explicit upgrade API. Do not overwrite an unrelated object. No monitoring in a development target Use a shared mode: production target; development deliberately bypasses enrollment and monitoring. Set both monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema. Monitoring is enabled, or one name is set alone. Set both names for the target and redeploy, or set monitoring_enabled: "false" and clear both. Train and score succeed but nothing is monitored Setup left the catalog blank, so monitoring_enabled is "false". Set both names and monitoring_enabled: "true", then redeploy. New reports contain NULL counts Unmeasured values are unavailable. Keep measured zero separate.

New monitoring_results rows store unmeasured counts as SQL NULL: this applies to reference, current, scored and labeled rows, and drifted columns. An explicit zero remains 0. Failed or performance-only observations can omit these counts. Historical rows and retries keep their saved values; upgrading does not backfill old zeros. For custom queries over older reports, check report_json to distinguish an absent count from a measured zero rather than replacing every NULL with 0.

Each project keeps its own Core pin in deployment/requirements.txt. Projects on different pins can share one store, so coordinate view contracts across all of them before an owner upgrade.

docs.title: Look up online features before prediction
When you need it
docs.text:
An online feature model accepts entity keys, lets Databricks fetch current feature values, and then runs the saved Skyulf preprocessing and predictor. An explicit saved policy rejects missing or stale feature values before preprocessing can impute them. This workflow uses the native Databricks Feature Engineering envelope and Online Feature Store.

The saved guard supports raw pandas and Polars model execution. Endpoint admission retains the existing certificate requirement: the fitted artifact must use pandas and supported independent-row preprocessing. The initial online request contract supports non-temporal scalar source inputs. It does not omit required source fields to make an incompatible model appear to accept only keys.

docs.title: Follow the data through the system
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    D["Delta feature table"] --> P["TRIGGERED or CONTINUOUS publication"]
    P --> O["Existing online feature store"]
    K["Request keys and other required inputs"] --> L["Native feature lookup"]
    O --> L
    L --> F["Saved freshness and missing-value checks"]
    F --> M["Saved preprocessing and model"]
    M --> R["Prediction response"]

Training binds the offline feature source to the model. Publication copies the source's values into an online store. Endpoint setup verifies that the model's saved source has an accessible matching publication. At request time Databricks performs the lookup; Skyulf applies the saved validation and prediction logic.

Bundle choice What it adds What you must supply include_online_feature_lookup=true An unscheduled endpoint setup job and training lookup placeholders Lookup fields, freshness policy, registered version and existing publication include_online_publication=true A feature synchronization job Existing source table, source ID, destination and store name online_publication_mode=TRIGGERED Manual or scheduled synchronization; hourly schedule starts paused Run a sync and observe completion before relying on the new values online_publication_mode=CONTINUOUS Start/status/stop/restart controls for native synchronization Start once and inspect propagation and native pipeline health include_daily_rollout=true A separate gradual traffic controller Two serving versions, saved comparison and initialized rollout state

You can use online serving without this project's publication job when another owner publishes the features. Conversely, publishing features does not create a model endpoint. Continuous publication updates features; it is not a continuous prediction job. Rollout is optional for either publication mode.

docs.title: Prepare identities and resources
docs.text:
Use the template's matching Core and Feature Engineering dependencies. On a new workspace, arrange these before running the examples:

Resource or identity Required role in this flow Source and destination UC schemas Existing namespaces with access for the intended owners Offline feature table One row per key, declared non-null primary key, CDF and a feature timestamp Online store Explicitly provisioned and available; copy its exact name into the configuration Training identity Read observations/features and log/register the fitted native feature model Publication identity Read the source and manage its owned online publication Endpoint identity Read the published features and the registered package Endpoint caller Query permission and a request matching the saved input schema

The online store is backed by Lakebase. Provisioning chooses its name and capacity in the authenticated workspace; Bundle selection only references it. See Databricks Online Feature Stores for the current platform provisioning requirements. The examples below use the Skyulf adapter's stricter latest-value, non-temporal contract.

docs.title: Generate, train and set up an online Bundle
docs.text:
