Keep this configuration for scheduled runs; do not supply a period or source version on each invocation. A repeat at the already committed source version makes no target write (noop=True). If the source version advances without new inserts, scoring commits a zero-row receipt (noop=False, both row counts zero) to advance the CDF watermark without changing saved predictions or carry history. An initially empty source also gets this checkpoint. Monitoring treats it as no new prediction batch; configured delayed-label checks still run. If an append succeeds but its acknowledgement is lost, the next run reads its committed receipt and continues after that source version. Source updates and deletes, duplicate keys, a missing or expired change feed, and an unrecognized target commit fail without advancing the watermark. Key uniqueness must hold across all runs, not only within one batch. Oversized increments fail under the same local row/decoded-memory limits; increase the budget deliberately or handle such a source with a separate distributed path. The target receipt is in the same Delta commit as the predictions. This protects participating writers only; changes outside the admission protocol must be handled explicitly.

docs.title: Lag and rolling history across batches
docs.text:
LagFeatures and RollingAggregate default to history_mode="batch": only the supplied frame participates. Set history_mode="carry" in a preprocessing step to save a bounded training tail per entity. Put this step after splitting. The following is one preprocessing-step dictionary inside a pipeline configuration:

{"name": "recent_value", "transformer": "RollingAggregate",
 "params": {"columns": ["value"], "window": 5,
            "sort_by": "observation_time", "group_by": ["entity"],
            "history_mode": "carry",
            "history_max_rows": 1000, "history_max_bytes": 48000}}

Declare the observed value, clock and entity in input_columns. For the Databricks source contract, this clock must be distinct from the job's event_column and record keys. Drop or encode non-model columns after the temporal step. Inputs must be available at prediction time; target-history forecasting is not supported. The clock must be numeric or a typed datetime; parse JSON/string timestamps in an earlier preprocessing step before using them as temporal ordering keys.

  • The artifact seed stays fixed. Lag 3 retains three prior rows per entity; rolling window 5 retains four. Window 1 retains one ordering marker.
  • Training never reads its own saved tail. Temporal holdout and each CV fold use only their own training history. Carry mode requires Time Series CV (or nested Time Series); skipped gap rows do not enter history.
  • Missing or tied entity/time keys and observations at or before the saved entity time are rejected. New entities start with empty history. Returned rows keep request order. drop_na is disallowed; use an imputer instead.
  • Each chained temporal step stores its own input context. Context rows do not enter subsequent imputer/scaler/model fitting or returned predictions.
  • Limits apply across all entities per step: by default 10,000 rows and 1 MiB. Exceeding a limit fails explicitly; inactive entities are not silently evicted.

Incremental Databricks scoring: the default initial complete source snapshot reconstructs history from that snapshot, without prepending the training seed. With initial_scoring="from_now", context starts empty at the checkpoint and is built only from later admitted rows; excluded historical rows do not seed it. Later increments read temporal_history from the last prediction receipt. The new context, source watermark and predictions share one Delta commit. A failed write leaves the prior committed context; a retry reads the actual receipt, and replaying the same source version makes no write. Empty increments at newer source versions retain the committed history in their zero-row receipt. Receipts have a 64 KiB history budget. A changed model or a prior receipt without history requires a fresh target; contexts are never silently mixed across models. This is bounded local batch execution, not Spark worker or streaming state.

Period scoring: run_frame_batch(..., history_state=...) accepts an explicit earlier context. A successful result's manifest contains the next context. Period replacement does not automatically choose another period's history. Retry identity includes the supplied context, so conflicting retries fail.

Core continuation: use score_pipeline_with_history to receive a PipelinePrediction with frame and detached history. Pass that history to the next call. The complete history example shows model reload, JSON transport and equivalence with one complete request. Persist predictions and history atomically, and serialize writers or compare and swap the prior state. Ordinary prediction reuses the immutable training seed; it does not remember earlier calls.

The backend /deployment/predict accepts continue_history=true for the first request and history_state thereafter; its response returns the next state. The caller owns durable storage and request serialization. An HTTP error returns no next state. Custom group/window callbacks still need complete caller-supplied context; built-in carry mode does not create history for arbitrary callbacks.

docs.title: Saved scoring policies and project assets
docs.text:
The rest of this section configures a generated Bundle project, not arguments to WorkflowConfig. Generate it with the Bundle guide, then edit the named project files before training. Saved model versions capture these choices; scoring a prior version does not reload today's files.

Generated projects separate src/features/pre_split.py, preprocessing.py and optional scoring.py helpers. Scoring policy is in config/scoring.yml. Preprocessing fits transformations inside each training fold. Scoring has a three-way mode and an independent target-filter switch:

# config/scoring.yml
version: 1
mode: pre_split
skip_target_pre_split_steps: false
eligibility: []
outputs: []
combined: []

In pre_split or combined, set skip_target_pre_split_steps: true to skip target-reading filters while keeping other pre-split steps. This never changes the predicted target. For example, "price is present" is a training-label check; "floor_area is present" can also be useful when predicting an unknown price. A mixed target/feature filter is skipped whole, because deleting one field would change its meaning. Fixed edits are projected onto feature columns. Preview records skipped names and reused steps.

Reused rules use existing Core implementations and survivor guards on a copy. Accepted original rows go to the model, so its saved normalization runs once. Filter dependencies must exist in scoring input_columns; include a field there and remove it from model features in preprocessing if necessary. Deduplication checks the current batch only. Empty recipes in pre_split mode preserve ordinary output. These choices are saved per model version; changing a local switch does not change the behavior of an already registered model.

Use mode: custom in scoring.yml for custom rules alone, or mode: combined to run pre-split first and custom eligibility only on its survivors. First pre-split exclusion reasons are retained. Custom callbacks receive original accepted inputs; fixed model transformations still run once. All-excluded batches skip custom callbacks and the model; combined mode with no pre-split steps still uses custom rules. Both modes expose the same separate custom sections:

  • eligibility: checks before prediction. A null reason accepts a row; a text reason excludes it. The template shows both required-field and finite inclusive numeric-range checks, using feature_value as an editable example.
  • outputs: rules after prediction. Add fields such as a prediction band. They do not change model predictions or select training data.

Declare built-in checks, bands and custom callback selections in config/scoring.yml; the scoring guide contains a complete example. Empty eligibility/output lists activate no rules. The model captures the YAML and selected source before fitting; saved versions keep their policy after editable files change.

Python-only projects without scoring.yml retain exported build_model_rules() and build_combined_rules() hooks. Legacy build_scoring() remains supported; when both model hook names exist, build_model_rules takes precedence. Returning None explicitly disables scoring rules. Do not define/export these builders alongside scoring.yml; keep only the helpers selected with custom: scoring.fn.

For classification, the band rule can use probability_0, probability_1, etc.; class order comes from the saved artifact manifest. Callbacks are ordinary trusted project functions saved with the model. Eligibility receives (frame, params) and returns a Series of nullable reason strings: null means eligible. The first non-null reason wins in configured order. Output callbacks receive (frame, predictions, params) and return exactly their declared columns, types, rows and index. Supported output types: float64, int64, string, bool. Callbacks receive defensive pandas frames with a RangeIndex for both engines; Core preprocessing and model prediction retain the recorded engine. Rules cannot overwrite raw inputs, estimates, keys or publication metadata. Keep callbacks deterministic; use saved assets instead of mutable files, clocks or network data.

Every source key has an output row. With a scoring policy enabled, that row has scoring_status (predicted/excluded) and nullable exclusion_reason. Excluded rows have null predictions and business outputs. Receipts include predicted_count and excluded_count; output_count counts all outcome rows. An all-excluded increment is a successful atomic publication that advances the source watermark. Failed callbacks/writes advance nothing. Replays cannot publish duplicate keys. Existing targets require the exact output schema, so introduce a new scoring schema using a fresh target. Training, CV and holdout comparison still use the raw predictor and their independently defined population.

Eligibility precedes lag/rolling processing. Excluded observations never enter continuation history. All-excluded batches retain the previous history unchanged. The saved input schema still applies to excluded rows; normalize input types before scoring rather than relying on eligibility to reinterpret an incompatible schema.

docs.title: Deliver lookup files and external Python dependencies
docs.text:
src/features/assets.json includes detailed _help instructions and a files list, initially empty. Create your data file and add its feature-root-relative path, for example "files": ["assets/bands.json"]. The original plain-list format ["assets/bands.json"] also works. Help text is never embedded as model data. Assets can support pre-split, preprocessing or scoring; they do not automatically add a pipeline step. Inside saved code, read a declared file as bytes:

from skyulf.inference.project_package import read_project_asset

payload = read_project_asset(__package__, "assets/bands.json")

Code, encoded file contents and pins share the bounded 64 KiB source snapshot. Paths must remain inside the feature package and asset symlinks are rejected. Undeclared assets, large external model downloads and files outside the package are not embedded. Replacing a local lookup file cannot change an existing model.

Declare exact distribution==version pins in src/features/requirements.txt. Training/load verifies installed versions before executing package code or unpickling the model. The artifact manifest records the pins; MLflow includes them in its saved environment. Provision the same dependencies in the training and scoring job environments; prediction never installs packages. Ranges, URLs, recursive requirement files, options, extras and environment markers are rejected.

docs.title: Train independent target models in one job
docs.text: TrainingBranch and train_branches train several targets from one pinned Delta snapshot and register one candidate per branch. They do not move aliases. A generated multi_target project packages those candidates into one model set that is approved, rolled back and scored as a whole. The model set guide owns the SDK example, the model_set settings, output modes, the replacement rule and set scoring.

docs.title: Diagnose a workflow failure
docs.text:
Symptom Action Preflight model_unresolved Offline preflight cannot read the registry; use prepare_workflow when read access is allowed. Engine/schema mismatch Match the artifact's fit engine and exact raw column order/dtypes; keep keys outside model features. Row/byte budget exceeded Reduce the requested source population or deliberately review a higher limit. Do not silently truncate. Missing recorded dependency Install the saved exact dependency/build before loading; prediction does not install packages. UC permissions failure Verify source, model, target and admission permissions independently for the job identity. Source update/delete during incremental scoring Standalone single-model incremental scoring rejects it; choose a new/rebuilt destination deliberately. Model sets have an explicit rebuild policy. Stale publication or alias expectation Review the intervening commit/role change; do not refresh the expected version automatically. Context required Supply complete group/history context or use the saved carry contract; see context diagnostics.

For REST serving continue to online feature lookup and gradual serving rollout. These are separate endpoint/publication workflows; registering a model or publishing batch rows does not create an endpoint.

Renamed modules, the replaced runtime="local" value and model packages saved with older import paths are covered in project upgrades.

docs.title: Set up a model serving endpoint and SQL function
When you need it
docs.text:
This optional workflow deploys a concrete registered model version, then creates a Unity Catalog SQL function calling its endpoint through ai_query. The endpoint runs the saved preprocessing and prediction code. Callers supply the model's input features, including any features produced by upstream joins or aggregations. The function returns predictions; your application or SQL job owns source selection and destination writes.

Choose prediction_delivery: endpoint or both in detailed Bundle setup to generate the serving_endpoint job. It maintains one endpoint per project and target, then checks real REST and SQL predictions against the saved model. Quick setup defaults to batch. REST serving works independently of the SQL function. The notebook API remains available for explicit, create-only setup.

For a complete endpoint-only project, copy taxi_fare_endpoint. It uses the built-in NYC taxi data, automatically updates serving after champion promotion, and demonstrates SQL requests plus telemetry monitoring. Its serving walkthrough ends at the Online serving dashboard; no batch prediction table is created.

docs.title: Choose how predictions are produced
docs.text:
Setup choice Generated prediction jobs Monitoring batch (default) score Batch observations through the monitoring job endpoint serving_endpoint; no batch schedule, prediction table or score handoff The monitoring job reads logged requests after enrollment both score and serving_endpoint, independently Both sources in the same monitoring store

The monitoring job is retained in every mode. Changing delivery mode changes the generated job graph: regenerate and review the project before deployment. Endpoint-only projects retain config/inference.yml for the smoke source and, for model sets, the registered parent identity and composition settings.

Path Runs where Use it for Cost model Batch score job, batch_compute: single_node One Python process on job compute Scheduled or handoff scoring of a bounded table Job compute while it runs Batch score job, batch_compute: spark Spark workers via mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf; no endpoint Large scheduled scoring into Delta Job compute while it runs REST endpoint (this page) Databricks Model Serving Applications needing one request at a time Endpoint compute while provisioned; scale to zero is enabled by default SQL function with ai_query (this page) Model Serving, called from SQL Analysts, SQL jobs and dashboards querying the endpoint Endpoint plus the SQL warehouse or cluster

The batch job never calls an endpoint, and the endpoint never writes the prediction table: an ai_query caller decides where results go, for example CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT score_fn(...). Spark workers and endpoints both run the saved pandas pipeline on independent batches, so both admit only the steps and models listed in Spark scoring support.

Additional built-in models, voting/stacking and eligible preprocessing recipes need the training evidence described in built-in recipes and model evidence. Selecting the endpoint job enables defaults.allow_tested_custom_steps: true in config/training.yml. For an existing endpoint-only project, enable it before training. Spark and online-feature projects already enable it. prepare_pinned_endpoint recomputes the certificate from the exact registered package; changing a serving setting cannot admit an old model without evidence. Missing or changed evidence requires retraining and registering a new version. Inspect partition_probe.json in that training run: the model and built-in step records explain what was checked. Serving uses the same model_probed and apply_probed_builtin certificate actions as Spark.

flowchart LR
    A["prepare_pinned_endpoint"] --> B["create_pinned_endpoint"]
    B --> C["require_pinned_endpoint_ready"]
    C --> D["query_named_records: REST"]
    C --> E["create_serving_sql_function"]
    E --> F["SQL SELECT with ai_query"]

For entity-key requests, first prepare and publish the model's online features, then use the online setup commands on this page. Change traffic gradually through the separate daily rollout workflow.

docs.title: Raw-input models and optional prediction tables
docs.text:
The model's saved input schema determines what callers send. If the complete pipeline was fitted on raw columns, its admitted feature generation and fitted preprocessing run inside the model. Callers do not repeat those transformations or create a merged feature table. Spark joins and historical feature-table calculations performed before that pipeline are not automatically included.

Training does not require a prediction sink. Choose prediction_delivery: endpoint to omit the batch job and its output configuration. REST calls and SQL functions return results. A separate caller decides whether to publish them with a DataFrame write or CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
File or input Set before running config/serving.yml → serving_endpoint Enablement, automatic handoff, logging, compute, SQL function, caller grants and sample size config/inference.yml → score_source_table Existing table containing every raw input in the saved model signature deployment/requirements.txt Runtime matching the registered model's producer deployment/variables.yml / target overrides Serving job timeout, compute policy, cost attribution and job permissions config/serving.yml → online_feature_lookup Separate online-lookup setup, only when selected

Use deployment identities and access for the Bundle and the permissions below for REST/SQL.

docs.title: Run the Bundle serving job
docs.text:
Detailed setup → prediction_delivery: endpoint or both supports certified pandas single models, competition winners and model sets. Quick setup creates batch scoring; Polars training is not admitted. Online lookup and rollout are separate options.

After training and champion approval, run from the generated project. Substitute your target and authenticated profile:

databricks bundle validate --strict -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle deploy -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
databricks bundle run serving_endpoint -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE
# Explicit version instead of resolving champion:
databricks bundle run serving_endpoint -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE --params model_version=7
  • Automatic: completed champion initialization, promotion or rollback, including daily-rollout promotion, submits a separate serving run in every target. Personal development targets do too: their endpoint and SQL function names carry the per-user resource suffix, so each developer gets their own endpoint and never changes a shared one. They need cost_tag_value like any target. Pending/rejected/unchanged candidates do not. The receipt pins the numeric version; submission retries are idempotent.
  • Manual: follow_champion: false, or champion changes made outside the template. Batch follow_champion in config/inference.yml is independent when both is selected.
  • Check the child run: training waits only for submission and retains its timeout. Open the returned serving run ID and inspect serving_result.

The dispatch tasks exist whenever the endpoint job is generated. Toggle serving_endpoint.follow_champion in YAML and deploy that file; the toggle does not require regenerating the graph and does not compare against a frozen job value.

docs.title: Automatic monitoring enrollment
docs.text:
To enroll automatically, set the target's monitoring_enabled: "true" and use logging_mode: telemetry or ai_gateway. Configure monitoring_catalog and monitoring_schema before running the job; these are validated before endpoint changes when enrollment is enabled. After reference, REST and optional SQL parity passes, it enrolls the served concrete version in that existing monitoring store. A model set gets one registration per branch, with parent name/version/branch attribution. Reruns reuse the same identities; prior registrations for this endpoint and project/target are disabled after the new enrollment succeeds. Their history, unrelated endpoints and batch registrations are preserved.

The result reports enrollment status. With monitoring_enabled: "false" or an absent flag, it reports monitoring_disabled and skips all monitoring work, preserving existing registrations. Endpoint logging and verification still run. When monitoring is enabled, logging_mode: disabled reports logging_disabled. The target's paused monitoring schedule still remains paused. Enrollment alone does not create observations: send requests, wait for payload delivery, then run the monitoring job. The Online serving dashboard reads those saved observations. Performance needs matching outcome labels. See serving monitoring for access and label contracts.

docs.title: Three caller recipes
docs.text: Merge one recipe into the generated serving_endpoint section; retain its names and target bindings. Examples assume one amount input. For your model, copy the job's generated examples with every required field.

docs.title: SQL with ai_query
docs.text:
serving_endpoint:
  # SQL access without request logging tables.
  sql_function:
    enabled: true
  logging_mode: disabled
  permissions:
    - group_name: risk_readers
      level: CAN_QUERY

The job adds endpoint CAN_QUERY and function EXECUTE. Callers also need USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA, which the job does not grant.

SELECT main.ml.risk_score(`amount` => s.`amount`) AS result
FROM main.source.customers AS s;

docs.title: REST for applications
docs.text:
serving_endpoint:
  # Replace the application ID with your service principal's ID.
  sql_function:
    enabled: false
  logging_mode: disabled
  permissions:
    - service_principal_name: APPLICATION_ID
      level: CAN_QUERY

To capture requests, choose telemetry and fill the three logging destination keys below before creating the endpoint. Credentials stay in the environment:

curl --fail-with-body --request POST \
  "${DATABRICKS_HOST}/serving-endpoints/risk-test-endpoint/invocations" \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer ${DATABRICKS_TOKEN}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"dataframe_records": [{"amount": 12.5}]}'

docs.title: Python SDK for notebooks and jobs
docs.text:
serving_endpoint:
  # Use the notebook/job caller's group.
  sql_function:
    enabled: false
  logging_mode: disabled
  permissions:
    - group_name: risk_readers
      level: CAN_QUERY

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

result = WorkspaceClient().serving_endpoints.query(
    name="risk-test-endpoint", dataframe_records=[{"amount": 12.5}]
)
print(result.predictions)

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
All keys below belong to config/serving.yml → serving_endpoint.

Key Generated default Meaning enabled true when selected Enable the job's work follow_champion true Automatically update after a completed champion change in production; false means manual runs only endpoint_name Project + target + suffix Stable endpoint; personal suffixes use hyphens model_name Target's model or model-set name Concrete UC registered model identity tracking_uri / registry_uri databricks / databricks-uc Package lookup workload_type / workload_size CPU / Small Endpoint compute, independent of job compute scale_to_zero_enabled true Reduce idle compute; cold starts remain possible ready_timeout_s 3600 Endpoint readiness deadline logging_mode disabled No inference tables or captured-request monitoring; alternatives: telemetry, ai_gateway logging_catalog / logging_schema / logging_table_prefix Empty when disabled Separate payload sink, required for logged modes sql_function.enabled / sql_function.name true / target's score function Create and smoke-test SQL; false leaves REST/SDK only permissions [] Additive caller grants; one user, group or service principal per entry. A list applies to every target; a mapping keyed by target (test:, prod: ...) grants each target its own principals, and an unlisted target grants nothing verification.sample_rows 20 Collected sample size, from 1 to 1000

Use verification: {sample_rows: 20} to set how many source rows the job checks. Older smoke.rows and selection keys are rejected. The job uses the current champion unless you pass --params model_version=<version> for that run.

To change automatic updates, edit serving_endpoint.follow_champion in YAML and deploy the updated file. The endpoint job's existing dispatch tasks remain in place in either mode.

docs.title: Operational rules
docs.text:
• Input and proof: config/inference.yml → score_source_table must already contain the saved raw inputs after any upstream joins. Hash ordering spreads the bounded sample but still scans the source. Empty samples and infinite reference predictions fail before endpoint changes. The same records run through the saved pyfunc, REST and enabled SQL path. Counts, fields and discrete values match exactly; floats allow rtol=1e-10, atol=1e-12 for rounding. Null transport follows the saved package. No batch scoring or Delta write occurs.
  • Result: action, concrete model URI, logging destination, SQL action, comparison counts under verification and runnable examples. Output includes one sampled input record. This smoke check does not replace holdout evaluation or monitoring.
  • Ownership: one entity at 100% traffic; foreign names, pending updates, conflicting logging/runtime settings and rollout/online endpoints are refused. Reserve tags project, target, suffix, managed_by; use one deployment writer. SQL ownership comes from its managed comment. Only schema/transport changes replace its definition; caller arguments may then need updating.
  • Identity and grants: the job needs model/table read access, endpoint management and function create/update rights. Shared targets use the shared SP or, with separate identities, scoring SP. Preserve training's CAN_MANAGE_RUN in serving_permissions. Removing a caller from YAML does not revoke access; change endpoint permissions and explicitly REVOKE EXECUTE when needed. When groups differ per workspace, key permissions by target so each deployment grants only groups that exist there:
permissions:
  test:
    - group_name: test-callers
  prod:
    - group_name: prod-callers
    - service_principal_name: <application-id>

Every entry is validated in every target, and the project smoke check rejects a key that is not a target in deployment/targets.yml. SQL callers also need USE CATALOG/USE SCHEMA on the function's schema and a SQL warehouse; the job grants only EXECUTE and endpoint CAN_QUERY. - Compute and cost: job compute follows serverless/policy_cluster settings. Set cost_tag_value before serving, including serverless targets; its placeholder is rejected. Do not use an ownership key as cost_tag_key. Set Bundle serving_timeout_seconds (default 7200) to at least ready_timeout_s + 300 and redeploy. Endpoint, maintenance and SQL-call costs are separate from logging. - Logging and retirement: existing notebook/online APIs retain telemetry defaults. This job refuses changing an existing endpoint's logging mode; use a separately named endpoint. Before retirement, set follow_champion: false, deliberately delete the endpoint and drop its function. Bundle job removal does not delete these resources; retain logs according to your policy. - Recovery: a failed smoke can leave the new version serving. Rerun with --params model_version=<previous_version> from the deployment result or endpoint configuration history (failed runs may have no final summary). Recovery is explicit and leaves champion unchanged.

docs.title: The command
docs.text: This advanced path creates a new endpoint and SQL function explicitly. It keeps the create-only behavior; use the Bundle job above for managed version updates.

docs.title: 1. Inspect the model and prepare the endpoint
docs.text:
Install deployment/requirements.txt with uv pip install -r in your notebook environment. Use the same Skyulf source runtime that packaged the registered model: admission checks source provenance, fitted artifact digest, partition safety, named input/output signature and nullable transport. Updating the local library does not silently upgrade an old model package. Repackage and register a new version with the intended runtime when necessary.

Supported packages are certified local pipelines (including a selected competition winner) and model sets. Admission is stricter than “any MLflow model”. Spark-native models, stateful/batch-dependent preprocessing and native feature lookup envelopes are not automatically admitted by this bridge.

Edit the explicit identifiers below. Use a separate endpoint and function name for each release so existing callers continue to use their selected version.

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.serving import (
    PinnedEndpointSpec,
    build_serving_sql_function,
    create_pinned_endpoint,
    create_serving_sql_function,
    prepare_pinned_endpoint,
    query_named_records,
    require_pinned_endpoint_ready,
)

client = WorkspaceClient()  # Notebook workspace identity, never embed a token.
spec = PinnedEndpointSpec(
    endpoint_name="risk-v7",
    model_name="models.risk.customer_risk",
    model_version="7",  # Concrete numeric version, not @champion or latest.
    logging_catalog="ops",
    logging_schema="serving",
    logging_table_prefix="risk_v7",
)
endpoint = prepare_pinned_endpoint(spec, tracking_uri="databricks", registry_uri="databricks-uc")
print("Inputs:", endpoint.input_schema)
print("Outputs:", endpoint.output_schema)
print("Endpoint configuration:", endpoint.config)

function = build_serving_sql_function(endpoint, "models.api.score_risk_v7")
print(function.create_sql)  # Inspect complete DDL before creating anything.

Preparation reads the registry but creates no endpoint or function. The generated SQL uses the inspected schema, not an independently maintained feature list. Fields must have simple names (letters, digits, underscores; no leading digit) and must be unique ignoring case. Reserved words are quoted. Supported primitive types are boolean, int32/int64, float32/float64 and string, including supported pandas/Polars aliases. Unsupported types fail before SQL execution.

For CPU custom models, the helper configures telemetry_config with sampling_fraction: 1.0. Databricks creates the <prefix>_payload inference view over its managed <prefix>_otel_logs Delta table. A workspace may reject the ai_gateway.inference_table_config path; set logging_mode="ai_gateway" only for a workspace that supports it. The helper never falls back automatically. Retain the endpoint, concrete model version and payload view name together: registry aliases can move independently of logged requests. See serving observation setup, Databricks custom-model telemetry and fast inference tables.

docs.title: Payload logging and the inference table
docs.text:
Logging belongs to the endpoint, not to the caller: every request that reaches it is logged the same way, whether it comes from REST or from an ai_query SQL call. Choose it with logging_mode on PinnedEndpointSpec, or with online_feature_lookup.endpoint.logging_mode in config/serving.yml; setup does not ask.

logging_mode What Databricks creates in <logging_catalog>.<logging_schema> When to choose it Rollout and serving monitoring telemetry (default) Raw <prefix>_otel_logs, _otel_spans and _otel_metrics tables, plus a <prefix>_payload view over the logs. Every request is logged (sampling_fraction: 1.0). New projects; the custom-model telemetry path Databricks recommends Available ai_gateway A <prefix>_payload Delta table written by AI Gateway, plus usage tracking Your organization already standardizes on AI Gateway inference tables, or telemetry is unavailable Available; some workspaces reject this path for custom models disabled Nothing Callers store predictions themselves, for example with ai_query Rejected with an explicit error

Both logged modes expose the requests as <prefix>_payload, which is what Skyulf reads. A rejected mode fails endpoint creation; Skyulf never switches to the other mode automatically, so the log location stays explicit.

The payload view holds raw request/response records and arrives with a delay of minutes. The batch score job is separate: it never calls the endpoint and always writes its configured prediction_table.

docs.title: Serve without an inference table
docs.text: Set logging_mode="disabled" when callers own prediction storage, for example an ai_query job that writes its own table with CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT score_fn(...). The endpoint is created with no telemetry or AI Gateway inference table, and the logging_* fields may be empty. Readiness checks then reject an endpoint that does log payloads. Daily rollout and serving monitoring read those payload logs, so they reject a disabled endpoint with an explicit error.

docs.title: Write your own prediction table with ai_query
docs.text:
The SQL function from step 3 already wraps ai_query with the model's typed inputs: it sends numeric NULLs as NaN and nullable integers/booleans as text, so the saved imputation still applies (a bare ai_query would send a NULL number as 0). Every input row returns exactly one result; the endpoint never drops rows. A model with a fitted outlier step or PowerTransformer can return a result with an empty prediction, scoring_status = excluded and an exclusion_reason such as outlier:<step name> or invalid:<step name> (see rows that are not scored). Handle that case explicitly in the caller; do not treat the empty prediction as zero. Keep keys outside the call so results join back. call_sql() renders the call for a table alias:

-- Full refresh
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE gold.trip_scores AS
SELECT s.trip_id, s.pickup_month,
       models.api.score_fare_v7(`pickup_hour` => s.`pickup_hour`,
                                `trip_distance` => s.`trip_distance`) AS result,
       current_timestamp() AS scored_at
FROM bronze.trips s;

-- Monthly incremental: rerunning the same month replaces it instead of duplicating it
DELETE FROM gold.trip_scores WHERE pickup_month = 2;
INSERT INTO gold.trip_scores (trip_id, pickup_month, result, scored_at)
SELECT s.trip_id, s.pickup_month, models.api.score_fare_v7(...), current_timestamp()
FROM bronze.trips s WHERE s.pickup_month = 2;

For one row per key, MERGE INTO gold.latest USING (<the SELECT above>) AS s ON t.trip_id = s.trip_id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT .... Replace the argument list with your function's real call_sql() output. These tables are yours: Skyulf monitoring reads its own prediction tables or the endpoint payload logs, not caller-written tables.

docs.title: 2. Create the REST endpoint and check readiness
docs.text:
ready = create_pinned_endpoint(client, endpoint)  # Create once and wait for readiness.

Databricks builds the endpoint asynchronously. This helper polls for readiness using endpoint.spec.ready_timeout_s (3600 seconds by default), then returns the ready endpoint. It requires READY and NOT_UPDATING and checks the exact model version, workload and logging configuration. A failed native update or an API error remaining after the SDK's own retries propagates. The polling timeout does not interrupt an HTTP request already in progress: the injected SDK client's HTTP timeout and retry budget are separate. A ready response received from that in-flight request can complete the wait after the polling deadline. Configure the client's transport limits when elapsed request time also needs a tighter bound.

If the wait expires, TimeoutError leaves the endpoint intact. Inspect the endpoint page and its build logs. Resume waiting for the same admitted plan:

from skyulf.integrations.databricks.serving import wait_for_pinned_endpoint_ready

ready = wait_for_pinned_endpoint_ready(client, endpoint)

For one immediate check without waiting:

require_pinned_endpoint_ready(client, endpoint)

Prediction and SQL enrollment use this immediate check. Do not repeatedly call creation: an existing endpoint name is rejected. The helper does not overwrite endpoints or change model aliases.

The default is CPU/Small with scale-to-zero enabled. Idle endpoints can stop serving compute after the platform's inactivity interval, and the next request can incur a cold start. This is separate from SQL warehouse compute and billing. See Databricks custom model serving.

For an inspected model whose only input is x: float64, a REST probe is:

response = query_named_records(client, endpoint, [{"x": 1.5}])
print(response.predictions)

Replace that example with all and only your model's input fields. REST records use native JSON scalars except fitted nullable Int32, Int64, boolean and Boolean columns: those use canonical strings (e.g. "42", "true") or None, matching the saved package. The SQL wrapper handles this encoding for you.

docs.title: 3. Create the SQL function
docs.text:
Use a Databricks Spark session and SDK client from the same workspace:

create_serving_sql_function(spark, client, function)

The helper checks endpoint readiness/version before submitting CREATE FUNCTION. It never uses OR REPLACE or IF NOT EXISTS: an existing function is an error, so a stale implementation cannot be silently reused. SQL creation errors are propagated without retries. After successful creation, rerun the SELECT below as often as needed; creation is not part of every prediction query.

For a SQL warehouse, run require_pinned_endpoint_ready first and execute the printed function.create_sql in the SQL editor. This path requires a Pro or Serverless SQL warehouse; ai_query is unavailable on SQL Classic. Supported Databricks Runtime compute requires 15.4 LTS or later. Verify workspace/region availability in the ai_query reference.

The SQL wrapper calls the endpoint name, not a UC model URI. The model version is checked at deployment, but an endpoint administrator can change it afterwards. Restrict endpoint management rights and retain one endpoint per model release. The SQL function cannot atomically enforce the version on each call. Run require_pinned_endpoint_ready before a controlled batch as an additional check.

docs.title: 4. Call it from a table
docs.text:
# These names stand for your existing table with the model's input feature columns.
expression = function.call_sql(table_alias="source")
print(expression)
scored = spark.sql(
    f"SELECT source.customer_id, {expression} AS result "
    "FROM analytics.features.customer_inputs AS source LIMIT 10"
)
display(scored)

Copy the printed expression into your own SQL job. It uses named arguments, so source-table column order does not control feature order. The wrapper builds named_struct in saved model order and declares returnType explicitly. SQL arguments use the fitted types; nullable integer/boolean values are cast directly to canonical strings without a floating-point conversion. Their nulls stay null. For floating-point inputs, the wrapper represents SQL nulls as a same-width NaN before calling ai_query, so the saved preprocessing handles missing values. This prevents the numeric-null-to-zero behavior reproduced in native testing. It does not fill values with a new SQL-side mean or constant. Use matching source types: SQL's argument coercion is not a data validation layer.

result is the named per-row prediction struct, not the REST predictions array. Its fields match endpoint.output_schema: e.g. result.prediction, probability fields, model-set outputs and saved project-scoring status fields when present. A single model, a registered competition winner and an admitted model set use the same SQL API; the saved output schema determines the returned fields.

docs.title: Set up an online Bundle endpoint
docs.text:
First complete online Bundle training and publication. This endpoint setup job exists only when initialization selected include_online_feature_lookup: "true". It is unscheduled and never creates a publication.

Take the concrete registered version from the training result and complete online_feature_lookup in config/serving.yml:

online_feature_lookup:
  enabled: true
  exclusive_writer: true
  tracking_uri: databricks
  registry_uri: databricks-uc
  endpoint:
    endpoint_name: customer-online-v3
    model_name: models.risk.customer_online
    model_version: "3"
    workload_type: CPU
    workload_size: Small
    scale_to_zero_enabled: true
    ready_timeout_s: 3600
    logging_catalog: ops
    logging_schema: serving
    logging_table_prefix: customer_online_v3
    logging_mode: telemetry
  publications:
    - source_table: features.customer.customer_features
      source_table_id: "REPLACE_WITH_DESCRIBE_DETAIL_ID"
      online_table: features.online.customer_features
      online_store: customer-features
      publish_mode: TRIGGERED # Match the existing publication; use CONTINUOUS for a stream.

Use actual resolved UC names here; the source table must be the model's saved lookup source with the same Delta identity. Configure exclusive endpoint writer permissions before setting exclusive_writer: true. The setup identity must be able to inspect the source, publication and store; the serving identity also needs access to the online features. Grant visibility of all publications for these sources and prevent concurrent publication changes during setup. UC enumeration covers the setup identity's visible inventory, not hidden resources. Setup rejects missing, mismatched or ambiguous accessible publications and requires evidence of a completed first sync before admitting creation. It reports a validation error while the first sync is incomplete; it does not poll or republish.

databricks bundle deploy -t test
databricks bundle run online_feature_lookup_setup -t test

The setup result reports READY, model_uri, input_schema and a typed request_example derived from the actual native signature. Replace its example values with a real entity and all other required request values, then send that request body to POST /serving-endpoints/customer-online-v3/invocations or use query_named_records in the SDK example below. Endpoint readiness does not establish that every requested entity has current features; the saved lookup policy checks that at prediction time. Rerunning setup never overwrites an existing endpoint. On timeout, inspect the existing endpoint and resume an explicit wait; do not rerun creation with the same name.

Save the returned request_example object as request.json, replace its sample values, and query after the endpoint reports readiness:

databricks serving-endpoints get customer-online-v3
databricks serving-endpoints query customer-online-v3 --json @request.json

Required source metadata can survive in the native signature, even when excluded from estimator inputs. Inspect input_schema; do not assume every model accepts keys alone. Direct REST callers can override fetched values. Freshness validation checks the received values and does not attest their source.

docs.title: Endpoint compute and setup timeout
docs.text:
These settings belong to online_feature_lookup.endpoint. They are also keyword arguments of PinnedEndpointSpec for a regular endpoint without online lookup.

Setting Default Supported values and effect workload_type CPU CPU, CPU_MEDIUM, CPU_LARGE: CPU memory tiers. Availability depends on your Databricks workspace. GPU model packages are outside this setup. workload_size Small Small, Medium, Large: serving capacity. Larger sizes can cost more; choose using your measured traffic. scale_to_zero_enabled true A YAML boolean. Set false to keep serving compute provisioned while idle; true permits cold starts. Some workspaces require true; platform restrictions are returned as errors. ready_timeout_s 3600 A positive integer in seconds. Controls the setup wait only; it does not change request timeout or get sent as an endpoint setting.

For example, to keep a Medium endpoint warm and allow 30 minutes for startup:

workload_type: CPU
workload_size: Medium
scale_to_zero_enabled: false
ready_timeout_s: 1800

Place those four lines under online_feature_lookup.endpoint. A changed YAML file does not update an existing endpoint. Setup is create-only: use a new endpoint name and explicitly move your callers after verifying it. A daily rollout must use the same workload type, size and scale-to-zero setting for champion and challenger; each plan can have its own client-side wait timeout.

To seed these values during Bundle initialization, the answer-file keys are serving_workload_type, serving_workload_size, serving_scale_to_zero_enabled and serving_ready_timeout_s. All four are hidden from interactive questions but accepted in an answer JSON file. As with other initialization answers, use strings there (for example "false" and "1800"); the generated serving.yml contains typed booleans and integers. The generated setup job and task also have a total runtime cap, controlled by the existing Bundle variable monitoring_timeout_seconds (7200 by default). Keep that cap above ready_timeout_s plus model/publication inspection time. Increasing the wait in YAML alone cannot extend the Databricks job deadline. See Databricks endpoint configuration for the platform's compute and readiness behavior.

docs.title: Admit and query the registered package
docs.text:
The following SDK route is an alternative to the Bundle's online_feature_lookup_setup job. Register the native outer package, then inspect a concrete version:

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.serving import (
    PinnedEndpointSpec,
    create_pinned_endpoint,
    prepare_online_endpoint,
    query_named_records,
    require_pinned_endpoint_ready,
)

workspace = WorkspaceClient()
spec = PinnedEndpointSpec(
    endpoint_name="customer-risk-online",
    model_name="models.risk.customer_risk_online",
    model_version="3",
    logging_catalog="ops",
    logging_schema="serving",
    logging_table_prefix="customer_risk_online",
)
plan = prepare_online_endpoint(
    spec, tracking_uri="databricks", registry_uri="databricks-uc"
)
print(plan.input_schema)
create_pinned_endpoint(workspace, plan)  # Once, using a new endpoint name.

After deployment is ready:

require_pinned_endpoint_ready(workspace, plan)
response = query_named_records(workspace, plan, [{"customer_id": 42}])
print(response)

The example request is valid only if the inspected input schema requires exactly customer_id. Native Feature Engineering can retain excluded training-source columns in its outer signature. Supply every field reported by plan.input_schema, or train from a narrower source. Temporal/date and binary source inputs are rejected by this bridge. The endpoint identity must have permission to read the required online features.

The helper's exact schema excludes feature overrides. Direct native REST calls can still provide feature values, including a freshness value. The saved guard checks the values it receives; it cannot prove that those values came from the online store after enrichment. Restrict direct endpoint access or use an application boundary if your application must prohibit caller overrides.

docs.title: Validate your endpoint
docs.text:
The serving smoke reader converts Spark DECIMAL model values using the same float64 rule as training and batch prediction. The saved signature determines JSON numbers and SQL DOUBLE arguments. See conversion evidence and precision. deployment/serving-requirements.txt pins the tested Databricks SDK; install this job environment rather than relying on the SDK preinstalled in a compute runtime.

Compare direct saved-model, REST and SQL predictions using the same representative inputs. Include nulls, reordered named columns, integer limits and keys, and all component/composition outputs used by your application. Check strict and captured error behavior without treating an error result as a valid prediction.

Use the actual caller identity to verify access rules. For classification, inspect labels and every probability column; for production capacity, measure cold starts, scale-to-zero behavior and sustained load. Recipe admission does not establish these endpoint-specific properties. Keep the concrete model version and request schema fixed during the comparison.

Automatic enrollment for the Bundle job and manual enrollment for other endpoints are documented in serving observations and enrollment.

docs.title: Errors and privileges
docs.text:
Default fail_on_error=True stops the query on an endpoint error. To inspect row-level endpoint failures, create a different function with capture enabled:

capture = build_serving_sql_function(
    endpoint, "models.api.score_risk_v7_checked", fail_on_error=False
)
print(capture.create_sql)
create_serving_sql_function(spark, client, capture)

This function returns {response: <prediction struct>, errorMessage: STRING}. On endpoint success, errorMessage is null. On an endpoint error, response is null. Authorization, SQL and other non-endpoint failures can still fail the whole query. Preserve and inspect errors before writing accepted predictions. See Databricks error behavior.

  • The deployer needs appropriate model/endpoint creation and logging destination permissions. Existing endpoint preparation also needs registry/artifact access.
  • The function creator needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, CREATE FUNCTION in the function's schema, and endpoint CAN QUERY; the SDK readiness check also requires endpoint visibility. The endpoint must be in the SQL workspace.
  • Function callers need USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and EXECUTE on the function, plus permissions for their own source reads, destination writes and compute. Databricks documents the ai_query definer's endpoint permission; verify the intended caller identity in your workspace before sharing the function.
  • Skyulf does not grant permissions or create catalogs/schemas here. An owner can grant EXECUTE ON FUNCTION models.api.score_risk_v7 TO ... explicitly.

See Unity Catalog UDF permissions and SQL function creation.

Symptom What to check Preparation rejects source/digest/signature Correct concrete model package and matching Skyulf runtime; do not bypass admission. Endpoint not ready/config mismatch Endpoint deployment state, build logs and exact version/configuration. Function already exists Use a new release name or deliberately manage the old function yourself. SQL permission/unsupported feature error Caller/definer privileges, warehouse/runtime and workspace preview availability. Missing field or type error Compare source fields with endpoint.input_schema; inspect SQL coercions. Row returns errorMessage Endpoint response/build logs; preserve the failed row for diagnosis. First invocation is slow Cold start and endpoint capacity; retry only under your workload's policy.

For missing or stale online features, use the feature guard checks. For traffic decisions, inspect the daily rollout evidence.

docs.title: Monitor serving requests and logged predictions
When you need it
docs.text:
For REST deployment and typed SQL function/ai_query calls, follow Deploy and call a model. The optional helper uses one concrete registered model version and derives SQL input/output types from its inspected package.

The generated serving_endpoint job automatically enrolls its concrete version after successful verification when payload logging is enabled and the target's monitoring_enabled variable is "true". Configure the shared monitoring catalog/schema first. For a model set it enrolls every branch; updating the endpoint disables its prior registrations while retaining history. No separate enroll_serving run is needed for this job. Send requests and run the monitoring job to create observations; enrollment itself does not populate traffic charts. prediction_delivery: endpoint keeps monitoring without a batch score job.

Set monitoring_enabled: "false" in the target variables to skip automatic enrollment while keeping endpoint logging and REST/SQL verification enabled. An absent flag also disables enrollment. The serving result reports monitoring_disabled; no monitoring namespace, reference or inventory work runs, and existing registrations remain unchanged. Only exact "true" and "false" values are accepted. When monitoring is enabled but payload logging is disabled, the result instead reports logging_disabled.

For an endpoint created outside that job, first prepare and create a pinned endpoint with full payload capture. Keep its concrete model version, endpoint name and payload view together; a registry alias can move independently of requests already logged. Endpoint creation, runtime admission and logging-mode selection are described on that serving page.

Every inventory reader sharing that monitoring namespace must run a Core release with serving support before the first serving enrollment. This includes other projects' monitoring jobs and any custom inventory readers. A reader without serving support rejects the serving fields, even in another project's entry. The score job's prepare_monitoring task does not load the shared inventory, so it is not affected. A dashboard update does not change reader runtimes. Keep training/scoring runtime changes separate when their saved artifact certificates require the original packaged source.

flowchart LR
    A["Pinned endpoint with payload logging"] --> B["Payload view"]
    B --> C["Serving job enrollment or manual enroll_serving"]
    C --> D["Scheduled monitoring job: observe"]
    D --> E["Saved serving report"]
    E --> F["Dashboard: Online serving"]

This page covers enrollment and observations. Daily serving rollout is the single policy guide for traffic increases, holds, rollback and restart.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
Match environment and project to this job's target and bundle name. The job compares them with the deployed target and project and rejects a mismatch, so an entry with "environment": "prod" works only with -t prod. Set reference_namespace to its configured monitoring catalog and schema. The source and prediction names are the same inference payload view. For CPU custom models that object is the Databricks-managed risk_payload view; its backing risk_otel_logs is a managed Delta table. Grant the monitoring job read access to both the view and its backing Delta table, plus system.serving.served_entities for actual model-version attribution. The job also needs the usual catalog/schema usage privileges and read access to the configured labels and saved training references. Do not rename, replace, alter or delete either Databricks-owned object, including its schema or internal checkpoints. Monitoring verifies the pinned view and backing Delta identity before reading; enrollment does not copy or modify the serving logs. Enrollment validates the entire list (1-100 distinct models), prepares verified training references, and saves the enrollments to the shared inventory. It does not observe, publish an observation reference, or request training in that run. Later scheduled monitoring_action=observe runs select active batch and online enrollments together and use the existing report, policy and dashboard.

For manually enrolled endpoints with two served versions, add a separate entry for each concrete version and endpoint. A model-set branch needs its own entry with model_set_name, model_set_version and model_set_branch identifying the parent release and output. Labels are provided independently in a Delta table keyed by databricks_request_id and zero-based request_row_index, with the actual target column and UTC available_at. Skyulf does not generate outcomes or write them back to the training table. Missing or late labels remain unavailable until an eligible observation; choose mode: report first and make any retraining policy an explicit later decision.

Keep performance in report mode initially. The inline online policy determines its measured verdict; automatic requests also require the deployment gate described in guarded retraining. Retraining alone does not update an endpoint. After a completed champion change, the independently configured serving handoff can submit its update job in production mode.

To retire or pause one online enrollment, resubmit its complete JSON entry with enabled: false using monitoring_action=enroll_serving. Keep the endpoint, model/version and parent branch identity unchanged. Disabling does not require loading its model or preparing references, so an unavailable model or reference cannot prevent the pause. Other batch and online enrollments remain active.

This optional bridge covers pinned serving and monitoring; it does not imply that every serving or feature lookup flow is automatically deployed.

docs.title: The command
docs.text:
In Databricks Jobs, open the generated monitoring job and use Run now with different parameters for this enrollment action. Supply the job parameter names and complete JSON below; replace the example identities. This is a cloud operation.

Run this project's existing monitoring job once with job parameter monitoring_action=enroll_serving and monitoring_serving_enrollments set to a JSON list. One entry, for an endpoint whose telemetry prefix is risk, can be the following. It targets test, matching the run command below:

[
  {
    "environment": "test",
    "project": "risk",
    "model_name": "models.risk.churn",
    "model_version": "2",
    "serving_endpoint": "risk-v2",
    "source_table": "logs.serving.risk_payload",
    "prediction_table": "logs.serving.risk_payload",
    "execution_engine": "spark",
    "reference_namespace": "ops.monitoring",
    "label_table": "labels.production.serving_outcomes",
    "result_available_at_column": "available_at",
    "performance_policy": {
      "mode": "report",
      "metric": "f1_weighted",
      "direction": "higher",
      "baseline": {
        "kind": "training_holdout",
        "model_version": "2"
      },
      "tolerance": 0.05,
      "tolerance_mode": "absolute",
      "window_hours": 24,
      "label_delay_hours": 6,
      "minimum_labeled_rows": 20,
      "minimum_label_coverage": 0.8,
      "consecutive_windows": 3
    }
  }
]

After enrollment, run an observation from the generated project root:

databricks bundle run monitoring -t test --profile YOUR_PROFILE

Unpause the dedicated Spark monitoring schedule after enrollment. Individual HTTP requests do not launch monitoring jobs; observation reads asynchronously delivered logs on that schedule. Completed performance windows are revisited according to monitoring_revisit_windows so late logs and outcomes can update their evidence. If the target has a dashboard in deployment/monitoring.yml, its native Dashboard task refreshes the published dashboard after the monitoring flow completes with monitoring enabled; development targets never refresh. Without it, new Delta rows alone do not invalidate the dashboard's cached view. sampling_fraction: 1.0 requests full payload capture, but it does not make recorded counts a complete HTTP request count: custom-model 4xx or 5xx errors may produce no inference-log row. The dashboard reports captured successes, failures and latency. Empty or late windows can reflect asynchronous delivery; check serving endpoint telemetry separately before interpreting them.

docs.title: Online serving dashboard
docs.text:
All matching contexts are visible initially; choose Model to narrow them. Monitored version filters the component model's concrete version; Context narrows its monitoring registration. The identity table separately shows Endpoint, Served model, Served version and Branch. A model-set parent can have a different name/version from the monitored component. Explicit mismatched selections stay empty. Only enabled serving enrollments are included.

Table Scope Selected model and serving scope Selection guidance and number of matching current contexts. Endpoint and model identity Monitored model/version versus served model/version and branch. Latest observation per context Latest full observation per matching enrollment and current configuration, ordered by window end, measurement time and report ID. Observation history All matching saved full observations, with native pagination and an optional history window-end filter; there is no global 100-row cutoff.

Five charts above the detailed tables show captured requests, HTTP error classes, captured error rate, mean/p95 execution latency, and the latency distribution. Each model/version/context has a separate panel; Model (choose one for details), Monitored version and Context apply to all five. The history window-end control also filters the latency matrix, while the latest snapshot stays unchanged. The latency bar chart and matrix retain only the latest 12 observations per identity before the date selection; use the history table to inspect older windows.

Chart Reading the result Captured requests per window Number of logged requests, including failed responses. One request may contain several prediction rows. How many errors of each kind? Grouped bars with an HTTP error class legend: 4xx client (blue), 5xx server (red), and Other / class not recorded (gray). Value labels show captured counts. Zero means none captured; a missing class count stays blank. If an older report lacks complete class counts, its entire error total appears in gray. A date plus observation number keeps repeated windows separate. Captured error rate per window Captured errors divided by captured requests in that same observation. Missing counts, failed observations and zero requests leave it unmeasured. How long does the model take to answer? Two grouped bars per observation: blue is the average execution time and orange is approximate p95, in milliseconds per request (lower is faster). The last 12 observations per identity are shown separately, including repeated windows. Hover for p50, p99, maximum, timed sample count and exact window timestamps. Small samples can make p95 and p99 equal to the maximum; this is not a separate anomaly. Where do captured execution times fall? Nine duration ranges across the latest 12 observations per identity. Each valid column totals 100% of non-null timings. A shared 0-100% blue scale allows comparisons; hover for exact counts and window times. Old, failed, empty or invalid summaries produce no cells.

For example, a report with ten captured requests, two 4xx responses and one 5xx response has a 30% captured error rate. If only eight requests have a recorded execution duration, latency percentiles and distribution shares use those eight, including any failed responses with durations. A p95 of 250 ms estimates the 95th percentile of those captured execution durations; it is not the slowest request or an end-to-end service guarantee.

Timings use Spark percentile_approx with accuracy 10,000. The fixed distribution boundaries are 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500 and 1,000 ms: the first range is below 5 ms, each middle range includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound, and the final range is at least 1,000 ms. Null timings are excluded from both the percentiles and distribution. No request payloads are read by dashboard queries; these fields come from saved aggregate reports.

Latest/history tables also show class counts, p50/p95/p99 and timed sample count. Older reports retain the fields originally recorded; missing percentiles are blank in numeric tables and produce no bar. The latency chart's detail tooltip shows Not recorded for missing p50/p95/p99 and timed sample counts; a recorded zero remains zero. Only a new monitoring observation records these fields; refreshing or redeploying the dashboard does not backfill saved reports. The monitoring environment must match the runtime recorded in the registered model artifact. Updating the Core requirement alone can fail that runtime check; prepare a compatible model artifact before upgrading its monitoring jobs.

Recomputing an old window with added serving fields can create a new report identity, so history can contain both calculations. Dashboard charts display saved measurements; traffic and promotion policy are defined on Daily serving rollout.

Observation history also shows prediction rows per captured request when saved. Its denominator includes failed captured requests. Request counts and latency stay per observation: windows may overlap, and model-set branches may describe the same parent requests. Do not sum these rows as unique traffic or average their latency means into an endpoint SLA. Observation status describes the saved monitoring result, not live endpoint availability.

Logging is asynchronous and custom-model HTTP 4xx/5xx errors may be absent, so captured counts do not measure all endpoint traffic. Latency describes model execution durations recorded by the platform, not client/network round-trip time.

Window end describes the request-time observation window; measured_at in the saved dataset is when monitoring calculated the report. Shared health freshness uses the latest captured request time for online serving and the scoring commit time for batch predictions. Neither proves that the feature values themselves are recent: a new request or scoring run can use old source data. Refreshing the dashboard rereads saved results and does not obtain new measurements.

For accuracy, open Model performance and select the matching model, version and monitoring context. Missing or immature actual outcomes remain insufficient evidence; successful HTTP requests alone do not establish prediction quality.

The Online serving dashboard page shows Requests with logging errors beside Captured errors in Latest observation per context and Observation history - windows may overlap. Hover over a point in Captured requests per window to see the same count for that observation. 0 means the saved observation recorded no logging errors; Not recorded means the saved report has no count for it. For example, an observation can have 10 captured requests, no HTTP errors and 2 requests with logging errors: those two requests remain in the request count, but their payloads are excluded from drift and performance. Logging errors are not added to the HTTP error-class chart. Model, version and context selections continue to scope these values; overlapping windows must not be added together.

docs.title: Common errors and fixes
docs.text: What you see Next check awaiting_logs No applicable saved report exists. Check enrollment, the monitoring job and asynchronous log arrival; this is not a healthy measurement. failed Inspect the saved report and monitoring task error. A failed latest observation clears earlier counts instead of showing an older success. Blank counts or latency Check the report status and log coverage. Unavailable measurements are not zero requests or zero latency. no_data Inspect the selected request window and captured logs. An empty window does not prove endpoint health or absence of HTTP traffic. Captured failures or unexpected latency Inspect endpoint telemetry and serving logs for that endpoint/version. A healthy input-drift status does not certify request success or latency.

docs.title: Incomplete serving payload logs
docs.text:
logging_error_count counts captured requests whose payload log has one or more logging_error_codes. It counts requests, not individual codes or prediction rows. A logging error can occur even when the endpoint returned a successful HTTP response; it is separate from the captured 4xx/5xx error counts.

Monitoring keeps those requests in captured-request, HTTP-status and available latency summaries. It excludes their unusable payloads from feature and performance calculations and reports the missing-log count. A window that would otherwise be healthy becomes degraded; usable remaining records can still show drift or performance loss. The request charts describe captured telemetry, not a guarantee that every production request was logged.

For traffic rollout, read the incomplete-evidence rule on Daily serving rollout. A logging failure alone is not a retraining trigger; inspect native logging codes and payload-size behavior before changing model settings.

Serving monitoring keeps captured requests with logging_error_codes in the HTTP request and status counts, but excludes their input/output payloads from drift and model-performance calculations. Exact duplicate deliveries count once; conflicting copies of the same request still fail validation. A logging error does not turn a successful HTTP response into an HTTP failure.

An otherwise healthy observation becomes degraded; measured drift and no_data retain their existing status. Capture completeness is reported separately: the saved report's serving.logging_error_count counts affected requests, not individual error codes or prediction rows. The notebook's Observation notes shows the excluded count. For example, two usable predictions and one request with a truncated log retain the two predictions' metrics, with an explicit warning about the missing payload. If every payload is excluded, drift and performance remain unavailable.

Metrics on the retained subset may not represent the missing requests. Logging errors alone do not block retraining: statistically supported drift or a measured performance-policy breach can still request training, subject to the existing minimum data, label coverage, consecutive-window and cooldown checks. Candidate comparison still decides whether a newly trained model qualifies for promotion. The notebook's Performance policy evidence shows the affected request count for that policy's own window and warns when it uses a partial population. With no usable predictions or sufficient labels, the policy remains unavailable.

Missing identity, timestamps or HTTP status, and capture sampling other than 100%, still reject the observation. Old reports are not rewritten; recomputing a window with new summary fields can produce a new report identity. Captured counts describe saved logs rather than every endpoint request.

docs.title: Increase serving traffic and promote a challenger
When you need it
docs.text:
Use a daily rollout to introduce a registered pipeline version gradually. The default policy increases challenger traffic by 10 percentage points after at least 24 hours at each stage. After a passing observation at 100% traffic, the scheduled job automatically promotes that version to the champion alias.

flowchart LR
    A["Challenger stage"] --> C["daily_rollout evaluates evidence"]
    C --> D["ADVANCE after 24 h: add 10 points"]
    D --> A
    C --> E["HOLD: keep traffic and stage clock"]
    E --> A
    C --> F["ROLLBACK on FAIL, even before 24 h"]
    C --> G["COMPLETE: passing 100% stage, promote champion"]

The diagram uses default step/timing settings. ADVANCE and COMPLETE need the full stage time; ROLLBACK happens as soon as fresh evidence fails. A rollback ends that rollout; a hold is evaluated again with better evidence.

This workflow requires an existing champion, a staged challenger with a saved passing comparison, and two compatible serving packages. Train the challenger with promotion_policy: manual_approval so training leaves the current champion in place. The rollout owns the later automatic promotion. Both packages must use the serving-compatible Skyulf runtime used by the controller.

Automatic promotion supports one fitted pipeline per version. It rejects model sets before initialization. Spark-native models and preprocessing that needs other request rows are outside the existing endpoint certificate. Model-set traffic composition is available at the lower-level endpoint API, but the generated daily job requires the single-pipeline approval workflow.

docs.title: Choose the right release mechanism
docs.text:
Workload Does this daily rollout control it? What selects the version? Requests routed through the configured serving endpoint Yes Endpoint traffic percentages, then guarded champion promotion Requests explicitly targeted at a served entity No percentage routing Caller chooses the entity; the controller uses this for smoke checks Batch or incremental Delta scoring No The score job's pinned version/champion selection and publication policy Spark worker inference No The registered version resolved for that score invocation Online feature publication No Its separate TRIGGERED/CONTINUOUS publication job

If a batch scorer resolves champion, it can pick up the promoted version on a later run. That is separate from serving traffic and does not rewrite prior prediction rows by itself. An online store is needed only when the saved model requires online feature lookup; raw-input serving can use rollout without one.

The sequence is: train and stage a challenger, create the two-version endpoint, initialize durable rollout state, configure the generated controller job, test one invocation, then unpause its schedule. The snippets below form that sequence and require existing model versions and permissions; they do not train models.

docs.title: What to edit
docs.text:
File or input Required settings Challenger training promotion_policy: manual_approval and a saved passing comparison Endpoint and rollout initialization Two concrete compatible versions, durable MLflow run, saved DailyRolloutPolicy config/serving.yml rollout identities, approval, smoke records, health and monitoring settings resources/daily_rollout.job.yml Keep the single-writer queue; unpause only after inspecting a manual run

Use serving observations for telemetry and label collection. Their evidence feeds this controller; their schedules do not replace the rollout stage clock.

docs.title: Prepare an isolated endpoint
docs.text:
Use a new A/B endpoint name. Keep an existing SQL function's pinned endpoint separate; changing A/B traffic would change that function's prediction contract.

from dataclasses import replace
from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.serving import (
    PinnedEndpointSpec,
    build_rollout_endpoint,
    prepare_pinned_endpoint,
    rollout_endpoint_ready,
)

workspace = WorkspaceClient()
registry_options = {"tracking_uri": "databricks", "registry_uri": "databricks-uc"}
champion_spec = PinnedEndpointSpec(
    endpoint_name="risk-gradual-release",
    model_name="models.risk.customer_risk",
    model_version="7",
    logging_catalog="ops",
    logging_schema="serving",
    logging_table_prefix="risk_gradual_release",
)
challenger_spec = replace(champion_spec, model_version="8")
plan = build_rollout_endpoint(
    prepare_pinned_endpoint(champion_spec, **registry_options),
    prepare_pinned_endpoint(challenger_spec, **registry_options),
)
print(plan.config)

# Run creation once. The native create operation rejects an existing name.
created = workspace.api_client.do(
    "POST", "/api/2.0/serving-endpoints", body=plan.config
)

Creation is asynchronous. In a later cell, inspect the same endpoint:

endpoint = workspace.api_client.do(
    "GET", f"/api/2.0/serving-endpoints/{champion_spec.endpoint_name}"
)
ready = rollout_endpoint_ready(endpoint, plan, challenger_percentage=0)
print(ready)

Continue only when ready is true. Both model versions must be loaded, routing must be exactly 100/0, and the configured inference logging must be intact. Do not repeat creation after a timeout without inspecting the endpoint first.

docs.title: Initialize durable rollout state
docs.text:
Create an explicit MLflow run for this rollout. Use the comparison digest and quality settings from the challenger's saved training result. The approval settings below are examples; their metric, threshold and improvement must match that saved comparison.

Set the traffic step and timing in your generated project's config/serving.yml before initialization, then read that same file in the initialization cell:

rollout:
  # Keep the other generated rollout fields.
  traffic_step_percent: 10
  stage_minimum_hours: 24.0
  evidence_max_age_hours: 24.0

traffic_step_percent is an integer from 1 to 100; both hour values must be positive and finite. stage_minimum_hours applies to every stage, including the final 100% stage. evidence_max_age_hours limits how old the observation and its window end may be; it is independent of the stage's length. For an isolated test, stage_minimum_hours: 0.1 means six minutes; keep the 24-hour default for normal use. Shorter stages still require enough requests and request-keyed labels under health. They do not change the daily job schedule: invoke the job manually after each test interval or adjust its schedule while preserving one writer. Each invocation advances at most one step.

from pathlib import Path

import yaml
from mlflow.tracking import MlflowClient
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.data.admission import SingleWriterAdmission
from skyulf.integrations.databricks.serving import (
    DailyRolloutPolicy,
    MLflowRolloutStore,
    build_rollout_promotion,
    initialize_rollout,
)

registry = MlflowClient(**registry_options)
approval = {
    "model_name": champion_spec.model_name,
    "metric": "heldout_rmse",
    "min_improvement": 0.0,
    "quality_threshold": 5.0,
    "quality_gates": None,
    "max_rows": 10000,
    "max_input_mb": 64,
    **registry_options,
}
comparison_sha256 = "REPLACE_WITH_SAVED_COMPARISON_SHA256"
promotion = build_rollout_promotion(
    plan, approval, auto_promote=True, comparison_sha256=comparison_sha256
)
experiment_id = "REPLACE_WITH_EXISTING_EXPERIMENT_ID"
run = registry.create_run(experiment_id)
store = MLflowRolloutStore(registry, run.info.run_id)
# Use the deployed file's absolute /Workspace/.../config/serving.yml path.
serving_config_path = "/Workspace/REPLACE_WITH_PROJECT_PATH/config/serving.yml"
rollout_settings = yaml.safe_load(Path(serving_config_path).read_text())["rollout"]
