Omit tuning entirely to fit once. {} requests tuning; it does not disable it. An empty search_space asks Core to construct the selected model's registered space, with explicit fixed parameters pinned. The model catalog shows the registered grid/random families and halving resources. Supplying a nonempty space replaces the automatic axes. Model defaults still supply omitted constructor settings.

Each axis must be a nonempty list of finite JSON scalars: numbers, strings, booleans or null. At most 128 axes, 100 values per axis and 65,536 encoded JSON bytes are admitted. Use native YAML null, true and false. Distribution objects, Python callables, conditional list-of-dictionaries grids and arbitrary Optuna constructor options are not YAML search-space values. Unknown estimator parameter names fail admission. A list such as weights: [[1, 2], [2, 1]] is therefore not an accepted search axis; set ensemble weights structurally in model.params instead.

All strategies use these fields inside tuning; their cards explain which controls affect that strategy.

Field Type Default Accepted values and effect strategy String random grid, random, halving_grid, halving_random, optuna. metric String Required for a single model or branch; competition can inherit its objective Native Core task-compatible objective, for example rmse, mae, mse, r2, accuracy, balanced_accuracy, f1, f1_weighted, precision, recall, roc_auc. Do not use heldout_ names here. The wizard supplies rmse or accuracy outside competition. n_trials Integer 10 1 through 1000. Random/Optuna trial count or halving-random initial candidate count. Grid variants still validate this field but enumerate their grid independently of it. random_state Integer 42 0 through 4,294,967,295. Seeds search sampling, independently of workflow split and CV seeds. Does not automatically seed every estimator. max_candidates Integer 1000 1 through 10,000. Rejects an exhaustive grid whose Cartesian product exceeds this limit. It is not the random/Optuna trial budget. search_space Mapping {} Empty means the registered space; otherwise parameter names map to finite scalar candidate lists subject to the bounds above. timeout Number or null null Positive finite seconds, supported only by Optuna. Soft search stop, not an interrupt or a whole-job deadline. strategy_params Mapping {} Empty for grid/random; only the exact halving or Optuna controls in the cards below are admitted. tune_threshold Boolean false Legacy binary-classification threshold tuning, requiring enabled nested CV and probability output. Incompatible with an active decision_threshold policy. Prefer the explicit policy documented in the training reference.

The Bundle fixes search n_jobs to 1 and requires all explicitly configured estimator and nested-estimator workers to be 1. n_jobs, parallel_backend, custom scorers, refit, error_score, and CV keys are not accepted inside the YAML tuning mapping. Set shared CV fields at workflow/defaults level. This keeps candidate fits bounded; a valid configuration is not a promise that its grid is cheap.

Loss objectives such as RMSE are ranked with sklearn's negative-loss scorer. Saved tuning best_score can therefore be negative: higher is better in the search evidence. Final lifecycle metrics such as heldout_rmse keep their own meaning and direction. The final holdout is never the search validation set.

The complete admitted metric names are:

Task Native tuning metrics Regression mse, mae, rmse, r2, explained_variance Classification accuracy, balanced_accuracy, f1, f1_weighted, precision, recall, roc_auc, roc_auc_ovr, roc_auc_ovo, roc_auc_ovr_weighted, roc_auc_ovo_weighted, pr_auc, pr_auc_weighted, log_loss, matthews_corrcoef, g_score

These are admission choices, not a promise that every model/label distribution can compute every metric. Probability metrics need appropriate model outputs; multiclass AUC needs a compatible variant and class coverage. g_score requires imbalanced-learn. The wizard exposes a smaller common metric menu; edit YAML for the other admitted names.

docs.title: Common setup for the worked examples
docs.text:
In a generated single_model project, replace config/training.yml with this header followed by exactly one strategy card's complete models block. Keep the generated config/inference.yml, Python package and job resources. The source table needs unique nonnull BIGINT customer_id, numeric DOUBLE income and numeric DOUBLE revenue. Replace the illustrative table/model names and quality bound for your data.

version: 1
defaults:
  config_version: 1
  training_layout: single_model
  engine: pandas
  task: regression
  training_table: "{catalog}.{input_schema}.customer_training"
  training_table_version: null
  record_key_columns: [customer_id]
  input_columns: [income]
  target_column: revenue
  model_name: "{catalog}.{metadata_schema}.revenue_model{resource_suffix}"
  split_strategy: random
  training_window_mode: full_snapshot
  test_size: 0.2
  random_state: 42
  stratify: false
  filter_unavailable_results: false
  max_rows: 10000
  max_input_mb: 64
  cv_enabled: true
  cv_type: k_fold
  cv_folds: 2
  cv_shuffle: true
  cv_random_state: 42
  metric: heldout_rmse
  min_improvement: 0.0
  quality_threshold: 5.0
  promotion_policy: manual_approval
  preprocessing_recipe: default
  pre_split_recipe: default

Use this companion content in both config/pre_split.yml and config/preprocessing.yml. Empty recipes keep the examples focused on search; choose fitted preprocessing appropriate to your real data before training.

version: 1
recipes:
  default: []

After saving the selected example, run from the generated project:

uv pip install -r deployment/train-requirements.txt
python src/tools/smoke.py
python src/tools/preview.py --action train --catalog workspace --input-schema demo --output-schema demo --metadata-schema demo
python src/tools/refresh_training_graph.py

Use bindings for your intended target. Preview resolves model/search/recipe settings but does not read Delta or fit the model. Deployment and an actual run follow the Bundle walkthrough. The examples are locally exercised with 40 numeric rows, a separate 8-row final holdout and saved/reloaded predictors. Those checks do not create a table, deploy a job or establish Spark-worker/serving admission for a model or recipe.

docs.title: Grid search
docs.text:
Choose grid when every combination has a reason to exist. Four alpha values times two intercept values mean eight candidates, each evaluated on the configured training folds, then a best-model refit. Cost grows multiplicatively.

Control Grid behavior strategy Set grid; omission selects random. search_space Finite Cartesian product; empty resolves the model's grid defaults. max_candidates Default 1000; admission bound on that full product, not truncation. n_trials Default 10, still validated, but does not limit grid enumeration. random_state Default 42; does not randomize grid enumeration. CV and estimator seeds remain separate. strategy_params / timeout Only {} and omitted/null, respectively.

All other common fields retain the contract above. This four-candidate example deliberately has n_trials: 1 to make its non-capping behavior explicit:

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: ridge_regression
      params: {fit_intercept: true}
    tuning:
      strategy: grid
      metric: rmse
      n_trials: 1
      max_candidates: 4
      random_state: 42
      search_space: {alpha: [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}

Common mistake: reducing n_trials to shrink an expensive grid. Reduce its axes or use random search; raising max_candidates permits more work rather than making it faster.

docs.title: Random search
docs.text:
Choose random to explore several axes within a fixed candidate budget. With Bundle finite-list axes, sampled combinations are drawn without replacement; if the Cartesian product is smaller than n_trials, only that many distinct combinations are available. This is parameter sampling, not row sampling.

Control Random behavior strategy random, also the default. search_space Empty resolves the model's random defaults; nonempty lists replace them. n_trials Default 10; 1..1000 sampled candidates, limited by available combinations. random_state Default 42; seeds candidate sampling. max_candidates Validated but does not cap random candidates; use n_trials. strategy_params / timeout Only {} and omitted/null, respectively.

All other common fields apply. Four trials here exhaust the small example space; for a larger space they would select only four combinations.

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: ridge_regression
      params: {fit_intercept: true}
    tuning:
      strategy: random
      metric: rmse
      n_trials: 4
      random_state: 42
      search_space: {alpha: [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}

Common mistake: expecting a search seed to control the estimator's randomness. For a random forest also choose its fixed model.params.random_state.

docs.title: Successive halving over a grid
docs.text:
Choose halving_grid when ranking candidates with a smaller budget is a useful approximation to ranking them with the full budget. It begins with the grid, increases the resource by factor, and retains roughly one in factor candidates. An early weak candidate is eliminated even if it would have won at full resources. The chosen model is subsequently refitted on the training data.

The two halving strategies accept exactly these strategy_params:

Field Type Default Meaning and bounds factor Integer 3 2..10; resource multiplier and approximate elimination ratio. resource String n_samples Training-row resource, or a real compatible estimator parameter such as n_estimators. The wizard offers those two; custom YAML names must exist on the prepared estimator. min_resources Integer or string exhaust With n_samples: exhaust, smallest, or 2..1,000,000. exhaust selects a starting budget intended to use the last round efficiently; smallest starts at the estimator/task minimum. With an estimator resource, an explicit integer is required. max_resources Integer or string auto With n_samples: auto uses available training rows; integers 2..1,000,000 are capped to the current search population, including nested folds. Estimator resources require an explicit integer in that range.

ASCII decimal strings such as "16" normalize to integer resource counts. min_resources must not exceed max_resources or the available sample budget. Small numeric sample budgets must still leave viable training/validation folds and enough rows per class. There is no aggressive_elimination, n_candidates or other sklearn scheduler setting in Bundle strategy_params.

For an estimator resource, remove that parameter from both fixed params and manual search axes. For example, resource: n_estimators requires explicit min_resources: 10 and max_resources: 40 on a compatible forest, without a fixed/searched n_estimators. Automatic spaces remove the resource axis, but an explicit fixed value still conflicts. Non-count parameters may exist on an estimator yet be unsuitable resources; use a positive training-budget parameter.

Control Halving-grid behavior strategy Set halving_grid. search_space / max_candidates Same initial grid/product bound as grid search. n_trials Default 10, validated but does not cap the initial grid or later rounds. random_state Default 42; controls halving sampling where used. timeout Omitted/null; no halving timeout control.

All remaining common fields apply. With enough rows, this example evaluates four candidates at 8 rows, two survivors at 16 and one at 32: seven candidate evaluations, each with two CV folds. The resource describes the population budget before fold fitting, not eight rows per individual fold.

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: ridge_regression
      params: {fit_intercept: true}
    tuning:
      strategy: halving_grid
      metric: rmse
      max_candidates: 4
      random_state: 42
      search_space: {alpha: [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}
      strategy_params:
        factor: 2
        resource: n_samples
        min_resources: 8
        max_resources: 32

Common mistake: using the default max_resources: auto with n_estimators, or fixing the same resource in model.params. Both fail admission.

docs.title: Successive halving over random candidates
docs.text:
Choose halving_random when a full grid is too large and a small resource budget provides a useful initial ranking. It first samples up to n_trials candidates, then eliminates candidates and increases resources just as halving-grid does. Its registered automatic search space uses the random family.

Control Halving-random behavior strategy Set halving_random. n_trials Default 10; 1..1000 initial candidates, not total round evaluations. random_state Default 42; seeds initial candidates and resource sampling. max_candidates Validated but does not cap sampled candidates or later rounds. strategy_params Exactly factor, resource, min_resources, max_resources, with the same types/defaults/bounds as halving-grid. timeout Omitted/null.

All remaining common fields apply. The example has the same possible four, two, one round counts as halving-grid; a larger candidate space makes its first round a sample instead of an exhaustive grid.

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: ridge_regression
      params: {fit_intercept: true}
    tuning:
      strategy: halving_random
      metric: rmse
      n_trials: 4
      random_state: 42
      search_space: {alpha: [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}
      strategy_params:
        factor: 2
        resource: n_samples
        min_resources: 8
        max_resources: 32

Common mistake: treating n_trials: 4 as four total fits. Surviving candidates are evaluated again, and every evaluation includes the selected CV splits.

docs.title: Optuna search
docs.text:
Choose optuna for adaptive TPE/CMA-ES proposals or supported early pruning. The training environment needs optuna and the sklearn integration optuna-integration; CMA-ES additionally needs cmaes. Select the wizard's matching optional dependencies and check the generated training requirements. Installing Optuna alone is insufficient for Bundle admission.

Control Type Default Meaning n_trials Integer 10 1..1000 attempted trials; repeated configurations are possible. random_state Integer 42 Seeds the sampler; the common integer bounds apply. timeout Number or null null Positive finite seconds. A running fit is not interrupted; nested CV can start separate studies, so this is not a global deadline. strategy_params.sampler String tpe tpe, random, cmaes; no additional sampler-constructor kwargs. strategy_params.pruner String median median, hyperband, none; no additional pruner-constructor kwargs. strategy_params.pruning Boolean Omitted permits supported pruning; wizard emits true false disables pruning; pruner: none also disables it.

All remaining common fields apply; max_candidates does not cap Optuna. search_space: {} uses the registered random-family space. With TPE or the random sampler, each list is categorical, including numeric lists. CMA-ES instead converts a numeric list into an inclusive min/max integer range or a continuous float range. Thus [0.1, 10.0] can produce intermediate values under CMA-ES. Strings, booleans and null-containing lists remain categorical and use independent random fallback where CMA-ES cannot handle them.

Pruning depends on actual estimator capabilities and validation. Supported native boosters can report iteration checkpoints; incremental estimators can report training updates; ordinary estimators can prune between completed CV folds. A single complete fold has no remaining fold work to prune. The logs state which mode is available. Pruned and failed trials cannot become the selected model; if none completes, there is no winner to refit. Choosing a pruner does not guarantee that any trial will be pruned, especially in a small study with its pruner's default warm-up behavior.

This example disables pruning to make the four-trial local exercise predictable:

models:
  revenue:
    model:
      type: ridge_regression
      params: {fit_intercept: true}
    tuning:
      strategy: optuna
      metric: rmse
      n_trials: 4
      random_state: 42
      search_space: {alpha: [0.1, 1.0, 10.0, 100.0]}
      strategy_params: {sampler: tpe, pruner: none, pruning: false}

Common mistake: assuming numeric lists always mean discrete choices, or passing an Optuna distribution object in YAML. Check the sampler's semantics above.

docs.title: CV, nested CV and total work
docs.text:
All five strategies use the workflow's shared CV contract. Configure it beside task and target_column, usually under defaults, rather than inside tuning.

Workflow control Type/default Search behavior cv_enabled Boolean, false False still searches on one training-only 80/20 validation split. It does not disable tuning or use the final holdout. cv_type String, k_fold k_fold, stratified_k_fold, shuffle_split, time_series_split, group_k_fold, stratified_group_k_fold, nested_cv. cv_folds Integer, 5; 2..20 Fold/repeated-split count; outer-fold count for nested CV. cv_shuffle Boolean, true Must be false for temporal CV and true for shuffle-split. cv_random_state Integer, 42; 0..4,294,967,295 CV seed, distinct from search sampling and final holdout seeds. cv_inner_folds Integer or null, null; explicit 2..20 Nested search folds. Null chooses min(3, cv_folds - 1) when outer folds exceed two, otherwise two. cv_nested_type String, auto Nested only: auto selects stratified k-fold for classification, k-fold for regression. Explicit k-fold, stratified, time-series, group or stratified-group policies are supported. cv_group_column String or null, null Required for group policies; not a model feature. Group search requires enabled CV. cv_gap Integer, 0 Nonnegative row gap for temporal CV. cv_test_size Integer or null, null Positive validation-window row count for temporal CV. cv_max_train_size Integer or null, null Positive maximum training-window row count for temporal CV.

Temporal search additionally needs the workflow's explicit event_column and enabled CV; it preserves chronological boundaries. Stratified policies require classification. Group/time metadata, class counts and actual fold sizes are validated before fitting. Every admitted CV fold needs at least two training and two validation rows; model-specific requirements can be stricter. Learned preprocessing is fitted anew inside each training fold. Preprocessing splitter nodes are rejected because the Bundle owns splitting.

For nested CV, set cv_type: nested_cv, for example cv_folds: 3 and cv_inner_folds: 2. Each outer training partition runs its own search; its winner is evaluated on that outer validation partition. After outer evaluation, a fresh full-training search selects the saved model. The outer scores estimate the search procedure; the final search's best score is not the outer estimate. The untouched final holdout remains separate. Stacking/calibration internal folds add further fits; they do not replace these validation levels.

docs.title: Temporal and grouped evaluation
docs.text:
Time-series CV needs a selected observation window, an event_column and cv_shuffle: false. Normalized timestamps order the folds and are removed before preprocessing/model fitting. Equal timestamps across a fold boundary fail; adjust folds or aggregate observations instead of allowing time leakage. Nested temporal CV requires a temporal final holdout. cv_gap, cv_test_size and cv_max_train_size are row counts at both nested levels and the separate final search. A null maximum training size expands the window; an integer rolls it.

Grouped CV requires cv_group_column, excluded from model inputs. A random final holdout selects whole groups using the saved seed; test_size is the proportion of groups and stratify must be false. A temporal final holdout must also contain disjoint groups. Missing groups/classes or insufficient groups fail before fitting; row filters retain aligned group/time metadata.

During initialization, ordinary or nested temporal CV fixes the final split to temporal, hides random/shuffle questions and opens the clock/window questions. The default becomes a rolling-calendar holdout; explicit fixed-window dates remain pinned. Group and other non-temporal CV retain the selected final split. These wizard rules do not rewrite an existing config/training.yml. See nested-temporal-init.example.json and nested-group-threshold-init.example.json in the template's examples directory.

Nested binary tune_threshold generates inner out-of-fold probabilities for each selected recipe; outer and final holdout labels never choose its threshold. Multiclass or models without probabilities fail this legacy mode. Use the explicit decision-threshold policy for its supported alternatives. tuning.json records fold thresholds and provenance.

cross_validation.json separates outer selection scores, selected parameters and mean/std from the final search. Fixed-model CV retains stability diagnostics; historical artifacts without nested-search evidence remain diagnostic. Negative loss scorers stay negative and larger is better. The independent heldout_* metrics determine promotion. Search settings/results appear in tuning.json and the train_and_tune summary. pandas and Polars use this same evaluation path.

docs.title: Competition budget
docs.text:
In model_competition, candidates share CV and the selection objective. competition_max_candidates defaults to 8 (2..32); the wizard offers up to eight candidate slots. competition_max_trials defaults to 100 (1..10,000). It rejects excessive planned work before source access; it does not truncate candidates or measure CPU time. The trial bound is calculated as follows:

  1. A fixed model contributes one candidate evaluation. Grid contributes its Cartesian product; random and Optuna contribute requested n_trials.
  2. Halving adds survivor rounds to that starting count. With starting count N and factor f, it sums 1 + floor(log_f(N)) rounds, repeatedly retaining ceil(previous_count / f). This is conservative when resources stop early.
  3. Nested CV multiplies this count by cv_folds + 1, covering outer searches plus the final full-training search. Ordinary CV folds still multiply actual estimator fits; they are not another multiplier in this trial-bound field.
  4. Sum across all candidates. An active explicit decision-threshold policy can add independent outer policy fits/searches; allow for that extra work too.

For the four-candidate, factor-two halving example, the ordinary bound is 4 + 2 + 1 = 7; with two outer folds it is 7 * (2 + 1) = 21. A budget of 6 or 20 respectively is rejected even if one expects an early stop. A second candidate adds its own bound. Competition parallelism remains one candidate at a time. Review preview's effective settings before increasing the budget.

docs.title: Voting and stacking ensembles
docs.text:
An ensemble is one model candidate containing several learners. In contrast, competition evaluates separate candidates and selects one winner. The ensemble guide covers the voting_* and stacking_* model.params fields, nested member search axes, worked voting, stacking and calibrated examples, and the wizard questions for each slot.

Continue with the model catalog, training field reference, and preprocessing recipes to choose a complete training recipe. A successful local search does not grant its fitted preprocessing chain Spark-worker or online-serving support; use the selected inference mode's own admission and verification path.

docs.title: Tables and objects in your workspace
When you need it
docs.text:
Read this page when you open a project's schema after the first runs and want to know what each table is, who created it, whether you need it, and what grows over time. A Bundle project touches four kinds of objects: your data, its predictions, its registered models and the shared monitoring store. Skyulf never creates your data tables; the jobs create everything else when they first need it.

flowchart LR
    subgraph IN["input_schema: you own these"]
        T["training table"]
        S["scoring source"]
        L["outcomes (labels) table"]
    end
    subgraph OUT["output_schema"]
        P["predictions"]
    end
    subgraph META["metadata_schema"]
        M["registered model"]
    end
    subgraph MON["monitoring_catalog.monitoring_schema: shared by all projects"]
        D["4 Delta tables"]
        V["8 views"]
        R["4 reference tables per monitored model version"]
    end
    T --> TR["train job"] --> M
    S --> SC["score job"] --> P
    M --> SC
    P --> MO["monitoring job"]
    L --> MO
    TR -. "enrollment" .-> R
    MO --> D
    D --> V

The four locations come from deployment/variables.yml: input_schema, output_schema and metadata_schema for the project, and monitoring_catalog plus monitoring_schema for the monitoring store. They may all be the same schema, but separating them keeps each schema readable (see recommended layout).

docs.title: Your data: input_schema
docs.text:
Table Created by Purpose Training table (training_table in config/training.yml) You Rows the model learns from. Training pins a Delta version of it. Scoring source (config/inference.yml) You Rows to predict. It needs no target; Change Data Feed lets the score job read only new inserts. Outcomes table (monitoring_label_table in deployment/targets.yml) You Actual values that arrive later, keyed by the same record key, with the time each value became known. Optional: without it, monitoring measures drift but not performance.

These may be one table or several; see Choose a table layout. Check or create your source tables explains how to verify them before the first run. The prepared examples create them with their own loaders (load_nyctaxi.sql, real_data/load_data.py); a normal project uses tables you already have.

docs.title: Predictions: output_schema
docs.text:
Table Created by Purpose Prediction table (prediction_table in config/inference.yml) Score job, on its first run One row per scored source row: record key, prediction, probabilities for classifiers, model name, version and run, and, when the model can exclude rows, scoring_status and exclusion_reason. Extra output columns from scoring rules (for example no2_band) are added here. <prediction_table>_v<version> plus a view under the logical name Score job with on_model_change: rescore_all One physical table per model version; the view always points at the current generation. Older generations remain until you remove them.

The default on_model_change: score_new_rows mode keeps one table and appends new predictions. See Scoring.

docs.title: Feature tables (optional)
docs.text: Projects that use config/features.yml and src/features/groups/ also run a features job. It writes one output table per feature group and the merged feature table that training and lookup read. Online serving can add an online copy of a feature table. See Feature tables and online features. Projects without feature groups, such as the real_data examples, have none of these.

docs.title: Models: metadata_schema
docs.text: The train job registers the model as a Unity Catalog registered model (model_name in config/training.yml), for example air_quality_no2_model. It appears in the schema's model list, not as a table. Each training run adds a version; the champion alias marks the version that scoring uses. The MLflow experiment, with runs, metrics, SHAP and chart artifacts, lives in the workspace path from experiment_name, not in a schema.

docs.title: The shared monitoring store
docs.text: The first monitoring enrollment creates the store in monitoring_catalog.monitoring_schema. One store serves every project and model that uses the same catalog and schema; later projects reuse it instead of creating their own. See Store setup for permissions and upgrades.

docs.title: Four Delta tables (they hold data)
docs.text: Table What it holds model_inventory One row per monitored model in each environment and project: which model and version, which tables, and its monitoring settings. Enrollment writes it. monitoring_results One immutable row per monitoring observation: the full report with drift, quality and performance evidence. The monitoring job only appends. performance_actions For each performance-policy result, whether a retraining request was made or skipped and why, recorded without rewriting the observation. retraining_requests Every retraining request and its submission receipt, and the shared cooldown gate per train job, so two triggers cannot start training twice.

docs.title: Eight views (no data of their own)
docs.text:
They read the Delta tables above and exist for the dashboard and your own queries.

View Answers current_health What is the latest state of each monitored model? monitoring_issues Which quality, drift or performance-policy issues are open now? metric_history Every recorded metric as one row (column, metric, value, threshold, issue). The easiest place to query drift and performance values. performance_history Performance results together with the action taken for each. complete_observations Full observations, excluding the small late-label-only reports a policy writes. monitoring_identities Every model, version and context ever monitored, including earlier ones. model_version_details Lineage and saved metadata of each concrete model version, including its training summary. serving_windows Serving-endpoint observation windows used by the dashboard's serving charts.

docs.title: Reference populations per monitored model version
docs.text:
Drift and retraining checks compare new data with what the model was trained on. Rereading the training table on every run would be slow and could see changed data, so enrollment copies the needed populations into immutable Delta tables. New format-2 references use two tables per identity and a source table that can be shared. The identity binds the monitored model, version and verified training evidence; source sharing additionally binds its physical Delta ID/version, selected columns, exact schema and row values, including duplicate counts.

Part What it holds Used for monitor_ref_<identity>_population The seen rows plus a recorded boolean training-membership column. Temporal splits keep training rows; random splits also retain holdout rows. Drift selects training members; freshness checks use the complete seen population. The marker is removed before model/metric use and its name avoids feature collisions. monitor_src_<identity> The verified, selected training source population, including the target. Historical reconstruction; shared only when content and schema match exactly. _receipt One JSON record: the evidence these tables belong to, their table identities, the source table identity and the holdout metric values. Verifying the tables before use, and the training_holdout baseline of performance policies.

For N references with U distinct source populations, format 2 needs 2 * N + U tables. Two references using the same population need five tables. Four branches with four different target projections need twelve, even when their source table and Delta version are the same. A shared source table name alone never proves that its data can be reused.

Existing format-1 references still use _train, _seen, _source, _receipt. They remain readable and eligible for guarded cleanup; upgrades do not migrate or delete them. Both formats hold copies bounded by training limits. New projects with monitoring include a weekly cleanup job; protected references remain until unused and old enough. See retention and recovery.

docs.title: Recommended layout
docs.text:
Give every project the same monitoring schema reserved for the store (for example workspace.skyulf_monitoring), and keep each project's data, predictions and models in the project's own schemas. A project schema then holds only its own tables, and all monitoring objects sit in one place:

Schema Typical contents Project schema(s) Training table, scoring source, outcomes table, prediction table, registered model skyulf_monitoring The 4 Delta tables, 8 views, per-identity population/receipt tables and shared source populations; an audit table is added when maintenance records are written

The air_quality_no2 example uses this shared layout. A fresh installation has four project tables: observations_train, observations_score, labels and predictions. The store's four tables, eight views and per-version references are in workspace.skyulf_monitoring. The other two real_data examples keep their independent stores in their project schemas.

The single-table air-quality walkthrough uses three project tables: observations for both training and scoring, labels for outcomes, and predictions. Daily input inserts do not update old rows. It uses the same shared monitoring schema.

Changing monitoring_schema redirects future enrollment and observations; it does not move or delete an existing store. Redeploy, enroll the existing concrete model in the destination, and prepare its Spark references before observing. Verify the destination report before retiring old objects. For example, an older air-quality installation may still contain its original 20 objects until its 16 monitoring objects are separately reviewed and removed. Historical reports stay in that old store; they are not automatically copied to the new one.

docs.title: What grows, and how to clean up
docs.text:
Object Grows with Clean up Prediction table New source inserts Your retention policy; Skyulf does not delete predictions. monitoring_results, performance_actions, retraining_requests Monitoring runs and decisions Keep observation/action evidence for audit. Request status, job cooldown gates and the reserved reference-admission row also receive guarded updates. Reference tables New monitored identities and distinct source populations Use guarded reference cleanup; retained aliases, monitors, policy baselines and unfinished retraining protect references. Shared sources remain while another receipt needs them. _v<version> prediction generations New versions in on_model_change: rescore_all mode Drop old generations once consumers use the new view.

Views never need cleanup. Do not drop or recreate the store's tables while any project still monitors into them; other projects share them.

docs.title: Drift Monitoring
docs.text: Data drift occurs when the statistical properties of incoming (production) data diverge from the data the model was trained on. Skyulf provides a DriftCalculator to detect this automatically.

docs.title: When to use drift detection
docs.text:
• Before running predictions on new data batches.
  • As a scheduled health check in production pipelines.
  • After a data source change (new CSV, new API feed, schema migration).

docs.title: Using the Data Drift Analysis page
docs.text:
Upload raw data in the same format as the selected model's source dataset. Do not manually apply the pipeline's log transforms, scaling or encoding first. The page compares it with the raw loader snapshot saved during that job, before preprocessing and train/test splitting. It reads the saved snapshot rather than reloading a source file that may have changed since training.

The reference contains the rows actually loaded: a sampled loader keeps its sample, while an unsampled loader keeps the complete loaded dataset. Consequently, a model trained on 120 of 150 rows can show Ref: 150 rows in drift analysis; the model card's 120 rows still describes its training partition.

The target and columns explicitly named by upstream drop-column configurations are excluded on both sides. All other raw columns remain eligible, including categorical inputs that the model later encodes. Missing and new input columns still produce schema drift. Explicit drops follow the model bundle's exclusion convention; this is not a complete dependency analysis of generated features.

Existing jobs with a saved execution graph and loader snapshot work without retraining. If that graph has multiple upstream source datasets or its saved source is unavailable, the analysis records a failed check rather than comparing the upload with a transformed reference. Legacy jobs without graph metadata retain their original saved reference; ensure that reference and upload use the same preprocessing stage.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import polars as pl
from skyulf.profiling import DriftCalculator

# Reference = your training data
reference = pl.DataFrame({
    "age": [25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50],
    "income": [30000, 45000, 55000, 65000, 70000, 80000],
})

# Current = new production data
current = pl.DataFrame({
    "age": [60, 65, 70, 75, 80, 85],
    "income": [90000, 95000, 100000, 110000, 120000, 130000],
})

calc = DriftCalculator(reference, current)
report = calc.calculate_drift()

print(f"Drifted columns: {report.drifted_columns_count}")
for col, drift in report.column_drifts.items():
    print(f"  {col}: drift={drift.drift_detected}")
    for m in drift.metrics:
        print(f"    {m.metric}: {m.value:.4f} (threshold={m.threshold}, drifted={m.has_drift})")

docs.title: Drift metrics
docs.text:
String, Categorical, Enum and Boolean columns receive categorical drift metrics, including psi_categorical. They do not need encoding first. Rerun saved drift checks that previously omitted Enum columns to populate those measurements.

The page's Avg PSI and Highest PSI cards include both numeric psi and categorical psi_categorical, with one finite PSI measurement per column. For example, numeric PSI 0.01 and categorical PSI 5 produce average 2.5050, with the categorical feature shown as having the highest PSI. A measured zero is included; unavailable measurements are excluded. If none are available, the cards show — and No PSI available rather than claiming stability.

The DriftCalculator computes these metrics for each numeric column:

Metric What it measures Default threshold Wasserstein distance How much "work" to transform one distribution into the other, divided by the reference column's standard deviation 0.1 KS statistic (Kolmogorov-Smirnov) Maximum distance between the two CDFs (0–1) 0.1 PSI (Population Stability Index) Binned distribution shift 0.2 KL divergence Information-theoretic divergence 0.1

A distribution is flagged as drifted when both conditions hold:

  1. At least one effect-size metric exceeds its configured threshold.
  2. A statistical test supports a difference after correction for the number of tested features.

This prevents a noisy small sample from triggering retraining on its effect size alone, and a tiny difference in a huge sample from triggering it on its p-value alone. Threshold sliders change the first condition; they do not remove the evidence requirement. Schema changes are handled separately.

Each metric's value is reported on the same scale as its threshold, so value > threshold reproduces its effect-size has_drift flag. That flag alone is not the column verdict. Two caveats:

  • The Wasserstein value is the normalized distance — the raw distance is in the column's own units, so a single threshold could not mean the same thing for a column measured in cents and one measured in kilometres. The untransformed distance is kept in raw_value for display.
  • The KS p-value is reported as diagnostic ks_test_p_value, with no effect-size threshold. The column's structured evidence determines statistical support; the diagnostic metric is never an independent alarm.

docs.title: Statistical evidence and small samples
docs.text:
Numeric and temporal features use the two-sample KS test. Binary categories use Fisher's exact test. Larger categorical tables use chi-square when every observed and expected cell has at least five observations; sparse tables use per-category Fisher tests with a correction within the feature.

The significance level is 0.05, with Bonferroni correction across features having at least two valid values on each side and a finite test p-value. This family includes tests that cannot reach significance at their current sample size, which makes the correction conservative. Each column reports valid counts, the test, raw and adjusted p-values, and an evidence status:

  • supported: the corrected test supports a difference; an effect-size threshold must still be exceeded to declare drift.
  • not_detected: the test did not support a difference.
  • insufficient_data: there are too few observations, or the test cannot reach the corrected significance level with these sample counts.
  • unavailable: the statistical evidence could not be measured.

There is no universal 100-row minimum. Feasibility uses the test's attainable p-value bound. The KS bound assumes a continuous distribution; ties can make the actual minimum larger, so a tied small sample can read not_detected instead of insufficient_data. These tests also assume independent samples; they do not correct for time-series dependence or repeated monitoring windows. See SciPy's KS, Fisher and chi-square test contracts.

Databricks monitoring persists this evidence with its report. A report with insufficient or unavailable measurements is degraded unless another finding already establishes drift. Automatic retraining refuses incomplete evidence and older saved reports that lack the new evidence fields; rerun monitoring to obtain a current decision. The drift page labels older distributions as legacy and shows unknown risk for unmeasured evidence.

docs.title: Custom thresholds
docs.text:
report = calc.calculate_drift(thresholds={
    "psi": 0.15,
    "ks_statistic": 0.01,
    "wasserstein": 0.05,
    "kl_divergence": 0.2,
})

The keys are psi, ks_statistic, wasserstein and kl_divergence. Anything else is merged into the dict but never read, so a misspelled key silently leaves that threshold at its default.

docs.title: Schema drift
docs.text:
The report also detects structural changes:

  • report.missing_columns — columns present in reference but absent in current data.
  • report.new_columns — columns in current data that were not in the reference.
  • type_drift — a shared column whose current values cannot be compared under the reference column's numeric or categorical interpretation.

Numeric comparisons preserve fractional values and wider numeric types. For example, comparing integer reference values 0, 1 with current values 0.9, 1.9 measures the shift without truncating the current values to integers. Numeric text is accepted only when every non-null value can be parsed; a column containing "unknown" receives type drift instead of silently discarding those observations. Decimal values and parsed numeric text use Float64 precision for measurement. Infinite values, including text that overflows to infinity such as "1e400", stop the comparison with an error naming the affected column. Replace them with finite or missing values and rerun; the monitoring history records a failed check with that explanation.

Type drift counts as a drifted column and includes a dtype-specific suggestion. It has no numerical PSI measurement, so changing distribution thresholds does not remove that verdict. Columns with no non-null observations retain the existing policy of reporting no distribution measurement.

These changes count toward report.drifted_columns_count, which therefore covers distribution drift and schema drift. A vanished feature has no values left to compare, so it never appears in column_drifts — the count is the only place it shows up, and it used to be omitted entirely, leaving a report that claimed zero drift while the structural change was classified as critical.

docs.title: Report structure
docs.text:
DriftReport(
    reference_rows=1000,
    current_rows=500,
    drifted_columns_count=2,
    column_drifts={
        "age": ColumnDrift(
            column="age",
            metrics=[...],
            drift_detected=True,
            suggestions=["Consider retraining..."],
        ),
    },
    missing_columns=[],
    new_columns=["new_feature"],
)

docs.title: Data format
docs.text:
DriftCalculator works with Polars DataFrames. If your data is in Pandas:

import polars as pl

reference_pl = pl.from_pandas(reference_pd)
current_pl = pl.from_pandas(current_pd)

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: Drift calculation requires scipy (installed with skyulf-core by default).

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Run drift detection before prediction to catch issues early.
  • Log drift reports over time to track gradual distribution shifts.
  • If drift is detected, consider retraining the model on recent data.
  • Keep categorical labels intact when comparing their distributions.

docs.title: Automated EDA & Profiling
docs.text: Skyulf provides a powerful automated Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) engine powered by Polars, designed to handle large datasets efficiently. The EDAAnalyzer generates comprehensive statistical profiles, detects data quality issues, and provides actionable insights.

docs.title: The Easy Way (Automated Visualization)
docs.text:
Skyulf provides a EDAVisualizer helper that automatically generates a rich terminal dashboard and interactive plots.

Note: This requires the visualization extras: pip install skyulf-core[viz]

import polars as pl
from skyulf import EDAAnalyzer, EDAVisualizer

# 1. Load Data
df = pl.read_csv("your_dataset.csv")

# 2. Analyze
analyzer = EDAAnalyzer(df)
profile = analyzer.analyze(
    target_col="target",
    task_type="Classification", # Optional: Force "Classification" or "Regression"
    date_col="timestamp",       # Optional: Manually specify if auto-detection fails
    lat_col="latitude",         # Optional
    lon_col="longitude"         # Optional
)

# 3. Visualize
viz = EDAVisualizer(profile, df)
viz.summary()  # Prints Data Quality, Stats, Outliers, Target Analysis, Alerts to terminal
viz.plot()     # Opens Matplotlib plots (Distributions, Correlations, PCA, etc.)

docs.title: The Manual Way (Accessing Raw Stats)
docs.text:
For custom reports or application integrations, use EDAProfile for the raw result returned by EDAAnalyzer.analyze(). This is the recommended public name, available from both skyulf and skyulf.profiling.

The older DatasetProfile import remains the exact same Pydantic class: EDAProfile is DatasetProfile. Existing JSON schemas retain the DatasetProfile title, and saved profiles retain their original pickle path. The pipeline transformer id "DatasetProfile" still identifies the separate inspection node; use that unchanged id in pipeline configurations.

import polars as pl
from skyulf import EDAAnalyzer, EDAProfile

# 1. Load your data into a Polars DataFrame
df = pl.read_csv("your_dataset.csv")

# 2. Initialize the Analyzer
analyzer = EDAAnalyzer(df)

# 3. Run the analysis
# You can optionally specify a target column for supervised analysis
profile: EDAProfile = analyzer.analyze(target_col="target_variable")

# 4. Access the results
print(f"Rows: {profile.row_count}")
print(f"Missing Cells: {profile.missing_cells_percentage}%")

# Access column-specific stats
age_stats = profile.columns["age"].stats
print(f"Mean Age: {age_stats.mean}")

# Check for data quality alerts
for alert in profile.alerts:
    print(f"[{alert.severity}] {alert.message}")

docs.title: 1. Comprehensive Profiling
docs.text:
The analyzer automatically detects column types (Numeric, Categorical, Date, Text, Boolean) and computes relevant statistics: * Numeric: Mean, Median, Std Dev, Quantiles, Skewness, Kurtosis, Histogram. * Normality Tests: For performance, normality tests are performed on a sample of up to 5,000 rows. * Shapiro-Wilk: Used for N < 5,000. * Kolmogorov-Smirnov: Used for N >= 5,000 (on a 5k sample). * Categorical: Unique count, Mode, Frequency distribution. Unique and rare-label counts and the top categories exclude missing values, which are reported separately in the column's missing count and percentage. * Date: Min/Max date, Range, Year/Month distribution. * Text: Avg length, Common words, Sentiment Analysis (Positive/Neutral/Negative).

Native Polars Categorical and Enum columns are profiled as categorical, including their value frequencies. A column with dtype Null (only missing values and no declared type) is reported as Unknown: its missing count, missing percentage and quality alerts remain available, while type-specific statistics are omitted. An all-null column with a declared type, such as Float64, retains that type's profile.

Automatic date detection converts a string column only when the selected format parses every non-missing value in the full column. If a later value uses another format or cannot be parsed, the original strings remain available for profiling; parse failures do not become missing cells or trigger a false missing-data Drop recommendation. Normalize such a column explicitly before requesting temporal analysis. An all-null native Date/Datetime column retains its type and reports actual null minimum/maximum bounds. Regenerate saved profiles to apply these corrections.

String columns are treated as categorical when fewer than 5% of their non-missing values are distinct, or when they contain at most 20 distinct non-missing values with at least one repetition. This also recognizes small datasets with repeated class or city labels. Missing values do not count as labels or dilute the ratio; all-null strings and strings with no repeated values remain Text. A recognized string target receives classification statistics, associations and rule discovery when numeric features are available. Rerun saved analyses to refresh their inferred types and target results.

docs.title: 2. Smart Alerts
docs.text: Skyulf automatically flags potential data quality issues: * High Null Rate: Columns with >50% missing values. * Constant Columns: Columns with only 1 unique value. * High Cardinality: Categorical columns with too many unique values. * High Correlation: Pairs of features with correlation > 0.95. * Multicollinearity (VIF): Detects features with Variance Inflation Factor > 5.0. Nearly duplicated features still produce warnings when the correlation matrix cannot be reliably inverted. The calculation then uses a separate regression for each feature, preserving low VIF for unrelated features. A value of 999 is a finite warning marker for effectively perfect dependence, not a precise estimate or a cap on other VIF values. Rerun saved analyses to refresh these results. * Class Imbalance: Target variables with skewed class distributions. * Data Leakage: Features with 1.0 correlation to the target.

docs.title: Smart Recommendations
docs.text:
For highly skewed numeric columns, transformation advice follows the observed value range. Log or Box-Cox is suggested for strictly positive, right-skewed data. Columns containing zero or negative values, left-skewed columns, and profiles with an unknown minimum receive Yeo-Johnson advice instead. These are suggestions to evaluate; EDA does not transform the source data.

The clean-dataset message appears only when no drop, imputation, transformation, encoding or resampling action is recommended. It describes the outcome of these checks, without certifying that a dataset is ready for modeling. An informational balanced-target message can appear alongside it. Rerun saved analyses to refresh their recommendations.

docs.title: 3. Advanced Analysis
docs.text:
• Outlier Detection: Uses Isolation Forest to identify anomalous rows.
  • PCA: Computes Principal Components to visualize high-dimensional data structure.
  • Clustering (Post-Hoc Analysis): Uses KMeans to automatically discover segments (clusters) in the numeric data and profiles them.
  • Causal Discovery: Uses the PC Algorithm with Fisher-Z tests to estimate a partially directed graph among numeric variables.
  • Decision Tree (Rule Discovery): Uses a surrogate Decision Tree model to extract human-readable rules.
    • Classification: "If Age > 50 -> High Risk (Confidence: 85%)"
    • Regression: "If Age > 50 -> Value = 120.5 (Samples: 100)"
    • High Cardinality: Automatically groups rare classes into "Other" for readable trees (e.g. Top 10 Zip Codes).
  • Target Analysis: Analyzes relationships between features and the target variable (Correlations, ANOVA, Interactions).
  • Geospatial: Automatically detects Lat/Lon columns and computes bounding boxes.
  • Time Series: Detects seasonality and trends in datetime columns.

For a categorical or Boolean target, feature association uses the correlation ratio (eta), where 0 means no difference between group means and 1 means no within-group variation. Each numeric feature is evaluated using only rows where both that feature and the target are present. Missing values in another feature do not affect its score, and this calculation does not remove rows from your dataset. Features with no complete pairs are omitted; constant observed features keep a score of 0. Rows missing either value contribute neither to group sizes nor to the sums of squares used in this calculation.

Previously saved reports retain their recorded scores. Rerun EDA to refresh the association values and feature ranking after this correction.

Categorical and Boolean targets keep their original names and values. They appear in Target Analysis through category-aware associations and box plots; they are not converted to arbitrary numeric codes for Pearson correlations or causal discovery. For example, selecting species does not create a species_encoded variable. The web app explains this omission in the causal and correlation views, including when no numeric graph is available. Numeric targets classified as categories are treated the same way.

Target and grouping column names such as mean, n, min, median, count and group are supported without dropping their statistics or recommendations.

docs.title: 4. Task Type Control
docs.text:
By default, Skyulf automatically detects if your target is Classification (Categorical) or Regression (Numeric). However, you can override this behavior:

  • Force Classification: Useful for ID columns or numeric codes (e.g., Zip Code, Status Code) that should be treated as categories.
  • Force Regression: Useful for numeric ratings (e.g., 1–5) that you want to treat as measurements. String labels are not automatically converted into numeric ratings.
# Force Classification on a numeric ID column
profile = analyzer.analyze(target_col="zip_code", task_type="Classification")

An explicit classification task also excludes a numerically stored target from target Pearson and Fisher-Z analysis, while retaining categorical associations. An explicit regression task permits an existing numeric target even if its low number of distinct values led to a categorical profile type.

docs.title: Visualization Support (skyulf-core[viz])
docs.text:
PCA plots keep points whose target label is missing, showing them as gray crosses marked Unlabeled. If every label is missing, the plot still shows all points without a target colorbar. Categorical PCA and geospatial plots use a deterministic color mapping for the same set of category labels, even when row order or the Python process changes. Recreate existing plots with EDAVisualizer to use the corrected rendering; the saved profile can be reused. PCA treats text labels such as "nan" and "inf" as categories so their points remain visible.

The core library is designed to be lightweight. To use the EDAVisualizer and generate plots, you must install the optional visualization dependencies:

pip install skyulf-core[viz]

This installs: * matplotlib: For generating plots. * rich: For beautiful terminal dashboards.

docs.title: EDA charts in the web app
docs.text:
The PCA & Clusters, Bivariate scatter charts and Geospatial map share category colors. Colors stay stable when rows are reordered, provided the displayed category set stays the same. Adding or removing categories can change the mapping; the palette repeats for large category sets. Category labels use English alphabetical ordering, including case and accents, so the browser's language does not change their color or marker assignment.

The 2D and 3D scatter views use the same five repeating marker shapes: circle, square, diamond, plus (+) and diagonal cross (x). The legend shows the shape actually drawn for each category. Missing-label points use gray plus markers in both views.

Missing target labels form a separate gray Unlabeled group. Real values such as Other, Unlabeled, constructor and __proto__ remain ordinary categories. If Unlabeled already exists, the missing group is named Unlabeled (missing), with a numeric suffix if needed to keep names distinct. All-missing targets still show every point and a legend entry. Maps use circles and show their category legend, including a filter for long lists; they retain category colors above twenty groups.

Reload the web app to use these rendering fixes with existing saved profiles. The chart data table and CSV export retain the original label values.

docs.title: Filtering & Exclusion
docs.text:
You can refine your analysis by filtering rows or excluding columns without modifying your original dataframe.

# Run analysis on a subset of data
profile = analyzer.analyze(
    target_col="price",
    # Filter rows where 'region' is 'US' and 'age' > 18
    filters=[
        {"column": "region", "operator": "==", "value": "US"},
        {"column": "age", "operator": ">", "value": 18}
    ],
    # Exclude 'id' and 'timestamp' columns from the report
    exclude_cols=["id", "timestamp"]
)

Column exclusions also apply to explicit lat_col and lon_col selections. If either selected coordinate is excluded, profile.geospatial is None, so its points, bounds and centroid are omitted. Exclusions persist when you reuse an analyzer; create a new EDAAnalyzer(df) to start with all columns again. Rerun saved analyses to refresh their stored reports after an update.

Exclusions also take precedence over the selected target: an excluded target does not contribute associations, causal nodes, inferred task type or decision tree rules. Its name remains in profile.target_col to record the requested configuration; profile.causal_target_exclusion_reason is "excluded".

docs.title: Advanced Analysis Modules
docs.text: The EDAAnalyzer automatically runs several advanced analysis modules if the data supports them. Here is how to use and interpret each one.

docs.title: 1. Outlier Detection
docs.text:
Uses Isolation Forest to identify anomalous rows in your dataset. This is useful for cleaning data or detecting fraud/errors.

For more than 50,000 rows, detection uses a reproducible sample of 50,000 rows. Each returned index is the zero-based position in the analyzed dataframe after row filters, before sampling. Without filters, it is the position in the input dataframe. It is never the position within the randomized sample. The outlier count and percentage describe the analyzed sample when sampling is used.

if profile.outliers:
    print(f"Total Outliers: {profile.outliers.total_outliers}")
    print(f"Outlier Percentage: {profile.outliers.outlier_percentage}%")

    # Inspect the top most anomalous rows
    for outlier in profile.outliers.top_outliers[:5]:
        print(f"Row Index: {outlier.index}, Score: {outlier.score}")

        # See why it was flagged (feature contribution)
        if outlier.explanation:
            print("  Reason:", outlier.explanation)

docs.title: 2. Multivariate Analysis (PCA)
docs.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) projects high-dimensional data into 2D or 3D space to visualize clusters and structure.

if profile.pca_data:
    # Access the projected points (x, y, z)
    for point in profile.pca_data[:5]:
        print(f"x: {point.x}, y: {point.y}, Label: {point.label}")

docs.title: 3. Causal Discovery
docs.text:
Skyulf integrates causal-learn to run PC with Fisher-Z tests on eligible numeric measurements. PC can leave relationships unoriented, so the result is a partially directed graph. It is an observational estimate for exploring hypotheses, not proof that one variable causes another.

Categorical and Boolean variables are omitted from this method. A categorical target such as species remains available in Target Analysis; it is not given an arbitrary ordering to place it in the causal graph. Fisher-Z's linear-Gaussian assumptions still matter for the numeric variables you analyze.

The graph uses at least 50 and up to the first 5,000 complete rows across its selected columns. It includes all eligible variables up to a maximum of 15. Above that limit, an eligible selected numeric target is retained along with up to 14 features ranked by absolute Pearson correlation with it. Without an eligible numeric target, the 15 highest-variance numeric variables are selected. A feature named target or label does not override your choice.

New reports record profile.causal_graph.selection_method as "all", "target_correlation" or "variance". If the selected target cannot enter numeric analysis, profile.causal_target_exclusion_reason is "categorical", "excluded" or "unsupported"; this explanation is available even when the graph itself is None. Both fields are optional when reading older reports.

if profile.causal_graph:
    print(f"Graph has {len(profile.causal_graph.nodes)} nodes and {len(profile.causal_graph.edges)} edges.")

    for edge in profile.causal_graph.edges:
        # Types: "directed" (->), "undirected" (--), "bidirected" (<->)
        print(f"{edge.source} {edge.type} {edge.target}")

Directed edges preserve the orientation returned by PC. The web graph keeps distinct column names such as petal width and petal_width separate and shows both arrowheads for a bidirected edge. Loading a report with an empty graph clears the previous graph.

Reload the app for rendering corrections. Run Analyze again to regenerate saved causal graphs, target statistics, rules and outlier row indices: existing stored reports retain the results produced by their original analysis.

docs.title: 4. Geospatial Analysis
docs.text:
Automatically detects Latitude/Longitude columns and computes bounding boxes and centroids.

if profile.geospatial:
    print(f"Bounds: {profile.geospatial.min_lat}, {profile.geospatial.min_lon} to {profile.geospatial.max_lat}, {profile.geospatial.max_lon}")
    print(f"Centroid: {profile.geospatial.centroid_lat}, {profile.geospatial.centroid_lon}")

docs.title: 5. Time Series Analysis
docs.text:
Detects datetime columns and analyzes trends and seasonality. It automatically adjusts the resampling interval (e.g., 1s, 1h, 1d) based on the data duration to provide meaningful trend lines.

if profile.timeseries:
    print(f"Time Column: {profile.timeseries.date_col}")

    # Access trend data
    for point in profile.timeseries.trend[:5]:
        print(f"Date: {point.date}, Value: {point.values}")

docs.title: 6. Smart Date Detection
docs.text:
Skyulf uses a robust "Tournament Strategy" to correctly identify date formats in ambiguous columns (e.g., distinguishing between MM/DD/YYYY and DD/MM/YYYY).

How it works: 1. Heuristic Check: First, it checks column names for keywords like date, time, created_at to avoid expensive parsing on non-date columns. 2. Candidate Testing: It attempts to parse a sample of the data using multiple formats: * ISO Standard (YYYY-MM-DD) * Common US Format (MM/DD/YYYY) * Common EU Format (DD/MM/YYYY) 3. Entropy Selection: For ambiguous cases (e.g., 01/02/2023 could be Jan 2nd or Feb 1st), it calculates the Month Entropy (number of unique months) for each candidate format. * It selects the format that yields the highest number of unique months, assuming that real-world data typically spans more than just January.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: We provide complete, runnable scripts in the docs/examples/scripts/ directory. These examples demonstrate how to use Skyulf as a library with rich terminal output and visualizations.

docs.title: Prerequisites for Examples
docs.text:
To run these examples, you'll need a few extra libraries for visualization and pretty printing: 

pip install matplotlib rich scikit-learn

docs.title: 1. Time Series Analysis
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/eda_timeseries.py

This example generates synthetic sales data with a trend and weekly seasonality. It demonstrates: - Automatic date column detection. - Extracting and plotting the Trend component. - Identifying seasonality patterns (e.g., day of week).

Output: - A terminal table showing trend values. - A plot window showing the trend.

docs.title: 2. Geospatial Analysis
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/eda_geospatial.py

This example simulates store locations around New York City. It demonstrates: - Automatic detection of Latitude/Longitude columns. - Computing the Centroid and Bounding Box. - Visualizing the store locations and centroid on a map.

Output: - A terminal summary of spatial stats. - A scatter plot window.

docs.title: 3. Comprehensive Workflow (Iris Dataset)
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/eda_comprehensive.py

A full-featured example using the classic Iris dataset. It covers the entire Skyulf EDA pipeline: - Data Quality: Missing values and duplicates. - Numeric Stats: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Normality Tests (Shapiro-Wilk/D'Agostino). - Outlier Detection: Finding anomalies with Isolation Forest. - Distributions: Histograms for numeric features. - Correlations: Heatmap of feature relationships. - Target Analysis: Boxplots showing feature distribution by target class. - Scatter Matrix: Pairwise scatter plots of features. - PCA: Projecting data into 2D space for visualization. - Causal Discovery: Inferring causal relationships between variables. - Smart Alerts: Automatic warnings about data issues.

Output: - A detailed "Dashboard" in the terminal. - Plot windows for Distributions, Correlations, Target Analysis, Scatter Matrix, and PCA.

docs.title: 4. Automated Analysis (The Easy Way)
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/eda_automated.py

This example demonstrates the simplified workflow using the EDAVisualizer class. Instead of writing manual plotting code, you can generate a full report in just 3 lines.

Output: - A rich terminal dashboard. - All standard plots (Distributions, Correlations, PCA, etc.).

docs.title: 5. Time Series & Geospatial (Manual Config)
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/eda_timeseries_geo.py

This example shows how to handle cases where auto-detection might fail or when you want to be explicit. It demonstrates: - Manually specifying date_col, lat_col, and lon_col in the analyze() method. - Visualizing both Time Series trends and Geospatial maps in the same report.

Output: - A terminal summary including Time Series and Geospatial sections. - Plots for Time Series Trend and Geospatial Distribution.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: The profiler is built on Polars, making it significantly faster than Pandas-based alternatives like pandas-profiling or ydata-profiling, especially for datasets with millions of rows.

docs.title: Data Drift & Monitoring
docs.text: Skyulf includes Data Drift Detection module to monitor how your data changes over time, ensuring model reliability in production.

docs.title: Concept
docs.text: Data Drift occurs when the statistical properties of the input data (production) change compared to the data used to train the model (reference). This can lead to model degradation.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Skyulf calculates drift using four key statistical metrics for every numerical column:

  1. Wasserstein Distance (Earth Mover's Distance): Measures the "work" needed to transform one distribution into the other. Good for detecting shifts in shape and location. The reported value is the distance divided by the reference column's standard deviation, so one threshold means the same thing whatever unit the column is in; the untransformed distance is kept in raw_value.
  2. KS Test (Kolmogorov-Smirnov): A non-parametric test that compares cumulative distribution functions. The drift decision is made on the statistic (the maximum distance between the two CDFs, 0–1); the p-value is reported alongside it as ks_test_p_value for diagnostics but never decides drift, because it shrinks with sample size.
  3. PSI (Population Stability Index): A widely used industry standard for measuring population shifts.
    • PSI < 0.1: No significant drift.
    • 0.1 <= PSI < 0.25: Moderate drift.
    • PSI >= 0.25: Significant drift (Action required).
  4. KL Divergence (Kullback-Leibler): Measures how one probability distribution diverges from a second, expected probability distribution.

docs.title: Schema Drift
docs.text:
The system also monitors for structural changes: * Missing Columns: Critical alerts for features present in training but missing in production. * New Columns: Alerts for unexpected features appearing in production data.

Both count toward report.drifted_columns_count, so that figure covers distribution drift and schema drift. A missing column has no values left to compare and therefore never appears in column_drifts — the count is the only place it is reported.

docs.title: Using the Data Drift UI
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the Data Drift page in the ML Canvas.
  2. Step 1: Select a Reference Job (Training Job) from the list. This loads the statistical profile of the data used during training.
  3. Step 2: Upload your Current Data (Production Data) as a CSV or Parquet file.
  4. Analyze: Click "Run Analysis".
  5. Review Report:
    • Check the Drift Score and Schema Alerts at the top.
    • Expand any column row to see detailed metrics and Interactive Histograms comparing the two distributions side-by-side.

docs.title: Using the Library (Python API)
docs.text:
Script: docs/examples/scripts/data_drift_check.py

You can also use the drift detection engine programmatically within your own scripts or pipelines using skyulf-core.

import polars as pl
from skyulf import DriftCalculator

# 1. Load Data (Reference vs Current)
# Reference: The data your model was trained on
# Current: The new data from production
ref_df = pl.read_csv("training_data.csv")
curr_df = pl.read_csv("production_data.csv")

# 2. Initialize Calculator
calculator = DriftCalculator(ref_df, curr_df)

# 3. Calculate Drift
# You can optionally override default thresholds
report = calculator.calculate_drift(thresholds={"psi": 0.2, "wasserstein": 0.1})

# 4. Inspect Results
print(f"Drifted Columns: {report.drifted_columns_count}")

# Check for Schema Drift
if report.missing_columns:
    print(f"⚠️ Missing Columns: {report.missing_columns}")
if report.new_columns:
    print(f"ℹ️ New Columns: {report.new_columns}")

# Check for Statistical Drift
for col_name, drift_info in report.column_drifts.items():
    if drift_info.drift_detected:
        print(f"\n🚨 Drift detected in '{col_name}':")
        for metric in drift_info.metrics:
            status = "FAIL" if metric.has_drift else "PASS"
            print(f"  - {metric.metric}: {metric.value:.4f} [{status}]")

        if drift_info.suggestions:
            print(f"  💡 Suggestion: {drift_info.suggestions[0]}")

docs.title: Extending Skyulf-Core
docs.text: Skyulf-core uses a Calculator / Applier architecture: calculators learn parameters during fit, appliers apply them during transform. New nodes are registered via the @node_meta decorator and NodeRegistry.

docs.title: Add a new preprocessing node
docs.text:
1. Create a new module in skyulf/preprocessing/.
  2. Implement a Calculator (extends BaseCalculator) and an Applier (extends BaseApplier).
  3. Decorate the Calculator with @NodeRegistry.register() and @node_meta().

docs.title: Step-by-step example
docs.text:
from typing import Any, Dict, Tuple, Union

import pandas as pd

from skyulf import NodeRegistry
from skyulf.preprocessing.base import BaseApplier, BaseCalculator
from skyulf.core.meta.decorators import node_meta
from skyulf.utils import pack_pipeline_output, unpack_pipeline_input


class MyNodeApplier(BaseApplier):
    """Applies the learned transformation."""

    def apply(
        self,
        df: Union[pd.DataFrame, Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]],
        params: Dict[str, Any],
    ) -> Union[pd.DataFrame, Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]]:
        X, y, is_tuple = unpack_pipeline_input(df)
        columns = params.get("columns", [])
        # Apply your transformation to X using the fitted params...
        return pack_pipeline_output(X, y, is_tuple)


@NodeRegistry.register("MyNode", MyNodeApplier)
@node_meta(
    id="MyNode",
    name="My Custom Node",
    category="Preprocessing",
    description="A short description of what this node does.",
    params={"columns": "list[str] — columns to transform"},
)
class MyNodeCalculator(BaseCalculator):
    """Learns parameters from training data."""

    def fit(
        self,
        df: Union[pd.DataFrame, Tuple[pd.DataFrame, pd.Series]],
        config: Dict[str, Any],
    ) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        X, _, _ = unpack_pipeline_input(df)
        columns = config.get("columns", [])
        # Learn something from X...
        return {"type": "MyNode", "columns": columns}

docs.title: What happens under the hood
docs.text:
• @NodeRegistry.register("MyNode", MyNodeApplier) registers the Calculator and Applier classes so that FeatureEngineer can resolve "transformer": "MyNode" in a pipeline config.
  • @node_meta(...) attaches a NodeMetadata dataclass to the class, used for auto-documentation and the frontend node palette.

docs.title: Real-world reference
docs.text: See skyulf/preprocessing/encoding/one_hot.py for the OneHotEncoder implementation — it follows this exact pattern.

docs.title: Add a new modeling estimator
docs.text:
1. Implement a new Calculator (extends BaseModelCalculator) and Applier (extends BaseModelApplier), or subclass SklearnCalculator / SklearnApplier.
  2. Register with @NodeRegistry.register("my_model_key", MyModelApplier).

The model key can then be used as "type": "my_model_key" in the modeling config.

docs.title: Advanced: duck-typed steps without subclassing
docs.text:
Registering a node with @NodeRegistry.register(...) (so it's usable from a JSON pipeline config / the frontend palette) still requires subclassing BaseCalculator/BaseApplier as shown above — the registry and @node_meta decorator are built around those ABCs.

If you're calling StatefulTransformer directly in Python (not going through the registry — e.g. scripting an ad-hoc pipeline step, or wrapping a third-party object), you don't need to subclass anything. skyulf.core.protocols defines CalculatorProtocol/ApplierProtocol as structural (typing.Protocol) types — any object with matching fit/apply methods satisfies them:

from skyulf.preprocessing.base import StatefulTransformer


class MeanCenterer:
    """Plain class — no BaseCalculator/BaseApplier inheritance."""

    def fit(self, df, config):
        return {"mean": df["x"].mean()}

    def apply(self, df, params):
        out = df.copy()
        out["x"] = out["x"] - params["mean"]
        return out


centerer = MeanCenterer()
step = StatefulTransformer(calculator=centerer, applier=centerer, node_id="center_x")

This is useful for quick experiments or wrapping existing objects (e.g. an sklearn-like class that already has compatible methods) without writing an ABC subclass just to satisfy a type check.

docs.title: Testing guidance
docs.text:
Write integration tests that run the full cycle:

calc = MyNodeCalculator()
artifact = calc.fit(sample_df, {"columns": ["col_a"]})

applier = MyNodeApplier()
result = applier.apply(sample_df, artifact)

assert "col_a" in result.columns  # or whatever your node guarantees

Prefer real DataFrames over mocks — see tests/ for examples.

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning
docs.text: Skyulf wraps scikit-learn's search utilities and Optuna into a single hyperparameter_tuner model type. You configure tuning entirely through the pipeline config — no code changes required.

docs.title: Supported strategies
docs.text: Strategy Key What it does Grid Search grid Exhaustive search over every combination in the search space Random Search random Samples n_trials random combinations Optuna (Bayesian) optuna Uses TPE (Tree-structured Parzen Estimators) to intelligently explore the space Halving Grid halving_grid Successive halving — trains on small subsets first, promotes the best Halving Random halving_random Random sampling + successive halving

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
config = {
    "preprocessing": [
        {"name": "split", "transformer": "TrainTestSplitter",
         "params": {"test_size": 0.25, "random_state": 42,
                    "stratify": True, "target_column": "target"}},
        {"name": "impute", "transformer": "SimpleImputer",
         "params": {"columns": ["age"], "strategy": "mean"}},
    ],
    "modeling": {
        "type": "hyperparameter_tuner",
        "base_model": {"type": "random_forest_classifier"},
        "strategy": "optuna",
        "search_space": {
            "n_estimators": [50, 100, 200],
            "max_depth": [5, 10, 20, "none"],
        },
        "n_trials": 25,
        "metric": "accuracy",
        "strategy_params": {
            "sampler": "tpe",
            "pruner": "none",  # Random Forest does not support incremental fitting.
        },
    },
}

Note: "none" (string) in the search space is automatically converted to Python None.

For Logistic Regression searches restricted to penalty=["elasticnet"], an omitted or null L1 ratio uses 0.5 in every candidate and the final model. Explicit numeric ratios are retained, and the resolved value appears in the best parameters. Search Elastic Net separately when combining it with other penalties would leave this conditional ratio unspecified.

Named binary f1, precision, recall, and pr_auc metrics score the sorted-last training class, matching evaluation and decision-threshold tuning's classes_[1] probability column. For example, labels {1, 2} use class 2, {0, 1} use class 1, and {"no", "yes"} use "yes". Explicit scorer callables and explicit positive-label choices in threshold metrics retain the caller's choice. Multiclass metrics keep their existing weighted behavior.

When fold preprocessing filters validation rows, every tuning strategy scores the retained features and their matching targets. For example, if an IQR filter keeps 110 of 120 validation rows, the scorer compares 110 predictions with those 110 target values. This score describes the retained population. Preprocessing is learned only from the training fold and is applied once per score, including when a custom scorer requests several prediction methods. Target encoding keeps classification labels and probability columns in the scorer's original space.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text:
Missing feature values are admitted using the installed estimator's capabilities, including supported Random Forest, Extra Trees and Decision Tree configurations. Search overrides that can replace an incompatible fixed default are considered before rejecting the input. Each candidate's actual fit still enforces its restrictions, such as unsupported criteria or monotonic constraints. Models that cannot handle missing values require imputation; fold preprocessing can supply that imputation using only training rows. Missing targets and numeric infinity remain errors.

These keys go inside the "modeling" block when "type" is "hyperparameter_tuner":
